Sports.title: Bentley holds on for close decision win after fast start vs Mosley Jr
Sports.content:
Denzel Bentley knocked Shane Mosley Jr down heavily early, before being made to eke out a unanimous decision win at the Copper Box Arena.

Bentley, who'd seen the WBO strip him of their middleweight championship in the build up to this fight, looked to take out his frustration on a world-rated opponent.

For a moment, in the early going, it looked like Bentley was going to make swift, brutal work of his opponent, the son of Hall of Famer Shane Mosley.

Mosley would have been happy with the opening round. He took the centre of the ring and used his long left to marshal Bentley. Pressed into a corner and backed up, Bentley threw potshots.

But in the second round Bentley hit with electric intent. A solid right cross shook Mosley up badly and the following cross to the chin sent the American down into the canvas.

Image: Denzel Bentley is a former WBO world champion

Mosley managed to rise and Bentley set about him. But he couldn't land quite cleanly enough to put Mosley down or out and the American got through the round.

By the fifth round Mosley had regrouped as he worked on the front foot. His right pinged Bentley and he attacked the Londoner on the ropes.

Bentley was too static as dynamism drained from his work. It invited the American to come forward and work. Mosley finished the seventh round letting his hands go as Bentley spun away.

The Londoner fired off bursts of punches and a cut by Mosley's right eye did worsen. Single shots in the closing stages clipped Mosley, but Bentley didn't shake him up as he had earlier on.

It left Bentley with a nervy wait for the scorecards but he came through on a unanimous but close decision, 96-94, 96-93 and 95-94.

American heavyweight hope Da'Mazion Vanhouter was too powerful and had too much sheer speed for Ivan Balaz.

Balaz began jabbing, but his left was sluggish and Vanhouter smiled. He powered punches into the Czech's long body and then, with an audible crack, a left hook to the ribs dropped Balaz to his knee with a wince.

Vanhouter celebrated but Balaz just beat the count - only for huge shots to scrape across and plunge him back to the canvas.

Bravely Balaz rose, but Vanhouter ripped his right hook into the body and put him down a third time to end the fight. That was the 10th first-round knockout in the 21-year-old's 14-bout pro career.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Da'Mazion Vanhouter floors Ivan Balaz inside two minutes at Zuffa Boxing 12

Lucas Roehrig displayed fine finishing instincts to stop Connal McDonald in the seventh of eight scheduled rounds.

Roehrig's advantage in speed was clear in the opening round, when he lashed in a lead left hook flush.

He found openings for his rapid right cross but McDonald proved tough and could take his power early on.

The Scotsman pushed himself forward to apply pressure, chopping his left hook and jolting Roehrig with a right.

But the Londoner sucked in air and took his work up a gear in the sixth round, moving and jabbing well.

When he had McDonald hurt in the seventh he didn't let up, striking in shuddering head shots to hack McDonald off his feet and end it.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player George Groves protégé Lucas Roehrig landed a stunning KO on his Zuffa debut

Sam Hickey patiently fielded the attacks of Amaury Massenaux, blocking the Belgian's hooks with tight elbows. He tested out his uppercut and would use that shot as a weapon to hurt Massenaux.

Hickey had looked to counter, but upped the pressure on Massenaux in the fourth round. A one-two arrowed in and the Scotsman began to crank in powershots.

He applied more of the same in the fifth round. His right hook landed round the side of the head and a right uppercut-left hook combination fired home at close range.

Massenaux backpedalled and dropped to a knee. On resumption Hickey hunted him down and when the referee saw the Belgian hurt, he stepped in to end it.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Sam Hickey stopped Amaury Massenaux at Zuffa Boxing 12, but did the referee stop it too soon?

From the opening bell Kayla Allen waded into Julia Igel, clattering her onto the backfoot with unwavering aggression.

Igel covered up, blocked plenty of punches and threw back, but the assault from Allen kept on coming. Right hands from Allen poured in and she drove left hooks into the body.

Her pace only began to dwindle in the last round and Igel swung wildly as she briefly found herself on the front foot.

But she couldn't break through and Allen won 58-56 after six rounds.

Austrian southpaw Umar Dzambekov continued his unbeaten run with a tremendous one-punch finish to take out world-class contender Zach Parker.

The two were evenly matched, boxing with precision over the opening three rounds of their scheduled 10-rounder, Parker cleverly targeting Dzambekov's body with solid right hooks.

But in the fourth round, Dzambekov drilled him with a thudding left uppercut to the solar plexus. Parker folded over the punch, crumpled to the canvas and just could not beat the referee's count.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Masood Abdulah landed two huge knockdowns against Adan Palma in the opening bout of Zuffa Boxing 12

Masood Abdulah opened the show winning an excellent eight-rounder against American prospect Adan Palma.

A flashing left from Abdulah streaked across in the first round to drop the visitor on the seat of his shorts.

But Palma struck back in the fourth round. He popped Abdulah with a hard left hook and the Londoner's legs wobbled beneath him. Abdulah kept himself upright but he was hard-pressed.

In the fifth round Palma shook Abdulah up with a right but in the sixth round the home fighter managed to reassert control, dropping the American with another well-timed left hook.

Abdulah took a unanimous decision, 78-72, 77-73 and 76-74 on the cards.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Vinnie 'The King of Violence' Kemp made a big impression on his debut as he demolished Liam McElhinney and then demanded another fight from Dana White

Vinnie Kemp, nicknamed the "King of Violence," made an impression. He swaggered into the ring, was reprimanded for barracking Liam McElhinney and battered his opponent into the ropes with wide-armed punches, ending it inside the first round.

Sports.title: 'A different Noni?' Madueke finding a new level for Arsenal
Sports.content:
Noni Madueke lay sprawled on the turf, head in his hands, following his one-on-one miss late in Arsenal's 1-0 victory over Hull. His frustration continued to show even after the final whistle.

The winger's reaction showed the standards this "different Noni", to quote Mikel Arteta, is setting himself as he strives to reach another level. Bukayo Saka's injury was a significant setback to Arsenal. Madueke has made it his mission to soften the blow.

So far, he has filled in impressively. Arteta understood his demeanour after the game. "He knew he had three clear chances to score," he said, always demanding more. But there was also an acknowledgement of his crucial role in Martin Odegaard's goal.

Madueke's shot forced the Konstantinos Tzolakis save from which his captain scored. It was just one of many dangerous moments. His total of 13 touches in the opposition box was the most by an Arsenal in any Premier League game this season.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player FREE TO WATCH: Highlights from Arsenal’s match against Hull in the Premier League

Madueke also hit his highest totals in a game this term for shots and chances created, with a combined eight, and successful dribbles, with five. This was not a vintage attacking display from Arsenal but almost everything positive came through him.

The 24-year-old was one of only five Arsenal outfielders to start having also started in midweek in Prague, where he scored the opening goal. His importance to Arteta is growing. He has happily taken on the extra responsibility.

Madueke was left out of Thomas Tuchel's England squad in between the two games; a blow which might have knocked another player. But he was impressing for Arsenal even on the left before his return to the right after Saka's injury against Bayern Munich.

Arteta puts his progress down to his decision to train independently during the last international break after only starting two of Arsenal's first seven games of the season.

"The way he reacted to that I think is a great example for the rest of the squad, which is, 'I want to do more.' He went away, started to train and was a different Noni. He wasn't going to accept that situation, he meant business. Since then he has been incredible."

Madueke's determination to better himself is not new.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Jamie Redknapp explains why he sees Mikel Arteta's Arsenal retaining the title

He has worked on his game individually, mostly with specialist coach Saul Isaksson-Hurst, since his days as a young player at PSV Eindhoven. Isaksson-Hurst calls him as a "mentality monster".

But the benefits of his latest round of extra-curricular work are clear to see. Arteta still sees room for improvement. "There are still margins, there are moments that we can decide better, we can be more efficient and then the margin will be bigger," he added.

But it is striking how much Madueke's execution has improved. The former Chelsea winger has always been capable of causing chaos in opposition defences. But now he is far less erratic, offering clarity and composure in the final third instead.

It is illustrated by the sheer volume of chances he is creating.

Image: Noni Madueke is creating more chances than any other player

His average has more than doubled from last season, to 3.57 per 90 minutes, putting him top among all Premier League players - even above Manchester City's Rayan Cherki.

He ranks behind only Cherki's team-mates Phil Foden and Jeremy Doku, meanwhile, for expected assists, on 0.32 per 90 minutes, showing he is offering quality as well as quantity.

His threat is varied. He has shown his capacity to contribute from both flanks this season and there were other examples of variety inside the first few minutes against Hull; a teasing, diagonal cross with his left foot nearly converted by Gabriel, then a right-footed cut-back for Christos Tzolis after attacking the byline.

Later in the half, he could be seen crossing for Rice, who headed too close to Tzolakis. There was another cut-back to find Bruno Guimaraes, whose shot was blocked.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Mike Dean explains why Arsenal should have had a penalty for the foul on Kai Havertz which was overruled because of an offside

Decision-making has always been one of his friend and team-mate Saka's many standout qualities. Now Madueke is making the right choices with far greater frequency too. He has found a level of efficiency to balance his unpredictability.

The numbers bear it out. In the Premier League and Champions League, Madueke is losing possession far less frequently than last season. His dribble success rate has jumped from 50 per cent to 55 per cent. His pass success rate has gone 78 per cent to 87 per cent.

It is not because he is choosing easier passes. In fact he is directing a higher percentage of passes forward. There was an example 26 minutes in against Hull, when a superb, diagonal ball through the lines from deep in his own half allowed Declan Rice to counter.

Image: Noni Madueke has made significant improvements this season

He is completing a far higher percentage of those forward passes and there has also been a notable improvement in his crossing. His open-play cross completion rate has leapt from 14 per cent last term to 33 per cent. It all adds up to markedly better end product.

Madueke appears to have matured. He was making his 100th Premier League appearance against Hull, 67 of which have come with Arsenal. Some questioned his decision to become back-up to Saka but he has made a success of his move from Chelsea, providing more evidence of the mental strength apparent to his coaches.

In Arteta, he has a manager who will continue to push him - and encourage him to keep going the extra mile. "Now you are in that position, you need to hold it and improve it and he can still do that," he added. "So let's see what he does in this break."

Sports.title: There are very few reasons for Unai Emery to leave Aston Villa for Manchester United | Jonathan Wilson
Sports.content:
On Sunday afternoon, shortly before 4.30, Unai Emery will leave the tunnel at Old Trafford and walk along the touchline towards the bench. Will he glance around the grand old stadium – faded and leaking though it may be in parts – and think that he could have a part in restoring the club to former glories? Will he look at the home bench and imagine himself sitting there – or perhaps more plausibly, scuttling up and down in front of it – as the first Manchester United manager since Sir Alex Ferguson to land a league title?

Perhaps not. Emery is, after all, in “advanced talks” to extend a contract at Villa that already runs to 2029. However frustrating he may find the habitual summer churn, he is good at managing it. He feels the right fit for Villa, and that is arguably the most important factor in determining success. Yet all elite managers share a robust self-belief and there is a paradoxical sense that the worse the situation gets at United, the more appealing the job becomes.

Imagine being the manager who does sort it out. Imagine following in that brief lineage of United title winners: Ernest Mangnall, Matt Busby, Alex Ferguson … me? United remain the eighth wealthiest club by revenue in the world; imagine the resources that would be available if they were actually any good.

That is an allure that very few clubs in the world can match, no matter how good they were in the 1890s, and no matter how much the Villa owner, Nassef Sawiris, may dislike the fact. This is a point that cannot be made too strongly. Villa’s threat of legal action against Jamie Carragher was an outrageous attack on free speech. There is no way Carragher’s comment about the food chain of football could be construed as defamatory and, while it’s true he might have made the comment in less provocative terms, swearing is not a crime. This was a classic case of a legal threat being used to quell criticism and those fans – and, worse, journalists – who cheered it on should be thoroughly ashamed. The partisan blindness and persecution complex shared by fans of so many clubs is one of the most depressing features of the modern game.

But it’s also true United’s allure has come to look distinctly tarnished. No matter how bullet-proof a manager’s self-confidence, it would represent a remarkable risk to make the leap from Villa to United at this juncture. In almost every facet, from infrastructure to personnel, the modern Villa are better run than the modern United. And from Emery’s point of view, it’s not just that Villa are well run, it’s that they’re well run in his way.

He has the coaching staff he wants, while the president of football operations, Roberto Olabe, and the director of football operations, Damian Vidagany, are people he trusts and has worked with before. Emery would not have the degree of autonomy he has at Villa at many other clubs. United’s win over Roma on Tuesday may have eased the most immediate pressure on Michael Carrick, but nobody surely thinks that one good half against a depleted Serie A side cures all ills. (The question, obviously, is slightly absurd: nobody surely thinks Carrick is really the problem at United; it’s just that executives tend to get rid of managers because it’s what you do when there’s been a slump in form; it’s how a director acknowledges that he’s recognised there is a problem, while hoping desperately to deflect attention from his own shortcomings).

It doesn’t help that there is a clear precedent from five years ago, when a popular former United player saw his team come from two down to beat a Serie A side managed by Gian Piero Gasperini; Ole Gunnar Solskjær was sacked a month later.

View image in fullscreen Michael Carrick applauds the fans after Manchester United beat Roma in dramatic fashion. Photograph: MI News/NurPhoto/Shutterstock

The United crisis may have eased, but it is far from over. While Sir Jim Ratcliffe shows off architects’ plans and begs for public money to build a new stadium, Villa get on with building the new Trinity Road Stand. While United’s squad sags under the weight of its many contradictions, a weird mismatch of ill-fitting parts, Villa’s begins to take shape despite making 11 signings in the summer – even if the 3-0 defeat by Barcelona in midweek suggests there is still work to be done. They probably wouldn’t ideally have made such radical changes and would have preferred to keep Morgan Rogers and Ezri Konsa but, equally, there was an admirable sense of realism at Villa – a recognition of their place in the food chain, you might say – that when Chelsea or Arsenal come calling and offering huge contracts, there’s not much to be done other than to drive the price as high as possible.

Youri Tielemans is another player Villa might have liked to keep, but once United matched his release clause, the deal was done. Although Tielemans probably appreciates his new contract, it’s far from clear it’s been a good move for him from a football point of view, not least because United’s is a midfield that exposes his lack of mobility. Carlos Baleba was signed from Brighton to address that lack of dynamism in the United midfield but there were concerns about his tendency to drift in and out of games even before he suffered a hamstring injury on Tuesday.

It even feels as though Villa have been smarter about using United players than United have. Victor Lindelöf was brought in on a free transfer in summer 2025 and has excelled since and while Marcus Rashford and Jadon Sancho had less of an impact, Villa only signed them on loan. Rashford’s time, which featured four goals in 17 appearances in all competitions, was probably the more eye-catching, but Sancho made 39 appearances in his season at Villa.

In both cases, Villa got value out of a players whose futures were uncertain but without committing to having to take them on full-time.

It’s pretty hard to imagine at the moment, but at some point, United will start heading in the right direction. It may even be that Tuesday’s win prompts a surge of adrenaline that takes them into the top half of the table. For now, though, Villa look by far the brighter prospect, a club on the up, while United are in barely managed decline.

Sports.title: Enzo Maresca rues Manchester City’s lack of desire after defeat at Nottingham Forest
Sports.content:
Enzo Maresca blamed his side’s lack of desire and the way they were outgunned in duels for a third successive Premier League defeat. After winning their first seven games of the season, Manchester City’s 3-1 loss at Nottingham Forest extended their poor run.

Jair Cunha dispossessed Josko Gvardiol to score the opener, then Liam Delap struck twice with muscular surges on the break as Forest won their first home league game since April. “Today I think [the problem] has been general,” said Maresca. “It’s not about one player. In the first half we lost all the duels, all the contacts. Against this team, that is fighting relegation, if you don’t match them … it’s something we need to understand. In this kind of game, if you’re not able to win duels and second balls like in the first half, you struggle.

“You need desire and intensity to win second balls and duels. You require intensity or you struggle and we didn’t match their intensity. The second and third goals are copy and paste, lost duels first in the middle of pitch then at the edge of the box.”

City’s 100% record came to an end with a 2-1 defeat away by Aston Villa, and they followed that up last week with a 1-0 home reverse against Brighton. “They are all different,” said Maresca. “But if you look at chances, possession, chances inside box, in all of them we were much, much better but we lost all of them. We’re going to use this international break to clarify what we can do better. We know we need to improve things and avoid this kind of game.”

After his frustrated reaction to last week’s defeat at Brentford, Oliver Glasner was understandably delighted that his reset, ending what he had referred to as compromises, had paid off.

“The way we play football I think we’ve had many better games,” he said. “But how we defended, how passionately we defended, how tactically smart we defended, it was one of our better games.

“You should control everything and if you want to control it, you have to run because you have to be so quickly aware – they’re so good, such great players, such a good structure and they move the ball so quickly. Of course, you can just defend but you also need to go forward and this is what we did today in the right moments.”

Sports.title: Martin Ødegaard extends Arsenal lead at top with winner to break Hull resistance
Sports.content:
As most Arsenal supporters would testify, patience is a virtue. They needed plenty during the 22-year wait to be crowned Premier League champions and Mikel Arteta’s side certainly had to retain their composure as they tried to break down a dogged Hull side. They had not beaten Arsenal in 14 attempts since winning on their first visit to this ground in 2008. But with 20 minutes to play, there was still every chance that Sergej Jakirovic’s team could have pulled off one of the shocks of the season.

Arsenal had already been denied a penalty just before half-time for a shirt pull on Kai Havertz in the box a week after escaping the same crime against Liverpool at Anfield, in a moment of controversy that could have been the major talking point from this match. Martin Ødegaard had other ideas and the Arsenal captain’s fifth goal of the season was enough to ensure they will go into the international break with a healthy lead over Manchester City. Enzo Maresca’s side are up next here in the league after the international break, with Arsenal having matched their record tally of 27 points from their opening 10 games. The signs look ominous for the rest, even if they were made to work for the points throughout by their opponents.

“To the international break after winning is one of the best things for a coach,” said Arteta. “I need to praise the players and all the staff for the work that they are doing because it’s been very, very demanding. We have a very short time to recover from games but despite that the mentality and the quality of the team has shown: it’s incredible.”

Jakirovic had promised beforehand that his side would go on the front foot. “If you are passive, they will destroy you,” said the Bosnian. But while his bold 5-3-2 formation caused Arsenal’s much-vaunted defence some issues, Hull remain without a league victory since the end of August. “It’s a big experience for us,” was Jakirovic’s post-match assessment. “We can take some big lessons from this but we have shown we can compete at this level.”

View image in fullscreen Martin Ødegaard scores the decisive goal from close range. Photograph: Simon Dael/Shutterstock

Hull made the brighter start as John Egan headed wide from a corner. After losing to Brighton before the last international break, Arteta was taking no chances and reverted to the side that won at Liverpool last weekend. There was no William Saliba on the bench, with the France defender set to play for the under-21s on Sunday instead as he continues his comeback from a back injury.

Quick Guide How do I 

Yet aside from a set piece that resulted in Gabriel Magalhães just failing to connect with Ezri Konsa’s flick-on, the visitors’ low block frustrated Arsenal and they continued to cause problems on the break. Elliot Stroud forced David Raya into a save after Riccardo Calafiori surrendered possession cheaply.

Havertz’s failure to take a shot after being played in by a slide-rule pass from Ødegaard drew groans of frustration. A toiling Arsenal thought all their prayers had been answered just before half-time when the referee, Farai Hallam, was sent to the big screen by the VAR. Nobel Mendy was clearly pulling Havertz’s shirt inside the area yet the German was offside so the penalty was not awarded, even though it probably should have been according to the rules. They state that Havertz must be “attempting to play the ball, or challenging an opponent for the ball” to be penalised and because Mendy’s offence came first, that should have taken precedence, as it did when Newcastle’s Fabian Schär was awarded a penalty against Bournemouth in February 2024.

View image in fullscreen Kai Havertz is pulled back by Nobel Mendy but no penalty was awarded. Photograph: Simon Dael/Shutterstock

Pro Ref has yet to make a statement on the incident and Arteta admitted he had been left confused by the whole episode. “I don’t know what the interpretation is, I’m sure they will make that clear to understand,” he said.

The Arsenal manager’s annoyance levels continued to rise when Havertz could only head straight at Konstantinos Tzolakis on the stroke of half-time. Hull came out for the second half with a similar attitude and Jakirovic picked up a yellow card for protesting against another decision that went against his team. Declan Rice was withdrawn early, although Arteta insisted he was fine afterwards. Noni Madueke found space after a flowing Arsenal move but again his effort was straight down the throat of Tzolakis.

The feeling of desperation was growing. But Ødegaard has made a habit of coming to Arsenal’s rescue this season and the captain was quickest to react when Tzolakis spilled Madueke’s shot to finally break Hull’s brave resistance.

Sports.title: Okafor seals Leeds win but Tottenham complain to Pro Ref over Bogle tackle on Tel
Sports.content:
It is almost one year to the day when the Leeds manager, Daniel Farke, produced the tactical overhaul many observers believe saved his job. That day, Farke abandoned his trusted 4-3-3 when Leeds were 2-0 down at Manchester City and although they lost the game, the 3-5-2 he reverted to was the bedrock for the success that followed.

To suggest Farke was under similar pressure going into this game would be a stretch, but without a win in five Premier League games it was not unreasonable to suggest the Elland Road natives were getting slightly restless. Defeat going into the international break would have firmly extinguished what had been a positive start, with eight points from the first four.

So how fitting that with the stakes high once again, Farke’s tactical flexibility which he appears to have developed over the past 12 months laid the platform for a much-needed win for Leeds. His decision to go back to 3-5-2 heading into this meeting with Tottenham led to a largely stalemate opening 45 minutes, with the hosts cancelling out an in-form opponent.

But what happened at half-time was significant. Just like a year ago, Farke changed shape and breathed new life into his side. He switched first to a 4-2-3-1 and then into a 3-4-3, with a mountain of pressure ultimately producing the goal Leeds’ play deserved, as the substitute Noah Okafor’s late strike proved to be the difference.

It was a moment that clearly meant as much to Farke as it did the Elland Road faithful, the German punching the air in delight as his tactical tweaks paid off, with another substitute Harry Wilson the man to tee up Okafor for the winner. It was a successful afternoon for Leeds, who can look ahead with optimism once again after a tricky period.

“There’s no replacement for this winning feeling,” Farke said after. “All my credit goes to the boys for a terrific performance against an in-form Spurs side. It was important to be tactically spot on against their processes.”

Spurs may look back on this as a frustrating afternoon. They failed to create enough opportunities to trouble a well-organised Leeds side, but they will consider whether a crucial moment as half-time approached could have shifted the momentum firmly their way, with Jayden Bogle perhaps fortunate to avoid a red card.

View image in fullscreen Noah Okafor slots home the Leeds winner in the 79th minute. Photograph: Robbie Jay Barratt/AMA/Getty Images

Bogle caught Mathys Tel on the achilles, with replays showing a nasty contact that left the forward unable to continue. A lengthy video assistant referee stoppage led many to assume Bogle would follow Jean-Philippe Mateta in seeing red against the same opposition, but it was deemed the Leeds wing-back did not commit serious foul play. It later emerged Tottenham will submit a formal complaint to Pro Ref about the decision not to send off Bogle for the challenge.

In both halves Spurs’ attacking potency let them down and they never really truly tested James Trafford in the Leeds goal as their bid to win four successive Premier League games for the first time in three years came grinding to a halt.

“The second half we didn’t show the same spirit,” Roberto De Zerbi said. “We didn’t show the hunger we need for these types of big games. We have to analyse. Many games like this can be a problem for us.”

There were few clearcut opportunities in the first half, with the Bogle-Tel incident the undoubted talking point. But Farke reverted to a back four after the restart, and it led to a huge spell of Leeds pressure. Both Dominic Calvert-Lewin and Ao Tanaka had glorious opportunities, with Spurs struggling to contain Leeds’ new shape.

Quick Guide How do I 

The momentum remained with the hosts as the hour mark arrived, which prompted De Zerbi into a triple substitution to attempt to wrestle back control. The result was almost immediate as Conor Gallagher shot wide while at the other end Sean Longstaff was next to spurn a huge chance for the hosts.

It looked as though it would end goalless but Farke rolled the dice again. His next move was another change of shape with Wilson and Okafor introduced to support Calvert-Lewin. Within two minutes the two substitutes combined and Okafor rifled home past Kinsky to send Elland Road into uproar with a goal – and a result – their second-half performance undeniably merited. Leeds navigated any late drama with minimal fuss.

Sports.title: Muniz rescues late point for Fulham against Newcastle after Murphy stunner
Sports.content:
Questions over whether Álvaro Arbeloa and Matthias Jaissle have what it takes to succeed in the Premier League remain unanswered after these two young foreign managers watched their sides grind out a 1-1 draw at Craven Cottage.

Arbeloa’s Fulham lacked fizz, physicality and personality before rescuing a point thanks to a late equaliser from Rodrigo Muniz, while Newcastle displayed little of Jaissle’s high-octane philosophy and squandered the chance to move into the top half after failing to build on a vicious opening goal from Jacob Murphy.

A second consecutive away win in the league was on the cards when Murphy seized on an error from César Palacios and scored in the 80th minute. Jaissle has faced criticism over his tactics and training methods since replacing Eddie Howe just before the start of the season but the German was happy with elements of this Newcastle performance.

The 38-year-old saw “a complete commitment and togetherness in all phases of the game” and was entitled to argue the visitors had the better chances, an impressive feat given there was such little threat from Jaissle’s front two of William Osula and Yoane Wissa.

It remains a big problem for Newcastle, who are paying for their failure to fill the void left by Alexander Isak’s move to Liverpool last year. They witnessed another half-hearted display from Wissa before the £55m striker’s withdrawal in the 61st minute and were hindered by the bluntness of Osula, whose hopes of grabbing a rare goal were somewhat hindered by his failure to register a touch in Fulham’s area.

To make matters worse Osula was also partially responsible for the leveller. Newcastle needed the 23-year-old to hold the ball up but he was outmuscled near the halfway line, allowing Fulham to pounce. Palacios, who had given the ball away for Murphy’s goal, wriggled into the area and combined with another of Arbeloa’s substitutes by smuggling the ball across for Muniz to score his first league goal since August 2025.

Jaissle felt it was a “slapstick” concession. Arbeloa, who likes to play an expansive style of passing football, focused more on Muniz’s impact after the target man’s introduction in place of the smaller Gonzalo García. “Newcastle were marking us man to man,” Fulham’s Spanish head coach said. “They forced us to play long balls and Rodrigo is very strong in this situation. He got his chance. It is very important for us because I need a player like Rodrigo. He can score goals but create so many chances.”

It is encouraging that Arbeloa was willing to be flexible and more direct. However this was a poor game between two sides too close to the bottom three for comfort. Fulham also fretted over Josh King after the 19-year-old went off with a groin injury. The attacking midfielder is set for a scan and will hope not to have suffered any significant damage after earning his first England call-up on Friday.

Thomas Tuchel will be keen to have King available. Newcastle paid a lot of attention to the teenager, with Sean Steur and Nico González sitting deep in midfield, but they could not keep him quiet during the first half. King tested Lukas Hornicek with a volley from 20 yards and later missed a decent headed chance.

View image in fullscreen Jacob Murphy roars in delight after giving Newcastle the lead. Photograph: Peter Cziborra/Action Images/Reuters

Fulham were not at their best. Oscar Bobb and García went close after an error from Steur but Newcastle were comfortable. Jaissle, who made four changes after accusing his players of not following instructions during last Monday’s defeat by Everton, asked his side to play a patient game and was annoyed when they had a goal ruled out in the 33rd minute. Dan Burn did nothing wrong when he converted a cross from close range, but Wissa was penalised for a holding offence on Timothy Castagne off the ball.
