The inaugural edition of the CORFEPS journal is indeed a full, rich and exciting package that is sufficiently exciting to signal to the communities of service and practice that something new and challenging has arrived in the administrative space. This is because the editorial board went all out to create a splash especially with the range of topics covered, and even more specially with the array of contributors and their unique specialties. As is to be expected, CORFEPS pulled strongly from within its own ranks for reflections that combine past administrative experiences with current observations from behind the scenes. The majority of the contributors are retired permanent secretaries who have served in one capacity or the other, and who have faced one crucial challenge or the other with wide ranging levels of successes.

In this regard, the CORFEPS journal, in its inaugural edition, is drawing on the immense institutional memories and professional knowledge of its members to ventilate both diagnostic, recuperative and reformative insights. And this is salutary in ways that serve to complement the mediatory role CORFEPS has been playing as a staunch and energetic stakeholder in the civil service reform project in Nigeria. We now have an opportunity to listen and take note, outside of the usual high-power meetings, of the single-minded understanding of the civil service system from those who have manned its various aspects, especially the ministries, departments and agencies. Their reflections and analyses are complemented by others, critical watchers of the civil service, whose many years of dealing with the system make them significant participants in the ongoing efforts to transform it into a value-based, public-spirited, meritocratic and high-performing world class institution.

Topics

In terms of the range of topics and themes discussed in the inaugural edition, the CORFEPS journal becomes an automatic administrative keepsake. The inaugural edition is divided into eight parts. Each of the segments, with the exception of the last two, speaks intentionally to the most dominant issues involved in assessing and transforming Nigeria’s democratic governance experiment. This is indeed a well-thought out scholarly first step by the editorial board. Part one, titled “The Nigerian Civil Service,” has four essays; part two with seven essays is concerned with governance tools; part three has just one essay dealing with Nigeria’s infrastructural development; part four has two essays surrounding leadership and management; the two essays in part five are wrapped around the theme of health and lifestyle; part six is dedicated to three book reviews; part seven signals recent appointments and tributes to distinguished former public servants; and part eight speaks to the activities of CORFEPS itself. In all, these thematic segments are all-encompassing.

They are meant to lay on the table the diagnoses, prognoses and resolution frameworks for understanding the totality of Nigeria’s administrative and governance challenges and the ways forward to transcending them.

Without daring any in-depth review of each essay—which goes beyond the space of this piece—I will touch on some of the significant contributions. And of course, we start with the civil service system. This is key, even to the current advocacy responsibilities of CORFEPS itself. And the four essays in this segment did not disappoint.

Their different focuses are without doubt current and contemporary—the status of the public administrator within the civil service and governance framework; the relationship between the civil service and the task of nation building; the significance of the MDAs in the achievement of state capacity; and the relationship between administrative leadership and performance management system. These are issues that are critical in reflecting on the challenges the civil service system is facing—how can we instigate the emergence of a public manager with twenty-first competences and literacies who can supervise a civil service system that is flexible, agile, technology-based and result-oriented through performance management that transforms Nigeria’s productivity?

In the second segment of the journal, containing the most essays, the contributors engaged with governance matters that richly scope the depth of the key issues.

I am particularly thrilled by the essays that investigate (a) public financial management and development financing, (b) the intervention of the executive in the institutional autonomy of public institutions, (c) decentralization and local governance, (d) capacity development to achieve service delivery and (e) the significance of corporate governance in the public sector. These issues connect with the earlier one on the administrative system. Budgeting and the financial management discipline that must attend it are critical for servicing development planning. And this goes beyond merely increasing budget size to the fundamentals of ensuring transparency and accountability in financing and execution that speaks to sustainable outcomes.

I am also fascinated, as my many public interventions have demonstrated, with the place of local governance in Nigeria’s democratic governance. This also ties with the concern with the health of fiscal federalism in the Nigerian federation. Indeed, the author of the essay argues that constitutional autonomy to back the essence of local governance will be grossly less than optimal.

Rather, what is needed is what he calls the “Nigeria Local Governance Reform Framework (2026-2035)” meant to reposition the local governments as key drivers of grassroots development. This is right on point. Similarly, the authors of the essay on training and capacity development attempt to recuperate training programmes “as genuine capacity-building instrument, anchored on competency-based needs assessment, transparent procurement, post-training accountability and the professionalization of Nigeria’s training institutions.”

The third and fourth segments of the journal are tied together by the relationship between leadership and sustainable development. Sound leadership is the difference between successful and failed infrastructure projects. This then directs critical reform attention to the issue of leadership training and selection, the focus of the first essay in part four. Part five would seem to be off the path of a direct focus on administrative and governance subject matters in its focus on health and lifestyle. But that is not the case. Most reform blueprints, unlike the practice during the golden era of the public service in the 1970s, fail to factor in work-life balance in human capital development. This is crucial in the sense that when the public servant is healthy, it goes a long way in affecting performance and productivity. Thus, the two chapters on breast cancer and prostate health are key factor in institutional reform.

Reform

To recapitulate: the inaugural edition of the CORFEPS journal is really a mouthful! It is like a reader on institutional and governance reform that all MDAs and key parastatals must have in their libraries. More than this, the edition already raises the bar that the editorial board cannot afford to undermine, going forward. I have a series of recommendations in this regard. One, the journal must not attempt to be academic. It must rather be styled and intended as a journal for public administration and public service professionals. This then demands that the editorial board must give deep reflection, again, to the objective of the journal and its intended audience. The fundamental question in this sense would be: What does the CORFEPS journal aim to become in the next five years within the Nigerian communities of service and practice? This question impacts the idea of style and content. For example, every edition could then be themed around some specific subject matter of administrative and institutional reform, governance challenge, democratic consolidation, leadership, financial management, civil service mentoring, etc.

Contributions can then be sourced from seasoned experts, public servants, administrators, while online search can also be made for syndicated columnists with innovative ideas and initiatives that speaks to the concerns of the journals. Indeed, special editions can be proposed on any theme for which the guest editor is renowned.

Departments of public administration, as well as the MDAs, could serve as key studies for reflection on the overall health of the civil service system and public administration in Nigeria. Websites of other professional bodies will serve as veritable source of publishable materials to introduce new ideas, tools, techniques, etc. Young mentees, volunteers and analysts could also be enlisted and commissioned to write features on some current affairs that are relevant to public administration. Interviews and autobiographical notes are critical elements for understanding the progress and reform of the public service. The editorial board must therefore also think of segmenting the journals to give room for special features, from interviews to critical reform highlights in some of the MDAs.

I will end this piece with a note of deep appreciation of those who thought the idea of the journal into existence. This is no mean feat in the total scheme of things concerning institutional reform in Nigerian civil service system. Kudos, first, to Alhaji M. Yayale Ahmed, the National Chairman of CORFEPS and the distinguished publisher of the journal. And then to Ambassador Dr Godknows Igali as the chair of the editorial board. I recognize every member of the editorial board and commend the efforts that went into birthing this inaugural edition. We have commenced a journey into a legacy of reform activities.

*Olaopa, a retired Federal Permanent Secretary, is the Chairman, Federal Civil Service Commission, Abuja

World.title: AMERICA IS NOT NIGERIA: Why Trump’s midterm defeat cannot predict Tinubu’s 2027 fortunes
World.content:
By Kayode Akinmade

The sweeping defeat suffered by President Donald Trump’s Republican Party in the November 3 American midterm elections has predictably provided fresh ammunition for Nigeria’s opposition politicians, who are already attempting to draw parallels between the political fortunes of the American president and those of President Bola Ahmed Tinubu ahead of Nigeria’s 2027 general elections. While the comparison may offer an attractive political talking point, it is, at best, superficial and, at worst, a deliberate attempt to transplant the political circumstances of one country into another.

There is no doubt that the Republican defeat represents a significant setback for Trump. Democrats secured control of both chambers of Congress, delivering a powerful electoral rebuke to the Republican administration and signalling widespread dissatisfaction with some of its policies. The result has opened a new chapter in American politics and raised questions about the direction of Trump’s presidency.

However, the critical question is whether the circumstances that produced this outcome in the United States are sufficiently comparable to Nigeria’s political and economic realities to justify the conclusion that Tinubu is destined for a similar electoral fate in 2027.

The answer is no.

America is not Nigeria. Trump is not Tinubu. And the political dynamics of the United States cannot be mechanically imported into Nigeria’s electoral calculations.

Indeed, one of the most important factors behind the Republican Party’s defeat was the controversial war involving the United States and Iran, a foreign policy decision that has generated enormous economic, diplomatic and security consequences for the Trump administration.

The conflict, which has lasted several months, has heightened concerns about American military involvement abroad, increased pressure on energy markets and contributed to rising fuel prices. For American households already grappling with the cost of living, the war became another source of economic anxiety. Its financial implications, military casualties and uncertain strategic objectives also generated questions about the wisdom of the administration’s foreign policy choices.

Iran conflict

Significantly, the political consequences were acknowledged by the highest levels of the American government. Trump admitted that the Iran conflict contributed to his party’s electoral difficulties, although he maintained that the military action was necessary.

His Vice President, JD Vance, was considerably more direct, declaring that “the reason we lost is the war.”

That admission is particularly instructive. It establishes that the Republican defeat was not simply an abstract expression of public dissatisfaction with a sitting president.

It was substantially connected to identifiable policy decisions and their consequences for American voters.

The question, therefore, is why Nigeria’s opposition should expect the political consequences of Trump’s decision to engage Iran to automatically translate into an electoral liability for Tinubu.

Nigeria did not initiate the conflict. Tinubu did not authorise American military operations against Iran.

He does not determine American foreign policy, the direction of Trump’s trade tariffs or the domestic political calculations of the Republican Party. To suggest that the electoral consequences of these decisions constitute a direct verdict on Nigeria’s president is to stretch political analogy beyond its reasonable limits.

Of course, the opposition is entitled to draw lessons from developments elsewhere. Political parties routinely study elections in other countries, particularly when they reveal the relationship between public expectations, government performance and electoral accountability. But learning from another country’s political experience is fundamentally different from assuming that its electoral outcome must be replicated elsewhere.

There is an even more important distinction that deserves attention: the American midterm elections are not presidential elections.

The midterms are held halfway through the president’s four-year tenure and determine the composition of Congress. They frequently become a referendum on the sitting president and his party, as voters use the opportunity to express satisfaction or dissatisfaction with the administration. Historically, the party controlling the White House has often faced considerable losses during midterm elections.

Nigeria’s 2027 general election, by contrast, will be a presidential contest in which voters will choose the individual and political party they believe are best equipped to govern the country for another four years. The candidates will have to present their records, programmes, leadership credentials and policy alternatives before the Nigerian electorate.

The difference is fundamental. A congressional election in the United States, influenced by a controversial foreign war, cannot automatically become a reliable predictor of a presidential election in Nigeria.

But beyond the political comparison, there is a more substantive issue that Nigeria’s opposition must confront: the country’s economic circumstances and the choices available to any government seeking to address them.

Structural weaknesses

Nigeria’s economic difficulties did not begin on May 29, 2023. The country entered the Tinubu administration with longstanding structural weaknesses, including an expensive petrol subsidy regime, multiple exchange-rate arrangements, weak revenue mobilisation, infrastructure deficits, excessive dependence on imports and a productive sector constrained by years of economic distortions.

These challenges accumulated over successive administrations and progressively reduced the government’s fiscal room for manoeuvre.

The new administration decided to confront some of these problems through the removal of petrol subsidy, foreign exchange reforms, fiscal restructuring and efforts to improve domestic revenue generation. These were not politically convenient decisions. Neither were they painless.

Millions of Nigerians have experienced considerable hardship since the introduction of the reforms. The rising cost of food, transportation, electricity and other essential services has placed enormous pressure on households and businesses. No credible assessment of the Tinubu administration can ignore this reality, and no amount of economic statistics should be deployed to dismiss the daily struggles of ordinary citizens.

However, the existence of hardship does not eliminate the need to examine the structural problems that necessitated reform in the first place.

What would have happened if the government had continued to finance an increasingly expensive subsidy regime without addressing the distortions it created? What would have been the consequences of maintaining multiple exchange rates and the associated opportunities for arbitrage? Could Nigeria have continued accumulating fiscal liabilities while expecting its economy to become more competitive and attractive to investors?

These are legitimate questions that the opposition must answer if it wishes to present a credible alternative.

The more important issue is not simply whether the reforms have imposed hardship. It is whether they are correcting the structural weaknesses of the economy, whether implementation is sufficiently effective and whether the government is doing enough to ensure that the benefits eventually reach ordinary Nigerians.

There are already indicators suggesting that the Nigerian economy is experiencing some improvement in its macroeconomic fundamentals. The Federal Ministry of Finance’s macroeconomic dashboard reported real GDP growth of 4.43 per cent in the second quarter of 2026, compared with 4.23 per cent in the corresponding period of 2025.

Headline inflation declined to 15.39 per cent in August 2026 from 23.14 per cent a year earlier. External reserves also rose to approximately $54.7 billion as of September 18, 2026.

Federation Account revenue increased from approximately N15.2 trillion in 2024 to N21.9 trillion in 2025, representing an increase of about 44 per cent.

These figures provide evidence of improved revenue mobilisation and strengthening external buffers. They are significant developments in an economy that previously struggled with severe revenue constraints and foreign exchange pressures.

Context

Nevertheless, these improvements must be understood within their proper context. A decline in inflation does not mean that prices have returned to previous levels. It means that the rate at which prices are increasing has slowed. Similarly, stronger foreign reserves and increased government revenues do not automatically translate into improved purchasing power for households.

The real challenge for the Tinubu administration is to convert these macroeconomic gains into tangible improvements in the lives of Nigerians. This requires more affordable food, improved electricity supply, lower production costs, better security, employment opportunities and stronger social protection for vulnerable citizens.

It is here that the government must concentrate its attention as the 2027 elections approach.

The administration’s performance must also be assessed beyond the immediate cost-of-living debate. Its infrastructure programme, investments in transportation, efforts to strengthen food production, reforms in the education sector and initiatives to improve the business environment are all relevant components of national development.

Projects such as the Lagos-Calabar Coastal Highway and the Sokoto-Badagry Superhighway reflect the administration’s ambition to expand strategic transport infrastructure and improve national connectivity. Their ultimate value, however, must be measured by delivery, quality, economic impact and the benefits they provide to communities and businesses.

Governance is multidimensional. A country’s economic performance cannot be reduced to the price of a bag of rice, just as the success of an administration cannot be established merely by announcing infrastructure projects. Both household welfare and long-term national development must form part of a balanced assessment.

This brings the discussion to the responsibility of the opposition.

Democracy requires a credible opposition capable of questioning government policies, exposing shortcomings and offering alternative solutions. The economic difficulties facing Nigerians provide legitimate grounds for robust political scrutiny. The opposition should therefore be encouraged to challenge the government and present its own vision for the country’s future.

But criticism alone is not a governing programme.

Beyond celebrating Trump’s electoral setback, Nigerians deserve to know what the opposition intends to do differently. Would it restore petrol subsidy, and how would it finance such an arrangement sustainably? Would it return to the multiple exchange-rate system? What practical measures would it introduce to reduce inflation, improve food security, strengthen the naira, attract investment and create employment?

How would it finance the infrastructure Nigeria urgently needs without returning the country to unsustainable borrowing and fiscal practices?

These are not unreasonable questions. They are the minimum requirements of a serious political alternative.

The opposition cannot expect to win the confidence of Nigerians simply by drawing attention to the electoral difficulties of a foreign president. Nor can the Republican Party’s defeat serve as a substitute for a Nigerian economic manifesto.

There is also a lesson for the ruling APC. The American experience demonstrates that political loyalty, electoral victories and presidential popularity cannot be taken for granted. Voters ultimately respond to their lived experiences, expectations and perceptions of government performance. The fact that an administration considers its policies necessary does not automatically mean that citizens will accept the consequences indefinitely.

Communicating achievements

Tinubu and the APC must therefore understand that the 2027 election cannot be won merely by explaining why the reforms were necessary. The government must demonstrate what those reforms are delivering. It must communicate its achievements more effectively, address areas of public dissatisfaction and ensure that economic recovery becomes visible in the everyday lives of Nigerians.

The administration must also resist the temptation to dismiss legitimate criticism as opposition propaganda. Nigerians who are struggling with food prices, transportation costs, insecurity and unemployment are not necessarily political opponents. They are citizens whose concerns deserve attention and practical responses.

Ultimately, the 2027 election will be a contest of records, ideas, leadership capacity and public confidence. Tinubu will have to defend his administration’s performance, while the opposition will have to demonstrate that it possesses a more credible and workable alternative.

The American midterm elections may offer useful lessons about the consequences of unpopular policies and the importance of public accountability. But they cannot determine the outcome of Nigeria’s presidential election. American voters have made their choice based on American circumstances. Nigerians will make theirs based on their own experiences and expectations.

The attempt to turn Trump’s defeat into a prediction of Tinubu’s political future may generate headlines and energise opposition conversations, but it does not settle the more important questions about Nigeria’s economic direction and political choices.

The burden of persuasion rests on both sides. The government must demonstrate results, and the opposition must demonstrate capacity.

In the final analysis, America will judge Trump, just as Nigeria will judge Tinubu. Neither president can borrow the electoral fortunes or misfortunes of the other.

America is not Nigeria. Trump is not Tinubu. And the road to Nigeria’s 2027 presidential election will be determined not in Washington, but by the choices of Nigerians.

World.title: Countdown to 2027: Edo North is for Oshiomhole
World.content:
Adams Oshiomhole

By Allison Abanum

Adams Oshiomhole’s first term has been defined by a deliberate strategy of translating legislative power into tangible federal presence for Edo North.

As Chairman of the Senate Committee on Interior, he has leveraged his position to facilitate federal employment for constituents and ensure fair representation in federal institutions.

His legislative record includes moving over 10 motions and sponsoring many bills.

These are not abstract motions; they are institutional investments that will outlast any single political cycle.

On the ground, Oshiomhole constituency interventions have reached all wards in Edo North, a coverage rate that speaks to both reach and intentionality. Oshiomhole has moved from delivering roads to delivering accountability, and Edo North have seen the difference in both bricks and budgets.

Beyond infrastructure, his engagement with youth leaders and traditional rulers signals a recognition that representation must be relational, not transactional, a point underscored by his refusal to charge constituents for assistance and his warning against extortion in his name.

The political consolidation around Oshiomhole 2027 bid reflects a broader strategic calculation within Edo North.

Endorsements have since crossed traditional lines: From the market women in Auchi to the Artisan in Iyahmo, down to all the student bodies and community leaders, it is clear that it is no longer a question of whether Edo North is standing for Oshiomhole; it is a question of how loudly Edo North will say so. To the people in the rural areas of Edo North, they have risen from service, unity, and discipline: delivery that touches households, reconciliation that silences internal friction, and grassroots organisation that turns intention into votes.

The good people of Edo North on their own are moving ward by ward to get support for Oshiomhole.

The plough is heavy; the hands must be steady because the furrow ahead is 2027.

The message is clear: no retreat, no sideways glance, no nostalgia for old battles in Edo North.

A senatorial district that has seen the light and future must now prove it can cultivate it, row by row, ward by ward, state by state, until the harvest of triumph is achieved.

Every leader, every member, every supporter keeps eyes on the furrow, not on the noise.

So, let the word go forth: APC is on the plough, and there is no looking back until Oshiomhole is sent back to the Senate in 2027.

The task is not to boast of yesterday but to labour for tomorrow with humility, focus, and determination.

The harvest belongs to those who keep ploughing.

For a senatorial district that has historically oscillated between alignment and agitation, the emerging consensus is that Oshiomhole federal network is an asset too valuable to surrender.

Abanum lives in Abuja.

World.title: A Ballot on a Burial Date? Northern Nigeria Confronts the Symbolism of January 16
World.content:
By Hassan A Karofi

The choice of dates in politics is often presented as a matter of administrative convenience. Yet history teaches us that dates carry powerful symbolism, especially in societies where collective memories of tragedy and triumph remain deeply rooted. As Nigeria prepares for a presidential election scheduled for January 16, 2026, it is important to reflect on what that date means to millions of people, particularly in Northern Nigeria, where January 16 is associated with one of the darkest episodes in the country’s history.

The significance of January 16 cannot be understood without revisiting the events of the country’s first military coup. In the early hours of January 15, 1966, a group of young military officers launched Nigeria’s first coup d’état. By the morning of January 16, the consequences of the coup were evident. Several of Nigeria’s most prominent political and military leaders had been assassinated.

Among those killed were Sir Ahmadu Bello, the Sardauna of Sokoto and Premier of Northern Nigeria; Sir Abubakar Tafawa Balewa, Nigeria’s first Prime Minister; Brigadier Samuel Ademulegun; Brigadier Zakariya Maimalari; and other senior political and military figures. While leaders from different regions were affected, the perception in the North was that the coup disproportionately targeted Northern political leadership. This perception would profoundly shape political attitudes and inter-ethnic relations for decades.

The events following the coup further deepened Northern grievances. Major General Johnson Aguiyi-Ironsi assumed power and suspended parts of the constitutional order. In many parts of Northern Nigeria, suspicion and anger grew rapidly, culminating in the counter-coup of July 1966. The resulting instability ultimately contributed to the chain of events that led to the Nigerian Civil War.

More than six decades later, the memory of January 1966 remains alive. For many Northern families, historians, traditional institutions, and political observers, January 16 is not merely another date on the calendar. It is a reminder of a traumatic turning point that altered Nigeria’s political trajectory and claimed the lives of leaders who continue to be revered across the region.

Against this backdrop, the decision to hold a presidential election on January 16 raises legitimate questions. Whether the date was chosen for logistical, constitutional, or electoral reasons, policymakers should recognize that symbolism matters in politics. Elections are national events meant to unite citizens around a shared democratic purpose. When an election coincides with a date associated with historical mourning for a significant section of the country, there is a risk that the symbolism overshadows the democratic exercise itself.

This concern is not necessarily about rejecting the election or questioning its legitimacy. Rather, it is about understanding how political decisions are perceived. In diverse societies such as Nigeria, sensitivity to historical memory is an important component of nation-building. Governments regularly avoid scheduling major celebrations on dates associated with national tragedies. The same principle can reasonably be applied to major political events.

There is also the risk of misinterpretation. In an era of social media, symbolism can quickly become politicized. Political actors may exploit the coincidence to revive old grievances, reinforce regional narratives, or deepen distrust among communities.

What may have been intended as a neutral administrative decision could inadvertently reopen historical wounds.

Supporters of the January 16 date may argue that Nigeria cannot permanently suspend public activities because of historical anniversaries. They may also point out that democracy requires adherence to electoral timelines regardless of symbolism. These arguments deserve consideration. However, they do not eliminate the responsibility to assess whether alternative dates could achieve the same constitutional objectives without generating unnecessary controversy.

A mature democracy is not only defined by the conduct of elections but also by sensitivity to the historical experiences of its citizens. The memory of the January 1966 coup remains a significant part of Northern Nigeria’s political consciousness. For many, the date symbolizes loss, betrayal, and the beginning of a national crisis from which the country took years to recover.

As Nigeria continues its democratic journey, leaders should remember that national unity is strengthened when historical sensitivities are acknowledged rather than dismissed. The question is therefore not whether an election can legally be held on January 16. The more important question is whether it is politically wise and symbolically appropriate to do so.

History may not dictate the future, but ignoring its lessons often comes at a cost. For many in Northern Nigeria, January 16 remains a day of remembrance. Policymakers would do well to reflect on whether a date synonymous with mourning is the right day for a defining national political contest.

*Karofi can be reached via [email protected]

World.title: 2027: Between Okowa and Ochei, a Trojan horse race?
World.content:
By Emmanuel l. Nwagboniwe

Let’s not equivocate here. The indices and optics in the political space amply suggest that the electoral race to represent Delta North in the Senate in 2027 is a direct contest between the former Delta State Governor, Dr. Ifeanyi Okowa of the All Progressives Congress (APC ), and ex -Speaker of the Delta State House of Assembly, Victor Ochei of the National Democratic Party (NDC).

Evidently, the projection of a contest likely to throw up soap- box rhetoric, anxieties, euphoria, and political high drama, horse trading, and possibly, mudslinging, is a no-brainer: Okowa and Ochei have bounced into the political ring with unequalled superlatives and robust social capital.

Commendably too, these former political allies’ ‘roll call of honour’ tells a convincing story of remarkably impressive private and public service careers- years put in and sacrificed largely in selfless and people-centred engagements.

For instance, a studied glance at Dr Ifeanyi Okowa’s resume speaks volumes: medical doctor; council chairman; Commissioner of Health; Secretary to the Delta State Government (SSG); Senator of the Federal Republic of Nigeria; two- term Governor of Delta State, ex -Vice Presidential candidate of the People’s Democratic Party (PDP) in the 2023 General Election.

Conversely, Victor Ochei is equally a no fresher in the public cum political space.

He is a graduate of Chemical Engineering; Founder/ Chairman of Day Notch Nigeria Limited, an engineering firm of global status; Member, Delta State House of Assembly representing Aniocha North Council; Deputy Minority Leader; Speaker, Delta State House of Assembly; Executive Director, Maritime Labour and Cabotage Services at the Nigerian Maritime Administration and Safety Agency (NlMASA); President, Nigerian Tennis Federation, among others.

Without gas lighting, these political highflyers’ ‘selling points’ make any of them eminently qualified to represent the Anioma nationality in the Red Chamber.

However, one knows that making a choice out of these two top contenders, especially by voters in a dynamic and highly unpredictable democratic space like ours where selfish and primordial sentiments hold sway, is certainly a herculean task, yet a candidate’s ‘report card’ remains an added advantage.

For Okowa, he is majorly regarded as a grassroots politician who walks his talk in terms of mass mobilisation, especially across the nine councils that make up the Delta North Senatorial District.

Evidently too, the former governor’s enduring stay in the political trenches for over three decades tells a reassuring story of one who understands the undercurrents and dynamics of power ‘capture’.

Moreover, Okowa has other political assets to take to the electioneering field; he has a vast and extensive experience in the executive and the legislative arms of government, and no matter how hard his traducers knock him, he being an ex -state executive, has a chunk of tangible and verifiable score cards to present to his Delta North constituents.

As the campaigns intensify, he will readily reel out the dividends of democracy he provided as a sitting governor to his Delta North voters.

Even his consultative town hall meetings have been turned into endorsements of sorts by traditional institutions -though an exercise dismissed by Ochei’s camp as a mere smokescreen in a democratic dispensation anchored on one man, one vote mantra.

Moreover, for a political strongman believed largely to be an ‘Establishment’ candidate, Okowa would be waging a double barreled war against his contenders, as he will leverage not only on the state government’s mobilisation drive, but most likely as well as from its near inelastic financial muscle.

Truth is: Okowa’s opponents must be ready to deepen their resource base to be able to match him in the battle royale for the exalted Abuja seat.

At this juncture, therefore, one is tempted to ask: Are Okowa’s intimidating credentials and robust service- delivery profile over the years enough pointers to cow any of his opponents to throw in the towel and make a cautious and timely retreat from the political battle field.

In other words, can Ochei, a major contender, continue to tackle a man who has withered various political storms, tempest and near deadly intrigues?

Well, feelers one gets from those who know Ochei closely say, he is not one who easily runs away from political battles, many others describe him as a human dynamo and an incurable optimist who dares where even angels thread softly.

Moreover, he is coming to the electioneering arena with a dose of youthful dynamism and vibrancy.

At 57, Ochei is believed to leverage on his mass appeal among the youths, as his message of generational shift in leadership resonates far and wide in the nine councils of Delta North.

He and his teeming supporters are already taking a swipe at Okowa for allegedly foisting a clandestine political dynasty for his family and cronies.

Still, Ochei who flaunts his impressive performance as a former lawmaker for Aniocha North echoes that his mission to the Senate is to replicate that same feat in the entire Delta North, insisting he has the capacity and political sagacity to attract federal presence to Anioma land more than any other candidate.

Ochei and his supporters are equally taking his redemptive message to town, affirming that he is on a rescue mission, to bridge what they call the ‘huge infrastructural decay’ in Delta North despite the zone’s role in the electoral victory of the now APC -led administration in the State.

In his resolute bid to actualise his vision at the Senate if elected, Ochei has rolled out a 10 -point Agenda encapsulated in an all- inclusive governance, better security, power, job opportunities, infrastructure, agriculture, productivity, among others.

Also, the former Speaker is latching onto the integrity and impeccable qualities of his party’s Presidential candidate, Mr. Peter Obi, to drive his message of redemption home.

Moreover, the NDC flag bearer is making much capital from what he regards as the ‘suffocating hardship’ in the country occasioned by the removal of fuel subsidy by the APC- led federal government ,to market his candidacy.

Well, as the January 16, 2027 polls draws nearer, the most pertinent questions on many lips are: Between Okowa and Ochei, who blinks first? Can Ochei, a candidate described by Okowa’s many supporters as a feather weight, pull a surprise, and possibly upstage the steely ex-governor in the electoral contest? Or will the enigmatic Okowa clinch the coveted Senate seat seamlessly?

Well, let’s not beat our chest in certainty as to which direction the political pendulum will swing towards, after all the projections and permutations here are mere conjectures buried in the womb of time.

•Nwagboniwe, a journalist, writes from Lagos.

World.title: FG plans National Sports Commission office in Kwara – Magaji
World.content:
Fourth from right is Coach Bola Magaji Chairman Kwara state Sports Commission,in glasses, also in glasses beside him is the author Comrade Biodun Abdulkarim, Special Adviser and Counsellor governor to the governor Alhaji Saad Salahudeen and other dignitaries at the unveiling of a book titled “The Sardauna Ilorin in the eyes of History.”in honour of Governor AbdulRahman AbdulRazaq in ilorin.

By Demola Akinyemi

ILORIN – The Federal Government has concluded plans to establish an office of the National Sports Commission (NSC) in Kwara State, following the development of sports facilities by the administration of Governor AbdulRahman AbdulRazaq.

The Executive Chairman of the Kwara State Sports Commission, Coach Bola Magaji, disclosed this in Ilorin, saying officials of the NSC had been impressed by the facilities provided by the state government.

Magaji spoke at the unveiling of a book titled The Sardauna of Ilorin in the Eyes of History, written in honour of AbdulRazaq, who holds the traditional title of Sardauna of Ilorin.

The book was authored by Abiodun Abdul Kareem, a senior journalist and editor of Herald on Sunday, the Sunday publication of the Kwara State Printing and Publishing Corporation.

Magaji recalled that officials of the National Sports Commission visited Kwara about three weeks ago to assess the sports facilities developed by the AbdulRazaq administration over the past seven years.

He said the officials expressed satisfaction with the facilities at the state stadium complex and indicated that the proposed NSC office would be established in the state.

According to him, the development reflects the growing recognition of Kwara’s investment in sports infrastructure.

Magaji said the state’s stadium complex could boast of some of the best squash court facilities in the world, adding that Kwara contingents to national and international sporting competitions had recorded improved medal-winning performances.

He attributed the development to investments in sports infrastructure and efforts to promote sporting activities in the state.

Also speaking, the Special Adviser and Counsellor to the Governor, Alhaji Saad Salahudeen, said AbdulRazaq’s contributions to governance, politics, youth development and national development would continue to attract attention in the years ahead.

He said the governor’s footprints in public service would remain relevant and be referenced in the next 50 years.

Earlier, the Chairman of the Organising Committee, Mallam Umar Abdulwahab, said the event was designed to provide a platform for discussions on leadership, public service, governance and historical preservation.

He said the initiative was also aimed at documenting experiences and inspiring future generations.

The event was attended by several dignitaries, including the Emir of Ilorin, Alhaji Ibrahim Sulu-Gambari, who was represented by Magaji Ogundele; Alhaji Saad Kajola; Alhaji Yusuf Abdullahi; the Secretary to the State Government, Professor Mamman Jibril; Senior Adviser on Islamic Religion, Alhaji Ibrahim Danmegoro; and Senior Adviser on Political Communication, Alhaji Bashir Adigun, among others.

World.title: A DECADE OF ROYAL SPLENDOUR: Oba Ewuare II’s 10th coronation anniversary
World.content:
By Moses Stowe

There are moments in the history of a people when the past and the present meet in a compelling celebration of identity, pride and continuity. For the people of the ancient Benin Kingdom, the 10th Coronation Anniversary of His Royal Majesty, Omo N’Oba N’Edo Uku Akpolokpolo, Ewuare II, CFR, the Oba of Benin, represents one such moment.

A decade after ascending the revered throne, the monarch’s anniversary provides an opportunity to celebrate the enduring institution of the Benin monarchy, reflect on its contributions to cultural preservation and reaffirm the values that have sustained the kingdom across generations.

More than a ceremonial commemoration, the anniversary brings together culture, history, sports, intellectual discourse, community engagement and royal pageantry in a programme designed to showcase the richness of Benin heritage.

For Eagle Aromatic Schnapps, Nigeria’s Authentic Traditional Prayer Drink, culture is more than a reflection of the past; it is a living heritage that connects generations, reinforces communal identity and preserves the values that define a people. This belief finds meaningful expression in the 10th Coronation Anniversary of His Royal Majesty, Oba Ewuare II, CFR, the Oba of Benin Kingdom.

As a brand whose identity is rooted in Nigeria’s traditional heritage, Eagle Aromatic Schnapps recognises the significance of royal institutions as custodians of history, customs and cultural continuity. Its association with this historic milestone reflects the brand’s appreciation of the traditions that have sustained the Benin Kingdom and contributed to Nigeria’s diverse cultural identity.

Eagle Aromatic Schnapps identifying with the anniversary goes beyond participating in a royal celebration. It represents an opportunity to reaffirm the importance of cultural preservation, community engagement and respect for the traditional institutions that continue to shape the country’s social fabric.

Speaking on the significance of the anniversary, John Bamgbose, Assistant Brand Manager, Schnapps and Gin, Intercontinental Distillers Limited, described the occasion as an opportunity to celebrate the Benin Kingdom’s rich history and the values that connect generations. He said, The 10th Coronation Anniversary of His Royal Majesty, Omo N’Oba N’Edo Uku Akpolokpolo, Ewuare II, CFR, is a remarkable milestone in the history of the Benin Kingdom. It is a celebration of royal heritage, cultural identity, continuity and the enduring spirit of a people whose history has made a lasting contribution to Nigeria’s national identity.

At Eagle Aromatic Schnapps, we recognise that our cultural heritage is one of our greatest treasures. Our traditions tell our stories, connect generations and remind us of the values that make our communities unique. When we celebrate our traditional institutions, we are also celebrating the history, creativity and collective identity of the people they represent.

We are delighted to identify with this historic milestone and celebrate the Benin Kingdom as it marks ten years of the reign of His Royal Majesty. We recognise the importance of preserving our cultural heritage and creating opportunities for younger generations to understand and appreciate the traditions that have shaped our society.

For Eagle, cultural engagement is about recognising what connects us as a people. It is about respecting our traditions, valuing our communities and supporting meaningful occasions that keep our heritage alive. We believe that when culture is preserved and appreciated, it becomes a bridge between our past, our present and our future.

Bamgbose added that the brand values meaningful engagement with Nigeria’s cultural institutions and communities, recognising the importance of responsible corporate participation in traditional celebrations.

The anniversary programme, scheduled throughout October 2026, reflected these values through a rich blend of cultural displays, royal pageantry, sporting competitions, intellectual engagements and community-focused activities. From the Cultural Festival, to the Food Festival, Art Exhibition and Trade Fair, to the Wrestling Competition, to the Oba Erediauwa Memorial Lecture, to football match to the Durbar the programme presents multiple opportunities to celebrate the heritage, creativity and collective identity of the Benin people.

According to the Obasogie of Benin Kingdom:

The significance of the Oba of Benin’s 10th Coronation Anniversary extends beyond the marking of ten years on the throne. It lies in the opportunity to renew appreciation for an institution that embodies the history, identity and cultural continuity of the Benin people. The anniversary programme brings different dimensions of society into one celebratory framework, demonstrating how tradition can remain relevant while creating space for contemporary interests and future aspirations.

As the people of the Benin Kingdom celebrate this royal milestone, the broader lesson is that heritage thrives when it is understood, valued and passed on. Traditional institutions preserve the memories of generations, communities keep their customs alive, and responsible corporate engagement can contribute to a wider appreciation of the cultural identities that define the nation.

The Grand Reception on October 20, 2026, provided a fitting climax to the 10th Coronation Anniversary celebrations, attracting an impressive gathering of dignitaries, political leaders and distinguished guests. The occasion was graced by the Governor of Edo State, the Deputy Governor, members of the State Executive Council, including Commissioners, and other prominent personalities who joined the Benin Kingdom in honouring His Royal Majesty, Omo N’Oba N’Edo Uku Akpolokpolo, Ewuare II, CFR. The gathering reflected the significance of the Benin monarchy as a symbol of cultural heritage, unity and traditional leadership, while further underscoring the importance of the historic milestone. For Eagle Aromatic Schnapps, the occasion provided another opportunity to celebrate the enduring relationship between Nigeria’s cultural institutions, community identity and the traditions that unite generations.

For Eagle Aromatic Schnapps, these celebrations reinforce a simple but powerful message: when we celebrate our traditions, we preserve our identity; when we honour our cultural institutions, we strengthen the connections that bind generations together.

Also, cultural heritage remains one of Nigeria’s most valuable assets, deserving recognition, respect and preservation. By identifying with significant traditional occasions, the brand seeks to reinforce the importance of the customs, institutions and communities that continue to shape the nation’s cultural identity.

Ultimately, the 10th Coronation Anniversary is more than a commemoration of a decade on the throne. It is a celebration of continuity, collective pride and the enduring connection between a people and their heritage. As the Benin Kingdom honours its past and looks towards the future, Eagle Aromatic Schnapps celebrates alongside the wider appreciation of Nigeria’s rich cultural traditions.

World.title: Loud Whispers with Joseph Edgar
World.content:
Obafemi Hamzat: Lagos Best Bet?

I believe that true reforms in our country can only come from the inside. Before you scream, listen – the APC is so entrenched that nothing short of a full-scale war can dislodge them. Their entrenchment has come with so many things that I can’t mention here, but has equally thrown up a Sodom and Gomorrah scenario.

A Sodom and Gomorrah scenario is when man asked God, “What if there was one good person there, nko, will you still destroy the place?” So, for me, I look for that one good person and work with the person and hope that eventually reforms will come through.

We have achieved slow success. See how Ambode turned Lagos into an infrastructural wonder, and see how Sanwo-Olu moved, especially in taking on the establishment with his reforms and in all of these, Hamzat was in there serving these ‘reformist’ administrations.

Hamzat seems to have a serious approach to governance, clarity in the objective, ability to push cohesion to deliver for the common man, humility, concise and engaging policy formulation and execution and more.

Lagos truly deserves the very best in leadership because of its very complex challenges and its growing population, and for its very socio-economic importance not only to Africa but to the world. Of all the candidates presently thrown up, Hamzat seems the best possible choice for a serious engagement with Lagos and its many problems. Thank you.

President Tinubu: I am Confused

Another $7billion borrowing? Bringing the total to a whopping N29 trillion in borrowings. It is no wonder Atiku has called it an election slush fund.

Even I, sitting here, I don tire, I swear. How do you run a government by borrowing up and down without even looking at slowing down the government? The cost of government is still crazy high, compounded by loopholes and leakages being exploited by everyone. Parastatals run like casinos in Las Vegas and white elephant projects everywhere, with no end game in sight. See, just one Ebola, and we have thrown N10billion at it, and now the woman has carried her wahala to her country, and we don’t know if the funds were already disbursed and, if so, what will happen to it?

Why all these borrowings? The whole thing is now so scary. What is the collateralisation? The same crude oil? Na wa o, and Akpabio and his merry men will just be bowing and signing off.

Mr. President, haven’t you heard of austerity measures? Mbok, please slow down; some of us still have children and grandchildren. If you are not thinking about our generation, please think of the upcoming ones. What legacy would you be leaving for them? Kai!

Peter Obi: Please Take It Easy

When President Bola Tinubu said he would campaign in only 12 states, we all screamed. You see why his people always say that he is a master strategist. The man understands what they call pacing. He has looked at the voting blocks and decided to pace himself and be strategic. Why waste my time and little energy in a state where even if I get 100% of votes there will not help my case or in a state where I have it in full control. Why not concentrate on the areas that are swing states or not yet captured? This is how brilliant politicians play.

But our “messiah” is running around, playing to the gallery and now exhausted. From burial ceremonies, to the opening of a spare parts shop in Abiriba and back to a naming ceremony in Sokoto, Mr. Obi is everywhere, and now he has lost steam.

He had better calm down and slow down and be strategic in his moves so that he does not physically burn out. The thing is evident in his speeches and engagements, as he is now making mistakes, contradicting himself, and just talking anyhow.

He should take two weeks off, disconnect, fly to an island with his Gucci bag-loving wife and rest. Rest so that by the time he comes back, he will be full of energy because the journey is long and tedious.

Sorry, my brother, please check your blood pressure regularly, drink a lot of water, have sex and just calm down. Nigeria is going nowhere; it is not a matter of life and death.

With or without you, our sufferings will continue. Just do your own and leave the rest. Thank you.

Bimbo Ashiru: The Man, His Network and His Contributions

I have worked very closely with Otunba Bimbo Ashiru in the last one month. I have spoken to him like five times a day during the period, visited him almost on a daily basis and engaged with him. I have watched him in meetings and seen how he has built a solid reputation enmeshed with positive goodwill.

Otunba comes from the very well-respected Ashiru family, a family that has produced some very prominent Nigerians, and he has parlayed all of that to a position of influence that is nothing but very remarkable.

I sit down and listen to his phone calls – from the top, to state governors, prominent politicians, captains of industry, and all remain just one phone call away. It is no wonder that he is a permanent fixture on speaking podiums.

Otunba is in great demand to speak or attend one Masterclass or the other, and this is simply because, unlike the vast majority, he bestrides the world of politics and business with so much gusto. He is on the Board of over 16 companies.

Otunba had just come out of his lavish room at the Transcorp Hilton hotel, wearing an expensive and elegant-looking black loafer with green soles, and I asked him to ‘dash’ me the loafers but pretended not to hear. I asked a second time, and he still ignored me. Refusing to give up, I held his cloth and repeated, and he still did, like the network was not working. At this point, I began to wonder what kind of Otunba is this na. If this was MKO Abiola, he would have removed it and given me straight; now see this Ijebu Otunba behaving as if I am using a NITEL phone to call him because he does not want to give me shoes.

So, there you have it, the only one negative on this super beautiful Nigerian. It is no wonder that the 100-year-old Daily Times recently gave him the Changemaker Award. Brilliant.

Biodun Oyebanji: Running With a Winning Team

I have not reached out to my egbon, the brilliant governor of my adopted state, Ekiti, for a while. Bro, how have you been? Long, long time.

I recently received good news from my brother Niran Olatana on his reappointment as the State Chairman of its Revenue Service. Niran’s appointment did not come as a surprise, as his tenure has seen the quadrupling of the state’s internally generated revenue from a paltry N650million to over N3billion monthly. His reappointment evoked a lot of jubilation as his staff went out in song and dance on the streets.

While I was still ruminating about Niran, I also heard that my other brother Akin Oyebode has also been reappointed Commissioner of Finance. I am sure that with this appointment, Akin should immediately be seen as the longest-serving in this position in the country. His longevity is nothing but competence. If you know Akin very well, who is nephew to the great Gbenga Oyebode, you will not blame Governor Oyebanji for sticking to him.

There is nothing wrong with sticking with a winning team, especially one that comes with competence, passion and integrity. See ehn, Niran and Akin are two people that I can vouch for when it comes to integrity, and this shows very well in Oyebanji’s approach to public service because if he too were not a man of integrity, he would not put ram road honest people in these two very sensitive positions.

Congratulations, Your Excellency, on these reappointments. You are on the right path. As soon as I find time, I will come and visit you guys, but please no pounded yam again o. The thing used to give me constipation, Your Excellency. Just try, there must be someone in the whole of Ado-Ekiti that can cook afang na. Kai.

Bisi Adebutu: A Good Samaritan in Jeopardy

During the week, famous international investigative Reporter David Hundeyin reached out to me. He came out of hiding – you know he is under state protection in a West African country. “Edgar, I have been approached to investigate a matter, and I have heard that you are close to the matter.”

I panicked o. Me that I just wrote a sponsorship proposal to President Tinubu. This one wants to come and scatter it for me – you know how the enemy of my friend is my enemy- that is what Tinubu will do when he finds out that I am talking to this one in the night.

I rushed into the toilet to take his calls before my APC neighbours would hear me and report. “Bro, what is the issue?” I whispered, and he said, it is the matter between Bisi Adebutu and one “boy”. I just hissed.

My brother, they approached me to enter the matter. I went to beg Bisi to calm down, and they secretly recorded me and took the recording to court. My brother, imagine that rubbish, me that was begging on their behalf.

Apparently, these very scrupulous people had approached the brilliant Bisi Adebutu for a loan. Bisi preferred equity, and they took $1.5million from him and started doing “sarewagba” with him. Bisi dropped his assets as collateral, and now they have done “gbajue” for him, and the case landed at the EFCC, and they are now playing the ethnic card.

Ohhh, Bisi is using Yoruba to bully them; his father is Baba Ijebu, and that is why they have stolen our brother’s company and jailed him; IPOB will enter the matter, etc.

My brother, I have removed my hand, even though my sentiments are with Bisi, who has not only lost that whopping sum but has had his credit rating scattered by these people, I concluded. The man now said, Edgar, let me shock you. They have sent your recording to me too. Kai, I screamed. I thank God it is not my sex tape. These people would have shown the whole world my prized jewels. They should just go and face their fire; I am not their problem.

Me, the day I jam that their sister, the one that recorded me, I will do her something strong and hand myself over to the nearest female police officer to detain me. Thank you.

Kemi Badenoch: Not Our Child

My visa will soon expire, and I will be going for renewal, so I have to choose my words.

Till today, we don’t know why Trump cancelled my visa. That one is okay because I no kuku get money to buy that ticket, but this one, let me be cautious.

But this Kemi person just hits me totally differently. The way she talks sef, she will be doing mouth like those annoying brats that used to report us in primary school to wicked teachers. Her latest tirade on the slave trade is the lowest. That Britain should not pay reparations and that it is our fault that we were commodified and sold like geisha fish to them.

This one is crazy o, and I am very happy; shebi it is them that left very serious people this country has donated to them and picked this one to integrate and make her their conservative leader.

I wish them well; it is when they eventually make her their Prime Minister that they will know the market that they have bought. This one will slap King Charles one day in a fit o. This is the kind of Kemi we used to call “kemo la kan” in Shomolu those days. Na real “Kemo la kan”. Kai!

Jimi Odukoya: A Marriage in Controversy

Aburo got married and got Pastor Tunde Bakare to bless his marriage. Pastor Bakare, just recovering from a failed attempt at career change, came out of his hibernation to bless the union, and since then, Christendom has gone into a meltdown.

“Oh, you cannot remarry with your ex-wife still alive,” some Christians railed. “She even wore a nose ring,” others screamed, “and he is wearing an earring and has a tattoo and ‘dada.’”

My position is clear – hypocrisy. If this were their blood brother, would they support him at a very young age, never to remarry again? Would they prefer him to scourge the choir like some of his colleagues are doing?

The man, knowing that he cannot “hold” it, went and got a wife, which is a beautiful thing, and they are still shouting. What kind of people are these so-called “Christians”? This same Bible has King David and Solomon, who were very creative in their philandering ooo and yet this young man picks only one, and there is bedlam.

Mbok, let me send my encouragement and blessings to the new Pastor and Pastor Mrs. Jimi Odukoya. After all, them Oshoffa had plenty, and they are in heaven today. Mbok, enjoy your life; you have only one life to live. Where is the party, abeg?

World.title: Aisha Babangida: Championing Women’s Empowerment and Advancing Girl-Child Education Across Africa
World.content:
When some people discuss charitable donations and foundations, rarely do they gush about the work of Aisha Babangida. And that is because they are unaware of the sheer scale and precision of her contributions, both to women’s empowerment and girl-child education across Africa.

Lady Aisha founded Egwafin Microfinance Bank in 2016. It is a licensed institution that gives microloans, credit, and banking services to small-scale market women and others who cannot get them from commercial banks.

The bank is one of four organisations she founded or leads, each with a defined function.

The Better Life Programme for the African Rural Woman (BLPARW) was founded in 1987 by Maryam Babangida, during the military administration of her husband, General Ibrahim Badamasi Babangida. It was conceived to improve the social, economic, and educational circumstances of rural women, acknowledging that rural women are central to Nigeria’s farming economy, yet many have limited access to finance, education, and infrastructure.

Aisha took over in 2009, after her mother’s death and 22 years after the programme began. Under her, it runs adult literacy, vocational training, agricultural development, cooperative societies, youth empowerment, and educational support, and has added financial literacy, business skills, and links to funding.

The Women Enterprise Alliance (WenA), which she founded in 2018, invests in and mentors early-stage companies and small and medium-sized enterprises led by women across Nigeria and Africa. Her initiatives train cohorts of 1,000 women entrepreneurs at a time on building sustainable business plans.

The Tasnim Foundation, which she also founded, concentrates on girl-child education for girls from rural and disadvantaged backgrounds. It funds scholarships, builds small community schools and rehabilitates orphanages, and has supported healthcare facilities, vulnerable children, and displaced communities.

The programme Aisha inherited trains women in business skills, while the bank she opened in 2016 and the alliance she added in 2018 supply credit and investment.

The AIB Founders’ Award, which she hosts, gives direct corporate support to emerging African businesses.

These are registered or licensed bodies with set functions, so their work can be checked.

The soft-spoken lady continues to direct partnerships with government and international development groups through the Women Development Centre in Abuja, and the programmes remain active.

World.title: Jimmy Odukoya: Love After the Storm
World.content:
Wonders shall never end. The same is true for love and marriage. It is within this beautiful mix that we find Pastor Jimmy Odukoya, senior pastor of The Fountain of Life Church.

It started with Odukoya posting a picture of two hands wearing wedding rings on Instagram on October 31, 2026, with the caption reading “To New Beginnings”. Expectedly, speculations followed online.

The next day, at the Sunday service at the church’s headquarters in Ilupeju, Lagos, he explained it. Visibly delighted, he called his wife to the altar and presented her as Mo Jasyme, now Pastor Mo Odukoya, the church’s new first lady, to the cheering applause of the congregation.

The couple then knelt before Pastor Tunde Bakare, general overseer of The Citadel Global Community Church, and his wife, Olayide, who prayed for them and blessed the union. Bakare said the wedding itself took place in the United States, so the introduction in Lagos came after the ceremony.

The announcement drew wide attention because of the pastor’s standing in the Christian community. He told the congregation he had carried his pastoral leadership alone since his father’s death and had “found my bone of my bone”.

News lines are already carrying listicles about Mo Odukoya, like how she is the daughter of Reverend Titus Theophilus Daniel and Reverend Mrs Bolaji Daniel; and a designer and creative entrepreneur known in Christian creative circles for contributing to the look, visual identity, and production of various artistic projects.

What causes some readers to take a second look is that she was previously married to Mosadoluwa Adegboye, the British-Nigerian gospel producer and singer known as itsMOSA. That and how she also supports Manchester United, the English football club.

Meanwhile, it is Pastor Odukoya’s second marriage. His first, to Oluwakemi Folashade Banjoko, known as Kemi Odukoya, took place in March 2013 in England, and they have two children. But the couple are separated now.

All in all, love has come for PJ, as he is fondly called. With his PM (Pastor Mo) beside him, the journey continues.

World.title: Between Peter Obi and Tompolo
World.content:
On July 18, 2025, the Asset Management Corporation of Nigeria (AMCON) sold about 1.14 billion Fidelity Bank shares, roughly 2.3 per cent of the bank. The buyer was described only as a prominent Niger Delta oil and gas security businessman. Then capital market sources started speculating that the buyer is High Chief Government Ekpemupolo, known as Tompolo, who chairs Tantita Security Services Nigeria Limited. If reports are to be believed, he has continued to buy and now leads the shareholder register.

In recent times, new reports emerged that Tompolo wants a say in who succeeds Dr Nneka Onyeali-Ikpe, the Managing Director since January 2021. Her tenure ends on December 31, 2026. This is how Peter Obi, former Anambra State governor, comes into the picture. Obi was a pioneer major shareholder at Fidelity. In fact, he became the bank’s chairman in 1994. He always says that he does not own it, that his board seat is a professional duty. But the documents leave little room between the two men.

Fidelity’s 2025 annual report counted 525,912 shareholders and 50.2 billion shares at December 31, 2025, and said none held up to five per cent. With the July sale falling before that date, and with the bank calling the takeover story unsupported, people are left scratching their heads.

The claims about Obi meet the same difficulty. Reports on platforms such as SaharaReporters say he secretly holds up to 29.5 per cent through proxies, nearly six times that five per cent ceiling. Unnamed shareholders have made similar claims in other reports.

Those who see a contest have reasons. Obi is preparing a 2027 presidential run under the Nigeria Democratic Congress, and a chief executive’s exit is a decision any large shareholder would want to influence. Rivals also allege that the bank’s structures are being used to pool funds for him. The bank rejects that claim and says it is detached from partisan politics.

Essentially, it is all very interesting. Who would have thought that Obi would ever be affixed to the same table as Tompolo, being of—some might say—reverse dispositions. Still, perhaps the identity of the person the board puts forward to succeed Onyeali-Ikpe will make things a bit clearer.

World.title: Tayo Amusan: A New Landmark in Sports and Entertainment Emerges
World.content:
Full-sized trucks will drive straight onto the floor of the Lagos Arena through a marshalling yard, so that concert equipment can go up and come down quickly. The feature separates the building from halls in Africa that were designed for other uses and later fitted out for music.

Billed as Africa’s first purpose-built indoor arena of international standard, the $100 million project is led by Tayo Amusan, the billionaire chairman of Persianas Group, with the Nigerian Sovereign Investment Authority (NSIA), which holds 40.5 per cent.

Live Nation and Oak View Group, two global live entertainment companies, are partners. As commentators have pointed out, Lagos has never lacked artists or audiences; the shortage has been of venues built for their scale. But Amusan’s arena will seat 12,000, which makes it the largest indoor arena in Nigeria, and has 32 VIP boxes. Its seating tiers are designed to give every seat an unobstructed view.

The Turkish firm Yazgan Design Architecture drew a yacht-inspired building with cascading terraces and LED screens on all four exterior sides. It is going up in the coastal zone of Victoria Island and Lekki, beside The Palms Shopping Mall, which Persianas developed and opened in 2004, 20 years before the arena’s groundbreaking. The mall brought a modern shopping format to Lagos.

The venue is built for more than 200 events a year, from Afrobeats and global concerts to basketball, UFC, WWE, boxing, tennis, and futsal, the indoor five-a-side football game.

The master plan also includes an adjoining hotel and parking. Hospitality, transport, event production, merchandising, security, and technical services stand to gain from the crowds, along with jobs, and the benefits could reach well beyond the arena’s immediate surroundings.

Readers might recall that groundbreaking took place on February 24, 2024, with completion first set for December 2025. Delays at the foundation stage, which covers piling and soil testing, moved the expected opening to between late 2027 and the second quarter of 2028. Soon and very soon, Amusan will show Lagos’ brilliance to the world.

World.title: Senate Presidency: Yari Emerges as Prominent Contender
World.content:
In June 2023, Senator Abdulaziz Yari lost the vote for Senate President to Godswill Akpabio by 63 votes to 46. He had insisted on contesting against the APC’s zoned candidate, and reports say the Department of State Services (DSS) detained him in July 2023 and questioned him about election spending. Now Yari, a former Zamfara State governor who represents Zamfara West, is back in the conversation.

Yari is Director-General of President Bola Tinubu’s 2027 campaign council. Akpabio and Deputy Senate President Barau Jibrin serve on the same council as deputy directors-general.

To circle back, there are a few things working for and against Yari, starting with how he is a two-term former governor and a former chairman of the Nigeria Governors’ Forum, and is Geregu Power’s Chairman. Supporters say he has a wide network across the northern political bloc. Reports describe him as one of the north’s wealthiest politicians, so to that record of money-spending, his camp says all of it was legally earned.

It helps to know that while he led the governors’ forum, the Economic and Financial Crimes Commission (EFCC) raided his properties, froze accounts, and investigated him over N84 billion in shared funds. His supporters call the attacks smear campaigns by rivals who fear his stature.

Regional balance also counts against him. In 2023, the party zoned the presidency to the South-south and the deputy post to the North-west. But Yari is from the North-west, as is Barau. Tinubu’s closeness is an asset, but senators tend to vote for their own leaders. And those senators seem to have spoken.

On October 15, 2026, serving senators declared the presidency of the 11th Senate not vacant and vowed to return Akpabio and Barau unopposed. Senate Chief Whip Tahir Monguno said the post would not be open to contest.

In any case, the 11th Senate is due to be inaugurated in June 2027, months after the January general election. The next thing to watch is how many sitting senators win re-election.

World.title: Abdulsamad Rabiu: One of the Most Influential Men in Tinubu’s Corner
World.content:
Not many Nigerians can say they have stood inside the Holy Kaaba beside their president. Abdulsamad Rabiu, chairman of BUA Group, can. He was among those allowed in when President Bola Tinubu visited Makkah for Umrah, the lesser pilgrimage, and he called it a deep blessing.

That alone would not put a man in the President’s corner, but what about the record around it?

At a dinner for the delegation in Makkah, Rabiu said it was the third the group had held with Tinubu since arriving, and it is believed that he might have pledged the business community’s backing for the President’s re-election. It is the same back home.

In October 2026, Rabiu met Tinubu at the Presidential Office in Abuja to align his companies’ operations with government objectives. He has also called on First Lady Oluremi Tinubu to coordinate private-sector help with the administration’s Renewed Hope social initiatives.

Rabiu’s own footprint is industrial. BUA Group’s interests span cement, sugar, food processing, and infrastructure, and his investments have added to domestic production capacity and employment.

He speaks up for the policies too. After consultative visits to Aso Villa, he credited the administration’s reforms with improving the foreign exchange environment and pulling down food prices. It just so happens that both are important in the sectors his businesses occupy.

The Presidency returns the compliment. Tinubu has marked Rabiu’s birthdays, including his 65th and 66th, with state statements calling him “a partner in nationhood” whose investments complement the government’s economic agenda.

A presidential delegation draws business leaders, and Oando chief executive Wale Tinubu was in Makkah too, alongside governors and senior officials. A public appearance does not describe a private relationship, and Rabiu, one of Nigeria’s wealthiest businessmen, has a standing built on his own industrial record.

Still, three dinners with the President in one trip is a seat close to the table. The administration’s momentum that Rabiu has pledged to back is something that voters might have to consider in the general election in January 2027.

World.title: Dauda Lawal is Wining Hearts, Commanding Attention in Zamfara
World.content:
To say that Governor Dauda Lawal of Zamfara State is wining the hearts of people of Zamfara State is like stating the obvious. He is writing a compelling chapter of his political story. The hardworking governor has made governance the centre-piece of his administration, seeking to translate the enormous expectations of his people into tangible dividends of democracy.

Zamfara, a state whose aspirations stretch far beyond the horizon, has long yearned for leadership capable of translating promises into progress and political declarations into tangible dividends of democracy. For its people, the true luxury of governance is not found in the grandeur of official convoys or the glitter of state ceremonies, but in the assurance that their hopes are being taken seriously.

This is where Lawal’s political narrative becomes particularly intriguing. Beyond the ceremonial splendour that accompanies high office, the real test of his administration lies in the lives touched, opportunities created and developmental footprints it leaves behind. His supporters see a governor determined to make public service meaningful, with the prospect of a better tomorrow serving as an important thread in his administration’s story.

Indeed, politics may provide the stage, but it is performance that sustains the applause. The corridors of power may glitter with influence, yet the enduring jewels of leadership are public trust, visible progress and the confidence of the governed.

For Lawal, the challenge is to consolidate the gains of his administration, deepen the impact of its policies and ensure that the aspirations of Zamfara’s people remain at the heart of governance. Ultimately, the measure of his stewardship will be found not in the splendour of political ceremonies, but in the enduring difference his policies make to everyday lives.

World.title: Rassie Erasmus gets sweet birthday wish from old school
World.content:
Springbok coacj Rassie Erasmus receieved a special birthday message from his old school. Images via IG

Springbok coach Rassie Erasmus received a special birthday wish from his alma mater, Hoërskool Despatch, this week.

The rugby hero turned 54 on Thursday, 5 November.

RASSIE GETS EXCITING BIRTHDAY WISH FROM OLD SCHOOL

On their social media accounts, Hoërskool Despatch – the Eastern Cape High School where Rassie Erasmus matriculated more than 30 years ago – posted a special birthday wish to the Springbok coach.



In the clip, learners of the Afrikaans medium school performed an upbeat war cry for the rugby hero who turned 54 years old this week.

The school shared: “We are incredibly proud of you, your achievements and the inspiration you are to our learners, our community and South Africa”

Rassie responded to the post with a comment that read: “This is so special! Love Despatch and all of you. Blow the flame high ❤️ Despatcher for life”.

PASSION FOR RUGBY

While attending Hoërskool Despatch, Rassie Erasmus developed a passion for rugby.

In 2018, his former coach, Coenie Strumpher, told SABC News that the rugby hero was an exceptionally talented schoolboy.



He shared: “He was so talented. It didn’t matter in which position he played.”

His former coach, Coenie Strumpher, told SABC News in March 2018 that Erasmus was an exceptionally talented schoolboy.

He recalled moving him from eighthman to flyhalf, saying: “He was so talented. It didn’t matter in which position he played.”

Rassie went on to play professionally for the Free State Cheetahs and Gauteng Lions, before making his Springbok debut in 1997.

He had 36 test match appearances and played until 2001. As the national team coach, he’s helped the Springboks win back-to-back World Cup titles in 2019 and 2023.
