World.title: Africa: CANEX Opens Doors for Gambian Fashion Entrepreneurs Seeking Global Recognition
World.content:
For Gambian fashion entrepreneur Ndey Bassin Faye, building an internationally recognised brand begins with empowering women, celebrating local culture, and embracing African-made textiles. At CANEX WKND 2026 in Lagos, she and fellow entrepreneurs are looking beyond borders to build connections that could help transform their businesses and the continent's fashion industry.

When Ndey Bassin Faye discusses her fashion brand's global expansion, she also refers to promoting Gambian culture internationally.

The founder of Bassin's Couture, established in 2016, is one of three Gambian fashion and tailoring entrepreneurs, Mariama Jallow, Ndey Bassin, and Ida, attending the Creative Africa Nexus Weekend (CANEX WKND) 2026 in Lagos, Nigeria.Their attendance is sponsored by the Andandorr programme, with support from EU YEP – Tourism and Creative Industries.

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

For entrepreneurs, the four-day gathering is more than an opportunity to showcase their work. It is a chance to meet potential partners, connect with suppliers, learn from industry experts, and explore new markets for their businesses.

At the heart of Faye's work is a commitment to women and girls. Through Bassin's Couture, she uses fashion not only as a business opportunity but also as a means of empowering women to pursue entrepreneurship while promoting Gambian culture through design.

Like many African fashion entrepreneurs, she faces challenges that extend beyond creativity and craftsmanship. One of the biggest obstacles is accessing materials.

"One of the challenges we face is the difficulty of sourcing diverse fabrics, particularly those outside of Gambian culture," says Faye.

She highlights the challenges of sourcing materials from other African countries, noting that, in some instances, it is easier to access supplies from Europe and China than from within the continent.

While the continent is home to rich textile traditions, cotton-producing countries, and a growing community of designers, connecting the different parts of the value chain remains difficult.

For Faye and her partners, CANEX offers an opportunity to help bridge some of those gaps. She hopes to use the gathering to establish relationships with suppliers, meet fellow designers, and explore collaborations that could strengthen her business and expand its reach.

"I want us to go international. I want our brand to be seen and to be known internationally," she says.

She also wishes to see more African materials incorporated into African fashion.

The Gambia has a tradition of handweaving, and Faye is proud to work with locally grown cotton. By incorporating hand-woven fabrics into her designs, she is taking practical steps towards building a fashion business that promotes local resources while celebrating the country's cultural identity.

Building a fashion industry that supports African designers

The challenges facing entrepreneurs such as Faye are part of the bigger conversations at CANEX, particularly during different masterclasses offered by experts in the textile industry. In a masterclass about how African fashion businesses could strengthen their marketing management and expand into global markets, luxury brand consultant Anita Ehui highlighted the structural difficulties that continue to affect African fashion businesses, particularly in manufacturing, textiles, sourcing, quality control, and pricing.

"I think we have a big manufacturing problem, whether in textiles or production itself, and that makes things difficult," Ehui said.

She explained that while many designers aspire to manufacture their products entirely on the continent, achieving this can be challenging due to limitations in material availability, production capacity, and quality.

Designers are often forced to make compromises, whether on quality, pricing, or design, because the necessary resources and infrastructure are not always readily available. Ehui encouraged entrepreneurs to prioritise African sourcing and production wherever possible, arguing that increasing demand for locally manufactured products could help strengthen the continent's manufacturing ecosystem.

However, she also cautioned against some common mistakes made by emerging fashion businesses.

One common mistake is overcomplicating business decisions, such as designing and selling products based solely on personal preferences rather than genuine customer demand.

For African fashion businesses aiming for growth, identifying the correct market is crucial. Instead of trying to appeal to everyone, entrepreneurs should understand their target customers, their desires, and the most effective ways to communicate the value of their products.

She highlighted how CANEX provides an important platform for designers to connect with potential customers and fosters conversations that can lead to partnerships and new ideas.

"CANEX is giving fashion designers a platform. It is also connecting some of the brands with customers," she stated.

She added that gatherings like CANEX create opportunities for collaboration, knowledge-sharing, and has potential to expose creators to new perspectives.

"When we gather at CANEX, there is always a conversation that can spark a collaboration or even open your mind to something new," she said.

Close 

From Local to Global Markets

For the three Gambian entrepreneurs, these conversations are particularly important as they plan the next phase of their businesses. Access to industry experts through masterclasses, exposure to other African brands and suppliers, and opportunities to engage with potential business partners offer valuable insights into building sustainable fashion enterprises.

Organised by the African Export-Import Bank (Afreximbank) and hosted by the Federal Government of Nigeria, CANEX WKND brings together leading African and diaspora creatives, investors, and policymakers from various sectors including music, film, fashion, sport, publishing, gastronomy, and visual arts.

The four-day event is designed to facilitate partnerships, encourage investment, and expand access to international markets for Africa's creative industries.

For Faye, the journey towards that future is already underway. The vision is to reach international markets without losing the local identity that makes the brand distinctive. Faye and Ehui agree that African fashion can compete globally, but the continent must first make it easier for African creatives to work, source, produce, and grow together.

World.title: Africa: A Just Energy Transition Cannot Leave Water Behind
World.content:
guest column

As Africa weighs how to power its industries and expand electricity access, water must be part of the equation. Ahead of COP31, Dr Jonty Cogger and Paul Wani Lado draw on South Africa’s experience to argue that a just energy transition must test proposed fossil fuel investments against their water demands—and protect the communities whose supplies could come under pressure.

South Africa's energy debate often focuses on electricity supply, energy security and economic growth. Oil and gas infrastructure is increasingly presented as part of the answer to these challenges. This framing hides a key test for any proposed development: whether its promised benefits justify the strain it will put on scarce water, and whether affected communities will carry an unfair share of the costs.

South Africa is a water-scarce country. Local communities increasingly struggle with unreliable water services, crumbling infrastructure and growing demand for water. Given this, plans to expand fossil fuel infrastructure need far closer scrutiny than they usually get.

Climate change makes matters worse by bringing more heat, more drought and less predictable rainfall. Writing for the Endangered Wildlife Trust, Dr Ian Little warns that a strong El Niño during the 2026/2027 summer season could bring below-average rainfall, higher temperatures, lower river flows and less water reaching dams. It could also cut crop yields, strain livestock farming and increase the demand for irrigation. In a country where water and food systems are already under pressure, this combination of risks shows why water security, food security and climate policy must shape any decision to expand fossil fuels further.

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

Oil and gas are not just a matter of energy policy. Expanding them affects the environment, the climate, water security and the rights of local communities. Yet debates about new gas infrastructure tend to focus on the promise of energy and industrial growth, rather than taking a hard look at the environmental costs and the local communities that may pay them.

Calling gas part of a just energy transition does not make it just. More electricity or investment does not, on its own, tell us who benefits, who pays the environmental, social and economic costs, and whether those costs can be avoided. Nor does calling gas a transitional fuel solve the problems of building fossil fuel infrastructure that will last for decades.

The risk is that South Africa repeats an old development model under the banner of a new transition where powerful economic interests reap the benefits of resource-hungry industry and local communities are left to deal with the environmental costs.

Water makes this contradiction especially clear because it links national energy choices to direct local effects. A project sold as improving energy security may make others less secure if it competes with households, farmers and nature for a limited and increasingly unreliable supply of water.

Putting water at the centre of the just transition means treating it as a firm limit on development, not just one factor to consider after energy and investment decisions have been made. Government should assess from the outset how proposed fossil fuel and industrial projects would affect how much water is available, its quality, and the ability of communities and ecosystems to cope as the climate worsens.

As government considers expanding gas infrastructure and attracting energy-intensive industries, it must account for how much water these developments will need. The critical question is whether the combined demand from multiple developments, together with existing uses and worsening climate pressures, can be met without harming communities' access to water, the health of ecosystems or the needs of other lawful water users.

This scrutiny must be based on evidence that is public and can be independently checked. Decision-makers should disclose how much water proposed projects need, where that water would come from, the condition and capacity of the water systems involved, what would happen in a drought, and the combined demands of existing and likely future developments.

The same scrutiny must apply to the infrastructure needed to support these developments, including pipelines, power stations and related industrial facilities. Decisions about these projects cannot ignore the water systems and communities they depend on.

Close 

Local communities should not have to face less reliable water supply so that fossil fuel expansion and industrial growth can go ahead. If government is serious about a just energy transition, it must require open water assessments that account for climate change and the combined impact of all projects before approving new developments, and it must show that communities will continue to have enough reliable water. Economic benefits should not be assumed to outweigh environmental and social costs; they must be weighed against them.

Dr Jonty Cogger is a public interest attorney at the Centre for Environmental Rights whose work focuses on using legal strategies to challenge pollution and climate change.

Paul Wani Lado is an attorney at the Centre for Environmental Rights where his work focuses on the extractives industry, particularly mining and upstream oil and gas projects.

World.title: Africa: CANEX Aims to Empower African Creatives to Compete in Global Markets and Drive Economic Growth
World.content:
CANEX WKND 2026 opens in Lagos, Nigeria, an initiative of the Afreximbank aimed at boosting creatives from across the African continent.

Creatives from across the continent are gathering in Lagos, Nigeria, for the Creative Africa Nexus (CANEX). This initiative brings together Africa's creative talent, investors, policymakers, and industry leaders to unlock the economic potential of the continent's cultural industries.

Dubbed CANEX WKND, the four-day event attracted more than 15,000 registrations from across the global creative community, under the theme "One People, United in Culture, Creating for the World."

Hosted by the Federal Government of Nigeria and organised by the African Export-Import Bank (Afreximbank) through its Creative Africa Nexus programme, the event runs from 5 to 8 November. It aims to transform Africa's growing cultural influence into sustainable businesses, increased trade, investment, and employment opportunities.

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

"CANEX was established to offer a comprehensive suite of solutions aimed at developing the capacity of Africa's creators and enhancing the value retained within the continent, through CANEX finance," said Dr George Elombi, President and Chairman of the Board of Directors of Afreximbank.

From film and television to music, fashion, publishing, sport, gastronomy, and visual arts, CANEX WKND is positioning the creative economy as an increasingly important contributor to Africa's economic transformation.

For a continent with the world's youngest population, the creative industries offer significant opportunities to harness the talents, innovation, and entrepreneurial ambitions of young people. However, translating this potential into sustainable livelihoods requires more than talent and international recognition. It requires access to finance, skills development, markets, technology, and the commercial infrastructure necessary to build viable businesses.

This is the gap Afreximbank's CANEX initiative seeks to address.

The bank recognises that financing is not the industry's only challenge; a holistic approach is needed for the industry to thrive.

"We can put financing skills into music and movie productions, yet the value we derive could still be low. We must, therefore, focus on building the creative ecosystem, focusing not just on idea generation, creation, and production, but particularly on value capture from those activities that we now know attract the greatest value. These include vending and production, and CANEX was created for that purpose," said Elombi.

He noted that the budget has increased significantly since CANEX started to meet the needs and demands.

"When CANEX began, we had a budget of U. S$500 million for the creative economy. We soon found out that it was too small, so we raised it to U.S. $ 1 billion, and that was also too small. In 2024, we raised it to U.S.$2 billion," he noted.

One of the key discussions of this event is to encourage creatives and provide a platform for practical discussions on financing creative enterprises, commercialising intellectual property, and strengthening the continent's position in global creative markets.

"Africa already has its cultural influence; our challenge is to build economic power. Look at Afrobeats, Nollywood, our fashion, literature, and visual arts: our creativity is thriving more than ever before. However, recognition is not the same thing as ownership, and global popularity does not automatically translate into prosperity," noted legendary Nigerian actor Richard Mofe-Damijo.

Mofe-Damijo emphasised the need for access to better finance, stronger protection for intellectual property, reliable institutions that work, and businesses that can grow beyond success stories.

Financing will also take centre stage at the Creative Economy Finance Summit, presented by Afreximbank in partnership with the Creative Economy Practice at Co-Creation Hub. The summit will bring together financial institutions and investors to examine how creative-economy transactions can be structured, financed and de-risked.

Among many topics, discussions will also explore one of the world's most compelling topics, artificial intelligence, examining how African creatives can leverage digital technologies to develop products capable of competing internationally.

Close 

On the list of prominent figures from across the continent and diaspora are Nobel Laureate and writer Professor Wole Soyinka, Emmy Award-winning actor Uzo Aduba, filmmaker and actor Funke Akindele, actors Richard Mofe-Damijo and Thuso Mbedu, and former professional footballers Didier Drogba and Jay-Jay Okocha, musicians Davido, Fally Ipupa, Flavour, Libianca and Charlotte Dipanda.

Cultural ministers from across the continent are also in attendance, including from Côte d'Ivoire, South Africa, and Rwanda, alongside representatives from the International Finance Corporation and Afreximbank.

Speakers highlighted that strengthening access to financing, protecting intellectual property, and improving distribution channels are essential for African creatives to compete internationally and retain a greater share of the value they generate. For Afreximbank, supporting the creative industries is also part of a wider strategy to diversify African economies, promote intra-African trade, and strengthen the continent's participation in global markets.

World.title: Africa: Deadly Viruses Know No Borders, Nor Should Our Resolve to Stop Them
World.content:
Sjoerd Sjoerdsma, Dutch Minister for Foreign Trade and Development Cooperation, and Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, Director-General of the World Health Organization at WHO headquarters in Geneva, Switzerland.

guest column

In this guest column for AllAfrica, the Dutch Trade and Development Minister and the head of the World Health Organization stress that addressing viral health crises anywhere protects everyone everywhere. The government of the Netherlands is committing funding both for the current Ebola crisis and flexible funding to quickly respond to new or emerging global threats.

COVID-19 may feel like a distant memory to many. But the virus claimed millions of lives around the world, including approximately 50,000 in the Netherlands. The lesson is clear: preparedness is not optional.

Preventing health crises abroad is in the interest of all countries, including the Netherlands.

Governments everywhere face competing priorities and constrained budgets. But infectious diseases do not respect national borders. In an interconnected world, health threats that emerge in one place can quickly become risks for all of us. No country can safeguard its health security alone.

That lesson is evident today in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC), where a major Ebola outbreak is unfolding in a region already affected by insecurity, displacement and limited access to health services.

Already the outbreak has crossed national boundaries, underlining how quickly a health threat in one country can become a shared international concern.

Responding effectively requires rapid action, strong local leadership and international solidarity. Under the DRC Government's leadership, the World Health Organization (WHO) is working closely with the Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention, local authorities, communities and partners to contain the outbreak in the DRC and save lives.

Mystic Stock Photography / Shutterstock.com The MV Hondius, a cruise ship owned by the Dutch company Oceanwide Expeditions experienced a Hantavirus outbreak last year. The Netherlands and the World Health Organized collaborated to safely evacuate passengers and crew.

To support these efforts, the Netherlands is providing €7 million to WHO for the Ebola response. But responding to outbreaks requires more than emergency funding alone. It requires flexible, predictable financing that can be directed rapidly to where needs are greatest. That is why the Netherlands is also providing a new €10 million flexible contribution to WHO for future emergencies, enabling the WHO to rapidly respond to health threats while helping countries strengthen preparedness and prevent future outbreaks whenever possible. This is additional to the existing €9.6 million yearly core funding to the WHO.

No country can safeguard its health security alone.

Some may ask why the Netherlands, or any country, should invest in health emergencies far from its own borders when domestic health systems also face challenges. The answer is simple: diseases do not stop at borders. Supporting countries to detect and contain outbreaks early is not only the right thing to do. It protects local populations while reducing the risk of wider international spread. Investing in health security abroad is also an investment in health security at home.

Outbreaks are most effectively controlled at their source. Local leadership is essential. National authorities understand their communities, their health systems and the challenges they face. WHO's role is to support those efforts, coordinate international expertise and ensure that countries have access to the tools, funding and technical assistance they need.

International cooperation remains the foundation of effective health security. This year, for example, a hantavirus outbreak on a Dutch-flagged cruise ship was swiftly contained through rapid collaboration among countries and partners coordinated through WHO. During an earlier outbreak caused by the "Sudan virus" species of Ebola in Uganda, investments that helped advance an Ebola vaccine developed by the International AIDS Vaccine Initiative (IAVI) and Batavia Biosciences contributed to global preparedness efforts. These examples demonstrate that cooperation works.

Dany Bitita/WHO Two new candidate vaccines to join Ebola trial as treatment research advances.

Yet this progress cannot be taken for granted. The international health system is under growing strain, even as health threats continue to increase. Climate change is altering the distribution of infectious diseases. Europe has already seen growing concern from vector-borne diseases, including West Nile virus, while other diseases such as dengue and malaria are expanding into new regions. At the same time, funding for global health, including for WHO, is declining.

Diseases spreading to new areas amid decreased global health funding is dangerous.

This is a dangerous combination. The need for cooperation, preparedness and rapid response is growing, just as the resources required to sustain them are coming under pressure.

We therefore call on European governments to strengthen their support for global health security by increasing flexible and unearmarked contributions to WHO. Such investments enable outbreaks to be detected earlier, contained more rapidly and addressed where they begin, before they become larger regional or global crises.

No one can rule out the possibility of another pandemic. . But we can ensure that we are better prepared for the next one. Strong health systems in the DRC, and in countries everywhere, are not only vital for the local communities. They are an investment in a safer, healthier and more secure future for us all.

Sjoerd Sjoerdsma is the Dutch Minister for Foreign Trade and Development Cooperation. Dr. Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus is Director-General of the World Health Organization.

World.title: Kenya: Kenya Cult Leader Paul Mackenzie Sentenced to 200 Years
World.content:
Paul Mackenzie was found guilty in October of the murder of 190 children.

A court in Kenya has sentenced Paul Mackenzie to 200 years in prison for the murders of 190 children and an adult. He told them to starve themselves to death as part of his apocalyptic religious cult.

Kenyan religious sect leader Paul Mackenzie was sentenced to 200 years in prison on Friday, at the culmination of a trial following the discovery of hundreds of corpses in the woods.

A self-proclaimed pastor and longstanding leader of a new age Christian apocalyptic cult called the Good News International Church, Mackenzie was convicted in October of 191 counts of murder in the deaths of one adult and 190 children.

Justice Diana Kavedza said the sentence was comprised of 100 years for 183 counts of murder by starvation and another 100 years for eight counts of murder by direct homicide.

He could have faced the death penalty, which is still technically on the books in Kenya.

However, like several countries that have kept capital punishment in their legal code but stopped actually using it, Kenya has not executed anybody since 1987.

While the charges against Mackenzie pertained to 191 deaths, some 400 people were found dead in what became known as the "Shakahola Forest Massacre." Mackenzie's so-called church had been operating since 2003, based in the coastal town of Malindi.

Mackenzie had denied the charges, saying that he did not force the cult followers to starve.

A total of 28 accomplices were given various prison sentences for their roles in the deaths.

World.title: Tanzania: Tanzania Opposition Leader Lissu Cleared of Treason but Jailed for Incitement
World.content:
A Tanzanian court on Friday sentenced opposition leader Tundu Lissu to four years in jail for inciting unrest, after earlier in the day clearing him of treason - meaning he avoided a possible death sentence. The verdict follows a disputed presidential election and a deadly crackdown on protesters, in a case that has drawn international condemnation and raised concerns about political freedom in the country.

A panel of three judges at the High Court in Dar es Salaam, Tanzania's commercial capital, convicted the 58-year-old leader of the country's main opposition party, Chadema, over remarks he made calling for electoral reforms.

"We are satisfied that through his statements, the accused intended to disrupt elections and instigate violence," a judge told a courtroom packed with supporters, French news agency AFP reported.

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

Lissu has been detained since April 2025. He has denied any wrongdoing, arguing that his campaign was lawful and the charges against him politically motivated.

Facing heavy security, Tanzania protesters fear repeat of election violence

Campaign in the dock

His arrest came six months before the October 2025 vote, shortly after he launched a drive for changes to Tanzania's electoral system under the slogan "No Reforms, No Election".

Prosecutors argued that his statements were intended to disrupt the vote and threaten the government, amounting to treason.

Lissu, a lawyer who represented himself during the trial, maintained that his comments had been taken out of context and that he had committed no crime.

"My hope is that you will carry that heavy historical burden without bias, with courage and with the dignity carried by your judicial oaths," he told the panel in his closing arguments.

Tanzania's Hassan makes historic Russia visit amid frayed ties with West

Criticism abroad

The trial drew criticism from British and European Union lawmakers, who described it as politically driven and called for Lissu's immediate release.

"The use of capital punishment against a political opponent risks turning the justice system into an instrument of political repression," they wrote in a letter to President Samia Suluhu Hassan.

Security was tightened across Dar es Salaam and around the courthouse ahead of Friday's verdict, as Lissu's supporters gathered for the hearing.

Groups were mobilising to travel to the city, police said on Wednesday, warning against "those who want to stage a coup".

Elections, coups and crackdowns: Africa's mixed democratic record in 2025

Close 

Death toll in dispute

Lissu's arrest, Chadema's disqualification and alleged abductions of government critics helped fuel protests during last year's presidential election.

Hassan won with 98 percent of the vote after her two main challengers, including Lissu, were excluded. The opposition dismissed the result as a "mockery" of democracy.

A government-appointed commission put the death toll at at least 518, blaming protesters for the violence. Opposition groups and human rights organisations say the authorities killed thousands.

Accusations that security forces used excessive force have been rejected by the government. The election was fair and transparent, Hassan has insisted, blaming foreigners for the unrest.

(with newswires)

World.title: Namibia: Distance No Longer a Death Sentence
World.content:
Namibia's air ambulance is expected to reduce some journeys that take hours by road to minutes or a few short hours by air, depending on the distance and emergency.

A 12-year-old boy who needed urgent medical attention died while waiting to be transferred from Katima Mulilo to Windhoek, a tragedy that has now become one of the reasons behind Namibia's first State-owned air ambulance service.

The boy's death, followed by the loss of patients who could not be transported quickly enough after a road accident along the Otjiwarongo road, exposed the cost of delays in Namibia's emergency healthcare system.

Health minister Esperance Luvindao recounted the painful experiences on Wednesday as the country officially launched its first State-owned air ambulance service,

a move expected to reduce the time critically ill and injured patients spend travelling to specialised hospitals.



"Unfortunately, in the early hours of the next morning, I got a call that this 12-year-old boy had passed away," Luvindao said, recalling the incident involving the patient from Katima Mulilo.

"This was heartbreaking. Because I knew that a young life had just been lost," she narrated. The minister said another emergency occurred in April 2026 when a road accident along the Otjiwarongo road left patients needing urgent transportation to Windhoek. "Unfortunately, this was not possible and lives were lost," she said.

The experiences, she said, forced the health ministry to look for solutions that could save lives while the government continues with plans to build more hospitals.

The launch, officiated by Vice President Lucia Witbooi in Windhoek, marks a major change in how the country intends to respond to medical emergencies, particularly in remote areas where patients face long journeys to reach referral hospitals.

For patients who need urgent specialist care, the difference between reaching a hospital in time and waiting hours could determine whether they survive.

Witbooi said the service was intended to ensure that a person's chances of survival were not determined by where they live.

"No Namibian should lose their life simply because they live far from a hospital," she said.

She added that the country's vast geographical size and the distance between remote communities and referral hospitals had long created challenges for emergency medical care.

The air ambulance is expected to reduce some journeys that take hours by road to minutes or a few short hours by air, depending on the distance and emergency.

The service includes a Learjet air ambulance equipped with medical equipment to provide critical care during flights.

Government Air Transport Services will provide aircraft and pilots in collaboration with the ministries of health and works and transport. It will also use helicopter evacuation services through cooperation with the Namibian Police and the Namibian Defence forces to respond to emergencies in areas where helicopters are needed.

Specialised medical personnel will accompany patients requiring urgent care, while emergency service centres at national referral hospitals will help ensure patients receive treatment immediately after landing.

Luvindao said the service was developed as a practical response to the country's healthcare challenges, rather than waiting for the construction of more referral hospitals.

"While we build those hospitals, Namibians want service. While we build those hospitals, there is another 12-year-old boy that might have severe head injuries and need urgent transportation. And so it is our role to make a plan, not just for the future, but for now," she said. She said the government was working towards constructing four hospitals in the coming years, but acknowledged that such projects require substantial financial resources and time.

Close 

The air ambulance, she said, would complement existing ground ambulance services and provide an additional option for patients whose conditions require urgent specialist intervention.

The ministry has also activated an emergency callcentre to coordinate requests, verify referrals and dispatch the service.

Luvindao said the centre would serve as a single point of coordination to ensure that patients with justified medical needs are transferred promptly.

The service will prioritise patients who require urgent specialist treatment, including those with serious trauma, neurological, cardiac and obstetric emergencies, as well as patients whose conditions make road transport unsafe or too slow.

The initiative requires cooperation between the health sector, aviation authorities, emergency responders and security institutions. - [email protected]

World.title: Africa: All of Africa Today - November 6, 2026
World.content:
Guinea-Bissau Cancels Controversial Newborn Vaccine Trial

Guinea-Bissau has cancelled a proposed hepatitis B vaccine trial on newborn babies following international criticism that it was unethical and potentially exploitative. The trial was funded by the US, under Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., who has a long record of expressing scepticism about vaccines. The study planned to involve 14,000 newborns, with half receiving the vaccine and the other half being denied the shot, despite WHO recommendations. Health experts warned that withholding the vaccine could expose babies to infection in a country where nearly one in five people has hepatitis B. The government had previously prohibited vaccine trials involving children, while police have seized a batch of vaccines from the research centre at the centre of the controversy.

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

Atiku Vows to Fight Court Ruling Sidelining His 2027 Presidential Bid

Former Nigerian Vice-President Atiku Abubakar has vowed to challenge a Federal High Court ruling invalidating his nomination as the African Democratic Congress (ADC) presidential candidate for the 2027 elections and nullifying the party's David Mark-led leadership. Atiku accused the ruling All Progressives Congress of using the courts to undermine his campaign, insisting that his campaign would continue despite the judgment. The ADC Presidential Campaign Council says its legal team is preparing to seek interim relief, including a stay of execution, while pursuing an appeal. The ruling followed a legal challenge by former ADC deputy chairman Nafiu Bala Gombe over the party's leadership transition.

UN Warns of Growing Drone Threats in Abyei

The United Nations has warned that drone attacks in the disputed Abyei region are adding a new dimension to security threats, following strikes that killed at least 30 people and injured about 59 in October. UN peacekeeping chief Jean-Pierre Lacroix told the Security Council that the attacks, the first of their kind in the area, highlight growing threats influenced by wider regional conflicts and armed groups. The warning comes amid rising tensions following deadly intercommunal clashes that killed 124 people in September. Meanwhile, the UN has raised concerns over continued drone strikes on infrastructure in Sudan, including power and water facilities, while warning that funding shortages could force the closure of a key border clinic serving about 100,000 people.

Attacks on Water Systems Triple in Conflict Zones, UNICEF Warns

Attacks on water and sanitation infrastructure in conflict zones have tripled from 2021 to 2025, putting millions of children at greater risk of disease, malnutrition and violence, according to a new UNICEF report. The report documented more than 135 attacks across 15 countries in 2025, compared with fewer than 45 incidents across eight countries in 2021. It highlights damage to water treatment plants, pipelines and other essential facilities in countries including Sudan and the Gaza Strip. UNICEF Executive Director Catherine Russell said that attacks on water and sanitation systems "deprive children of safe drinking water and the essential services that rely on water to function effectively". UNICEF is calling on parties to conflicts to protect water infrastructure, workers and civilians, warning that repairing damaged facilities cannot replace the protection required under international humanitarian law.

WHO Adds Two Ebola Vaccines to DR Congo Trial

The World Health Organization has announced that two additional Ebola vaccine candidates will join clinical trials in the Democratic Republic of Congo as the country battles its largest-ever outbreak of the Bundibugyo strain. The vaccines, developed by Oxford University in partnership with the Serum Institute of India and US-based Moderna, will be evaluated for the first time during an outbreak of this Ebola strain. The DR Congo has been battling a deadly outbreak of Ebola disease for nearly six months. It has become the largest in the country's history. As of 1 November, the outbreak had recorded more than 10,500 confirmed cases and 5,126 deaths. The WHO said that the new candidates could provide an important tool in controlling the outbreak, although they will require national approval before joining the ongoing trial.

Close 

Six More Bodies Found in Kenya Building Collapse

Rescue teams in Nairobi have recovered six more bodies from the rubble of a collapsed multi-storey building in the Eastleigh neighbourhood, raising the death toll from the disaster. Kamukunji MP Yusuf Hassan confirmed the latest recoveries. He expressed condolences to families still waiting for news of missing relatives. Four people were previously rescued alive. Police have maintained that multi-agency teams are supporting the operation. They urged members of the public to keep away from the affected area to allow emergency responders and specialised equipment to operate safely. The search operation remains focused on recovering those still believed to be beneath the debris.

World.title: Alabama finally puts it all together, dominates LSU and leaves Lane Kiffin staring at $40 million CFP disaster
World.content:
Alabama spent the past five days taking heat from across the country over its No. 5 ranking in the initial College Football Playoff poll released Tuesday.

On Saturday, Kalen DeBoer’s Crimson Tide took out its frustration on Lane Kiffin and LSU in front of a stunned crowd in Baton Rouge, delivering a result that could have major ramifications for the Tigers’ playoff hopes.

This page may contain affiliate links to legal sports betting partners. If you sign up or place a wager, FOX News may be compensated. This content was created by a team that works independently from the FOX newsroom.

We all spent the past week arguing over why the Tide would be ranked eight spots ahead of No. 13 Tennessee after the Vols won the head-to-head matchup last month in Knoxville.

COLLEGE FOOTBALL PLAYOFF RANKINGS: MIAMI TAKES TOP SPOT, INDIANA CRACKS TOP FIVE IN FIRST OFFICIAL RELEASE

The nonstop chatter around Alabama struggling to find an identity behind head coach Kalen DeBoer had become a hot-button topic around college football, while LSU fans were under the impression that Lane Kiffin was turning a corner in the Bayou.

Boy, how quickly the tables have turned.

LSU spent more than $40 million building its roster this season, acquiring a group of stars through the transfer portal. Now, the Tigers enter the second weekend of November with three losses and their CFP hopes hanging by a thread.

On the other side of the field, not worried about Kevin Costner or other celebrities making the walk into a game alongside the head coach, Kalen Deboer has now finally pieced it all together for a squad that has the talent to compete for a national championship.

This is the Alabama team the CFP committee thought should be ranked 5th in the country, and the Tide backed up their thinking in a dominant second half way in Baton Rouge.

Where did this Alabama performance come from? It's been bubbling

Maybe it was the return of Ryan Coleman-Williams or multiple starters on both sides of the ball, but Alabama finally looked like the type of team we thought would grace our television screens on a weekly basis without the hiccups.

In front of over 100,000 fans inside Tiger Stadium, it was Alabama's Keelon Russell who fully came out of his shell in what will turn out to be a massive game in terms of his team making the playoff.

Three touchdowns and over 200 yards passing, offensive coordinator Ryan Grubb provided his freshman quarterback with the ammunition needed to put Alabama in a spot to win this game.

But, winning 31-13 in "Death Valley"?

LANE KIFFIN FUMES OVER ALABAMA KICKOFF TIME, ACCUSES SEC OF NOT WANTING LSU TO WIN

That's a massive slice of humble-pie served up to Lane Kiffin, and the ones that doubted the heart of this Alabama football team, by a Crimson Tide defense that held LSU to just one touchdown on four redzone possessions.

Sure, LSU was moving the ball on offense, but that did not translate to points in Alabama's bend but don't break mindset that had Lane Kiffin shrugging his arms in frustration along the sidelines throughout the third and fourth quarter.

On the other hand, Alabama scoring 21 unanswered points put the final nail in this LSU football team that will host a much better looking Texas Longhorns squad next week in Baton Rouge.

LSU still has a path to CFP? It's hanging on by a thread with Texas incoming

Sure, the Tigers could upset Steve Sarkisian's football team, but there was nothing from the LSU offense that should give fans hope that they can hold up against a Texas defense that will get even healthier over the next week.

Obviously, this is the type of scenario that LSU fans were not expecting. The noise that comes with Lane Kiffin is just that — noise. Yes, the Tigers were good enough to have us all wondering how this game would turn out during the third quarter.

Fifteen minutes later, Kiffin's record against Alabama as a head coach was 0-6.

CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

Olivia Dunne and Paul Skenes walking with Lane Kiffin through the Tiger Walk makes for some fantastic social media content. But following that up by getting beaten in the trenches by an Alabama team that has been dissected all week for its flaws will not go over well in Baton Rouge.

A massive statement was made by Alabama on Saturday night during a week in which the entire country questioned just how good they actually were.

Now, everyone should be worried about what this Kalen DeBoer team can do over the next few weeks leading up to selection Sunday in the college football playoff.

World.title: Tim McGraw warns of ‘most dangerous’ times in marriage after 30 years with Faith Hill
World.content:

Tim McGraw shared his insight into what the "most difficult" part of marriage is, after being married for 30 years.

During a recent interview with Esquire’s "What I’ve Learned," the 59-year-old country star shared that as his three children with Faith Hill grow up and start their own lives, the two of them find themselves "stepping into a new phase of life."

"Sometimes that requires not talking about it and just moving on through," he said. "And sometimes it requires sitting down and talking about it a little bit, saying, 'Hey, we need to check in a little bit and see where we're at now that everything's changing.'"

He went on to say that "points of change in a marriage" can come "regularly throughout a long marriage," and these can often be "the most dangerous parts, I think, for a marriage."

GREAT RELATIONSHIPS HAVE 3 ESSENTIAL INGREDIENTS — AND ONE FACTOR THAT CAN RUIN EVERYTHING

"And not talking about things and not clearing the air and not sort of rediscovering each other at every chance you get," he said. "I think the best time to dive into each other and really rediscover each other at the worst times when you think things are falling apart."

In his opinion, it is important to have a strong foundation and "to always go back to it," because "the longer you wait to go back to it," there may come a time where it becomes "unreachable, and you never can cross that divide."

They have also recorded multiple duets together during their relationship, including "It's Your Life," the Grammy Award-winning "Let's Make Love" and "Speak to a Girl," which was featured on their first-ever collaborative album, "The Rest of Our Life."

World.title: Bridget Fonda spotted in rare LA outing 24 years after her final on-screen appearance
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

Bridget Fonda stepped out for a rare public outing in Los Angeles, 24 years after she last appeared on-screen.

The 62-year-old actress was photographed while out to lunch on Monday, Nov. 2, keeping it casual in black sweatpants and a white tank top, paired with a yellow collared button-up shirt.

She accessorized the look with a black crossbody bag and sunglasses, and styled her hair in a ponytail.

As the granddaughter of Academy Award-winning actor, Henry Fonda, known for his roles in "The Grapes of Wrath," "12 Angry Men" and "On Golden Pond," Bridget made her film debut when she was five years old, appearing alongside her father, Peter Fonda, in the 1969 movie, "Easy Rider."

'80S ICON KRISTY MCNICHOL MAKES RARE APPEARANCE 25 YEARS AFTER LEAVING HOLLYWOOD

She had her breakthrough in 1989, when she starred in the film, "Scandal," and continued to prove herself in films such as "Single White Female," "Point of No Return," "It Could Happen to You" and "Jackie Brown."

Although she found big success as an actress, she slowed down in the late 1990s and into the 2000s. Her final movie role was in the 2001 TV movie, "After Amy," and her final time on-screen was in two episodes of the miniseries "Snow Queen," in 2002.

According to the Daily Mail, she told paparazzi in April 2023 that she had no plans to return to acting, noting, "It’s too nice being a civilian."

In addition to her grandfather and her father, Bridget also grew up with Academy Award-winning actress, Jane Fonda, who is her aunt. She explained that coming from an acting family, it was hard not to be compared to one another.

"At one time, there was nothing the press would have liked better than to set up a me vs Jane thing," she told The Guardian in 2000. "They were desperate for us to be bitter rivals. They'd also try to set me against my dad, to use me as a dart to throw at someone else."

After stepping away from Hollywood, Bridget married film composer and frontman for the band, Oingo Boingo, Danny Elfman, in 2003, and the two welcomed their son, Oliver, in 2005.

World.title: Ohio State's College Football Playoff hopes take big hit with loss to Oregon, Jeremiah Smith shows frustration
World.content:
After being the No. 1 team in the preseason, Ohio State is proving why the games aren't played on paper.

The Buckeyes, 12th in the College Football Playoff rankings, were touchdown favorites against No. 23 Oregon but were dominated, 41-28, for their second loss in as many weeks.

This page may contain affiliate links to legal sports betting partners. If you sign up or place a wager, FOX News may be compensated. This content was created by a team that works independently from the FOX newsroom.

It looked like all Buckeyes early, as they got out to a 14-0 lead in the first quarter sans Julian Sayin, but someone lit a fire under Oregon's you-know-what, and they responded with 38 unanswered points.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE OUTKICK SPORTS COVERAGE

The Buckeyes were two-and-a-half minutes away from going into the locker room with at least a 14-3 lead, but the Ducks faked a punt on 4th and 10, which apparently was the turning point. Five plays later, they found the end zone to cut the deficit to four, and then Luke Fahey threw an interception near midfield, which Oregon turned into a 17-14 lead right as the first half ended.

The bleeding did not stop, as momentum, and the ball, was all in Oregon's hands to start the second half. Dierre Hill Jr. took a 48-yard scamper to the house to go up two possessions, and the Buckeyes were stumped. After a three-and-out in their first drive of the second half, their next four drives resulted in turnovers on downs, all while Oregon managed to put up two more touchdowns to go up 38-14.

Jeremiah Smith had a 57-yard reception in garbage time to make his stats pretty (seven receptions for 133 yards), but let his emotions out on the field as he may have watched his Heisman chances slip away. He was held to just four catches through three quarters, three of them in the first half.

The Buckeyes had been the first team out of the first edition of the College Football Playoff rankings, and they unquestionably now face an uphill battle to play in the postseason.

DUKE'S BEATDOWN OF NC STATE INCLUDED A MUST-SEE MISSED FIELD GOAL RETURNED FOR A 109-YARD TOUCHDOWN

This defeat is off the heels of last week's 30-18 loss to USC as the second-ranked team in the AP poll. Thus, the team is 0-2 without Sayin, who many had in the Heisman conversation at the start of the season.

Nine Ducks caught at least one pass from Dylan Raiola (25-for-40, 257 yards, two touchdowns). Dakorien Moore and Brandon Smith combined for 10 catches for 108 yards, each with a score, while Hill scored twice on his 13 carries for 75 yards.

Now needing a lot of help, Ohio State will host Northwestern next week before a trip to Nebraska and then finishing the season hosting Michigan.

Oregon, meanwhile, is now hoping to backdoor its way into the playoff — they wrap up their campaign with Michigan, Michigan State and Washington the rest of the way.

World.title: Chili's sold nearly 30 million margaritas last year — and a $6 favorite stands out
World.content:

Chili's dominated restaurant chains in margarita sales in 2025 and is set to sell even more this year as the company finds new ways to keep its signature drink program fresh, according to a new report.

The chain sold nearly 30 million margaritas in 2025 and says that many customers come in specifically for the drinks, Nation's Restaurant News recently reported.

"Guests are coming to Chili’s for 'margs,'" Mary Ellen Scott, Chili's senior marketing director, told NRN. "It’s part of who we are and part of the experience."

CHILI'S GOES VIRAL AFTER ROASTING FAST-FOOD PRICES: 'WHY LET THEM PLAY YOU LIKE THIS?'

Frozen margaritas have been a Chili's menu staple since 1975, back when they cost just $1.50, and the chain has revamped the offering in recent years. Frozen drinks now account for 25% of its margarita sales.

Last year, Chili's launched a line of premium-liquor frozen margaritas and in February, it introduced a Margarita of the Month Club that allows customers to track how many of the drinks they bought and buy related merch, which is available for anyone to buy.

CHILI'S REVIVES ICONIC RED BOOTHS AND CLASSIC DESIGN IN NATIONWIDE RESTAURANT OVERHAUL

Customers can collect a digital badge for each month’s margarita and Scott says the "diehard" fans are eager to collect them all.

The club builds on the rotating Margarita of the Month program Chili's introduced in 2018, which draws customers in part for its low price of $6.

BABY BOOMERS CROWN THEIR FAVORITE CASUAL DINING CHAIN AS GEN Z CHOOSES A DIFFERENT WINNER

"It’s value, newness and fun," Scott told NRN. "It's always $6, the drink is changing every month, and we're always looking for ways to make the experience more fun, whether it's a candy or a swizzle."

Examples include October’s Witches Brew, a green drink made with Lunazul Blanco Tequila, blue Curaçao, and Monin Granny Smith Apple Syrup served with a broomstick "swizzle," or decorative stirrer.

November’s StrawEddy Marg combines the tequila with Deep Eddy Lemon Vodka, strawberry purée and house-made sour.

The premium-pour margs go for $10 to $12, which is still a steal when cocktails in many major cities are going for around $20.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE LIFESTYLE NEWS

The chain also has a full bar, but Scott says the margaritas remain its "flagship."

Fox News Digital has reached out to Chili's for comment.

TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

World.title: Coach of NJ's top girls soccer team suspended for playoff game after champagne bottle celebration
World.content:
A New Jersey girls' soccer coach has been suspended for a playoff game for celebrating a milestone victory with a champagne bottle.

Paul VI coach Karen Anderson was seen on video celebrating her 100th career win, a 2-0 win over Notre Dame in the South Jersey, Non-Public A quarterfinals, by what appeared to be popping the bottle on school property after the game.

Anderson told NJ.com that she did not drink from the bottle, which was bought and given by parents of members on the team. Anderson did not say whether the bottle had alcohol in it.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE OUTKICK SPORTS COVERAGE

The New Jersey State Interscholastic Athletic Association (NJSIAA) rulebook states that "[p]layers and coaches involved with alcohol/tobacco/illegal substances during or after the game at the game site or on school property, including chartered buses, shall be suspended from NJSIAA tournament play for one year and be denied any championship rights." So, perhaps the punishment is rather lenient.

Anderson told the outlet that she was "not surprised" that the video was coming to light "given our success."

"It’s really unfortunate that there are people out there looking for an opportunity to ruin all the hard work that I’ve put into this program," she said of the video, which has since been deleted from social media.



"There sure are a lot of people that would look for a target to take an opportunity. It’s really unfortunate that somebody will find that one opportunity to jump on and try to take down everything that you have put into this."

"While Coach Anderson did not consume the contents of the bottle, Paul VI does not condone this behavior and recognizes the importance of upholding the standards of conduct expected of our coaches," Paul VI said Friday in a statement to the outlet.

CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

Paul VI's girls' soccer team is the top-ranked team in the state and is two wins away from clinching its third-consecutive Non-Public A state championship.

An ex-NYPD police officer accused of murdering a Brooklyn jogger was seen being out of the 62nd Precinct police station in handcuffs on Saturday.

Sayed Mohassib has been charged with second-degree murder in the stabbing Oct. 30 death of Katie Suarez at the Shore Parkway Greenway.

He is also charged with physical evidence and criminal possession of a weapon.

Mohassib, who wore a red Van Dutch jacket, black top and jeans, showed little emotion as he was escorted by police.

NYC WOMAN CRITICALLY INJURED AFTER BEING STABBED MULTIPLE TIMES WHILE JOGGING ALONG BROOKLYN WATERFRONT

He told police that he woke up covered in blood with no memory of the attack, adding that he threw the knife in the garbage, according to the New York Post.

Suarez, 28, was running along a waterfront path around 8 p.m. when she was stabbed in her neck.

She had been on the phone with her parents before the attack and when they got cut off, they went looking for her along the path where they found her in critical condition.

She died of her injuries at the hospital.

COPS RETURN TO NEW JERSEY MOTHER'S HOME MONTHS AFTER SHE WAS FOUND STABBED AND HUSBAND CALLED 911

Mohassib briefly served with the NYPD before he left for the Marines, where he was deemed unfit for service, the Post reported.

The 27-year-old was most recently working as a public school aide.

The New York City Department of Education told FOX 5 that Mohassib has been suspended and will be fired depending on a conviction.

World.title: College football fans and media rip SEC refs over controversial forward fumble call in Texas-Missouri game
World.content:
Apparently, you can throw an incomplete pass beyond the line of scrimmage and recover the ball for a first down in college football if you’re Arch Manning and the Texas Longhorns.

This page may contain affiliate links to legal sports betting partners. If you sign up or place a wager, FOX News may be compensated. This content was created by a team that works independently from the FOX newsroom.

During Saturday's Texas-Missouri showdown, a matchup with massive College Football Playoff implications, the Longhorns were trailing 20-13 late in the third quarter when Manning dropped back on 3rd-and-10, appearing to throw an incomplete forward pass while getting hit. To the nation watching, it looked like Manning's arm was clearly moving forward before he lost control of the ball, but the officials apparently saw something the rest of America didn't.

ARCH MANNING, TEXAS ESCAPE MISSOURI AFTER WILD OFFICIATING CONTROVERSY SENDS SEC SHOWDOWN INTO CHAOS

One SEC sideline official called it an incomplete pass, while another allowed the play to continue, which isn’t too uncommon during a bang-bang play like this. Ultimately, the crew let the play stand and ruled it a forward fumble, allowing Texas receiver Emmett Mosley V to recover the ball 14 yards downfield for a first down.

During the review of the play, ABC/ESPN play-by-play announcer Joe Tessitore said astonishingly, "Are they saying this is not a forward pass and instead, a fumble?!"

Color commentator Jesse Palmer was also shocked.

Worst of all: The officials reviewed the play and somehow still decided it was a fumble. Three plays later, Texas scored the game-tying touchdown.

This obviously caused the college football world to melt down.

REFS' CRUCIAL NO CALL LOOMS LARGE OVER GEORGIA'S VICTORY OVER ALABAMA

One X user said they were "Questioning the integrity of this officiating crew."

Former referee, now rules analyst Terry McAulay said, "This is clearly and obviously an incomplete pass. He loses control after the hand moves forward."

Former Missouri and NFL quarterback, Chase Daniel was irate. "This is the most ridiculous call I’ve ever seen….you have the rules analyst and Jesse Palmer on the broadcast completely flabbergasted."

Outkick College Football Reporter Trey Wallace said, "This was called an Arch Manning fumble, and Texas picked up the 3rd down with a 12-yard gain. What the heck is happening at Missouri."

Former Missouri wide receiver T.J. Moe felt similarly saying, "This call knocked Mizzou out of playoff contention. Absolutely ridiculous. In what world is this not a forward pass?"

On3 personality David Pollack stated, "That was the craziest fumble forward I have ever seen for Texas."

Former NFL player Breiden Fehoko posted, "Real rigging going on Texas/Missouri game. Real talk this is so nasty."

FROM PHANTOM PASS INTERFERENCE TO IGNORED FACEMASK CALLS, NFL OFFICIATING FAILURES DEFINED WEEK 3

Many college football fans shared similar sentiments, calling it "rigged" and that the SEC was favoring Manning and the Longhorns for "ratings" and more accusations.

Just pencil this in as yet another officiating scandal that will continue to make fans and the media alike question the integrity of the game.

After the game, Missouri head coach Eli Drinkwitz wasn't particularly interested in donating his paycheck to the SEC by criticizing the officials, suggesting he'd be fined if he said what he really thought.

CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

Texas ultimately scored 21 unanswered points to win 34-20, but the controversial call left Missouri fans wondering whether they had just witnessed a football game or a creative interpretation of the rulebook.

World.title: New fallout from White House staffing shake-up after midterms
World.content: There were new reactions Saturday after President Trump elevated his longtime adviser Stephen Miller as his new White House Chief of Staff, marking the president’s first major staffing shake-up since Republicans lost control of the House and Senate. NBC News’ Julia Ainsley reports.Nov. 7, 2026

World.title: Trump offers press secretary position to UFC head Dana White
World.content:
President Donald Trump on Saturday said on Truth Social that he had offered the job of White House press secretary to Dana White, the CEO and president of the Ultimate Fighting Championship.

“I am pleased to announce that the Great Dana White, a violent Fighter and Warrior, has been offered the job of Press Secretary of the United States,” the president wrote.

Trump suggested in his post that White should bring several UFC fighters, including Khabib Nurmagomedov, Justin Gaethje and Amanda Nunes, as assistants to defend against the “Lunatic Left.”

“Dana will be a Press Secretary like none other. Dana, please take the job!” he added.

White said at a boxing event in London Saturday evening that he was heading to Washington, D.C., that night and had a meeting scheduled with the president Monday.

Asked whether he could speak about conversations he has had with Trump so far, White declined.

“We have a meeting on Monday, so sure, I’ll have more to talk about after that,” White said.

When Trump posted on Truth Social earlier Saturday, it was unclear whether his offer to White was a serious one.

Shortly after Trump posted, White posted on Instagram what appears to be an AI-generated image of himself behind the podium in the White House briefing room, captioned, “On to the next chapter.”

White also added a screenshot of Trump’s post to his Instagram story.

Trump and White have long been friends and the president has attended many UFC fights while serving in the White House.

Earlier this year, White also organized a UFC fight on the South Lawn of the White House, an event that was part of a slate commemorating the United States’ 250th birthday.

Many Trump administration officials and Republican lawmakers attended the fight in July.

A spokesperson for the White House did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

The position has been vacant since Katie Zacharia departed the role after just five days in October.

Zacharia had replaced Karoline Leavitt, who served as White House press secretary since Trump returned to office in January of last year. Leavitt announced in August that she would leave her post to spend more time with her family.

The White House had another staff shake-up on Friday, when Chief of Staff Susie Wiles said she would be stepping down from her post. Trump named longtime aide Stephen Miller as her replacement.

Wiles’ departure made her the seventh woman to leave the Trump administration this year. So far, all of the women who have left have been replaced by men, with the exception of Zacharia and Leavitt, as a press secretary has not yet been named.

World.title: The ‘slam dunk’ that wasn’t: Promising cholesterol drug fails to prevent heart attacks or stroke
World.content:
An experimental drug that held great promise in driving down a dangerous form of cholesterol didn’t show any measurable impact on heart attack or stroke in a clinical trial. The failure of the Novartis drug pelacarsen to help people who have high levels of lipoprotein(a) stunned researchers, who called it a massive blow to preventive cardiology.

Results of the clinical trial of pelacarsen, an injection, presented Saturday at a meeting of the American Heart Association, found there were zero decreases in stroke, heart attack, cardiovascular deaths or the number of procedures to open blocked arteries or restore blood flow to the heart.

“I really thought that this was going to be a slam dunk,” said Dr. Amanda Doran, an assistant professor of medicine in the division of cardiovascular medicine at Vanderbilt University Medical Center. Vanderbilt was one of nearly 800 sites involved in the clinical trial, called Horizon. “We were pretty invested, so it obviously hurts.”

Pelacarsen targets a stealthy and particularly lethal form of cholesterol called lipoprotein(a), or Lp(a). Much like low-density lipoprotein — LDL, or the “bad” cholesterol — Lp(a) causes plaque to build up in arteries. But it also helps form blood clots, and unlike LDL, it is entirely genetic.

About 1 in 5 Americans have high Lp(a), according to the American Heart Association. Most don’t realize they’re at risk.

Because people are born with those high levels, diet and exercise have no effect. That’s why heart experts have been so keen to find a drug that would handle the problem.

The Horizon trial included 8,322 people with high Lp(a) levels and who’d already had a heart attack, stroke or other heart problem within 10 years of starting the trial.

The drug did reduce Lp(a) significantly, by 78%, compared to a placebo drug that cut levels by 13%.

But that huge reduction ultimately meant nothing in terms of cardiovascular health.

Dr. Steven Nissen, the chief academic officer of the Heart, Vascular & Thoracic Institute at the Cleveland Clinic, led the trial. He said the dismal results took him by “extreme surprise.”

“Everybody, me included, believed that lowering levels of lipoprotein(a) substantially would reduce the risk of major cardiovascular events,” he said. “There is simply no evidence here that people that got more reduction did better.”

The findings, also published Saturday in the New England Journal of Medicine, confounded Nissen and other cardiologists who’ve long known that controlling other markers of heart health — LDL and blood pressure, for example — provides clear benefits.

“I have not seen a more shockingly neutral trial in a while,” said Dr. Karol Watson, co-director of the UCLA Program in Preventive Cardiology and a professor at UCLA’s David Geffen School of Medicine. Watson was not involved with the research.

There are several theories as to why the drug didn’t work as anticipated. It’s possible, Watson said, that the therapy was given too late in life to make a difference. The average age of Horizon’s study participants was 60, and they were followed for an average of five years.

“Remember that Lp(a) is a genetic disorder, so from the time a baby’s conceived, their Lp(a) is high. If we just swooped in in the last five years, maybe that’s too late,” Watson said.

Study participants were also treated aggressively in other ways to drive down their LDL cholesterol and get blood pressure readings into a healthy range. Participants may have also been taking aspirin because of a history of heart attack or stroke, which could have lessened Lp(a)’s clotting risk.

“How much of the Lp(a)-associated risk was remaining? We just don’t know,” Watson said.

Does Lp(a) still matter as a marker of heart health?

Doctors have only recently begun screening for it. Earlier this year, the American College of Cardiology and the American Heart Association released guidelines that every adult should have their Lp(a) levels measured. It’s a blood test that’s done once because levels are fixed and don’t change over time.

Experts stress that Lp(a) remains an important and valuable indicator of heart disease risk, even though the Horizon study failed to show any health benefit to driving down Lp(a) levels.

“None of that invalidates Lp(a) as a robust marker of cardiovascular disease risk,” said Dr. John Wilkins, a cardiologist at Northwestern Medicine and a professor in the division of cardiology at Northwestern University’s Feinberg School of Medicine. Wilkins was also one of the authors of the Lp(a) guidelines.

“It’s still worth testing for Lp(a) because it can help identify individuals with a higher probability of an event, and we do have other interventions that can help reduce their risk,” Wilkins said. “It’s just that at present, at least with this particular drug in this particular group of patients, we did not see benefit. That doesn’t mean that we might not find something or some way to lower Lp(a) that reduces risk. We just need more science to figure that out.”

UCLA’s Watson and Vanderbilt’s Doran agreed. “We have really good data to show that Lp(a) levels are predictive of disease,” Doran said. “People who have high Lp(a) need to be aware of that in order to pursue aggressive prevention strategies.”

What’s next in treating Lp(a)?

No further study of pelacarsen is planned, Nissen said, but similar drugs are in the pipeline: Eli Lilly’s lepodisiran, Amgen’s olpasiran and Silence Therapeutics’ zerlasiran.

All are injections that work by blocking the liver’s ability to produce Lp(a), but use different approaches. Pelacarsen is what’s known as an antisense oligonucleotide. The others use a technology called small interfering RNA, or siRNA, and may have fewer side effects, such as injection site reactions, Nissen said, than pelacarsen.

Like pelacarsen, all reduce Lp(a). Clinical trials to show whether they have any real-world heart health effects are ongoing.

Eli Lilly is also studying an oral drug called muvalaplin, and CRISPR gene-editing technology designed to permanently switch off the gene that produces Lp(a) is in early development.

“I’m still so hopeful,” Doran said. “We’re going to get it in the end.”

World.title: We want to hear your experience with changes to student loan repayment plans
World.content:
President Donald Trump’s “big, beautiful bill” has transformed the sprawling federal student loan system — and student borrowers are feeling the effects of the most consequential changes.

This year, the approximately 7.5 million student borrowers under the Biden-era Saving on a Valuable Education, or SAVE, plan had to select a new one. So far, about 2 million borrowers have done so, after the Education Department warned that the SAVE plan was “illegal” and would be discontinued. The remaining borrowers who did not select a new plan were set to start receiving notices this month informing them that they missed a final deadline and were automatically moved to a new plan.

The Trump administration has said ending the SAVE plan would help streamline repayment programs while ensuring borrowers are paying off what they owe to the federal government. But student advocacy groups fear lower-income borrowers who had benefited from smaller monthly payments — or even qualified to make no payments at all based on their income — will end up with significantly higher bills under the other available plans.

We want to hear from you, whether you’re in this situation or are facing another challenge related to the recent student loan changes. Please share your experience by filling out the form below.

World.title: Man arrested outside LeBron James’ L.A. home claiming to be his son
World.content:
A man found outside LeBron James’ Los Angeles home was arrested on suspicion of felony stalking, police said.

Police were called to the scene just after 9:30 p.m. Friday on a report of a possible burglary suspect at the basketball legend’s home in the affluent neighborhood of Brentwood on the city’s west side, Los Angeles police said.

Security personnel had spotted a man on surveillance cameras and called police, law enforcement sources told NBC Los Angeles.

Responding officers located the man, who claimed to be James’ son, sources told NBC Los Angeles.

The man was arrested on suspicion of felony stalking, police said. Authorities did not identify him.

James was not home at the time. He was in Cleveland playing for the Philadelphia 76ers.

World.title: 1 dead, at least 12 injured after elderly driver plows into group of cyclists in North Carolina
World.content:
One cyclist was killed and at least 12 others were injured after an elderly driver, suspected to be impaired, plowed into a group of cyclists in North Carolina.

Donald Robert Morris-Jones, 76, was driving on Optimist Farm Road in Wake County Saturday morning when he crossed the center line and struck the group of cyclists, the North Carolina State Highway Patrol said. The incident unfolded about 14 miles southwest of Raleigh.

After striking the group, the vehicle traveled away from the scene then ran off the left side of the roadway and crashed into a ditch a half a mile away from the cyclists, officials said.

The North Carolina State Highway Patrol responded to the scene just after 9:30 a.m.

One cyclist died as a result of the crash and at least a dozen more were hurt, authorities said. Their injuries range from minor to serious, and several were transported to hospitals for treatment.

Morris-Jones was taken into custody and booked on a charge of driving while impaired, according to Wake County Sheriff’s Office inmate records.

“Impairment is suspected to be a factor in the crash,” the agency said.

World.title: NYPD arrests suspect in stabbing death of Brooklyn jogger
World.content:
A New York City Department of Education employee is facing murder charges in the stabbing death of a 28-year-old woman last week in Brooklyn, authorities announced Saturday.

Katie Suarez was stabbed while jogging along the Shore Parkway greenway in Brooklyn on the evening of Oct. 30.

Her father found Suarez injured along the path. She was rushed to the hospital with a stab wound to her neck but ultimately died from her injuries.

On Saturday, the NYPD said it had arrested 27-year-old Sayed Mohassib, of Brooklyn. Mohassib is charged with second-degree murder, tampering with physical evidence, and criminal possession of a weapon. Mohassib, wearing flip flops and a red jacket, did not answer any questions when police walked him out of the 62nd Precinct Saturday afternoon.

The circumstances leading to Suarez's killing were not immediately clear. It also wasn't immediately clear what led police to Mohassib.

Katie Suarez NYPD

The suspect is an employee of the New York City Department of Education. Police sources say he worked at Public School 200 in Brooklyn, and that he was also a member of the NYPD in field training in the Bronx from October to November 2022.

"The safety of our students is our very top priority. We have suspended this individual and will move to terminate employment pending the outcome of the conviction. We are supporting the NYPD in their investigation however is needed," the Department of Education said in a statement.

Mohassib's employment with the DOE has raised questions by elected officials. City Councilmember Kayla Santosuosso, State Sen. Andrew Gounardes and Assemblymember-elect Chris McCreight said in a joint statement Mohassib "was evidently a mentally disturbed man with no criminal record" who had been "an ex-NYPD officer and ex-Marine who was discharged from the military on psychiatric grounds."

"Troublingly though, at the time of the attack, he was a DOE employee, serving as a teacher's aide in a public school," they said. "This last revelation raises serious questions about how he came to be employed in a local public school and warrants a full investigation into the circumstances of his hiring and continued employment."

Suarez's killing prompted shock and outrage throughout New York City, along with an intense search by the NYPD for her killer.

Pedestrians on the greenway reacted to word of the arrest Saturday.

"I think it's a little bit of relief. I guess relief and hopefully, potentially, some closure for her family," one person said.

Earlier this week, Katie's anguished mother Yasira Suarez had called on the suspect to turn themselves in, saying "you took an angel."

World.title: 2 licensed skydivers die after midair collision in California
World.content:
Two female skydivers who were taking part in an organized skydiving event in California were killed after colliding midair and plummeting to the ground.

The accident occurred Friday and involved two licensed, experienced skydivers at Skydive Elsinore, the company said in a statement. The Riverside County Sheriff's Department said deputies were dispatched late Friday morning after reports of an air emergency. The skydivers were taken to a local hospital with critical injuries.

They were pronounced dead at the hospital, the sheriff said.

The Riverside County coroner's office later identified the victims as 29-year-old Levi Pimentel of Aurora, Illinois, and 56-year-old Georgia Jean of Box Elder, South Dakota.

Skydive Elsinore said the free-fall portion of the dive and the opening of the parachutes were normal, but as they were preparing to land, the two skydivers collided at about 150 feet above the ground.

"The collision caused their parachutes to become entangled, and both sustained critical injuries when they reached the ground," Skydive Elsinore said in a statement. The company said there was no evidence of equipment malfunction.

The skydivers were visiting from out of town to take part in an organized skydiving event, the company said.

Skydive Elsinore — which says they are the longest-running skydiving operation in North America — is located approximately one hour away from both San Diego and Los Angeles metropolitan areas.

World.title: This week on "Sunday Morning" (Nov. 8)

The Emmy Award-winning "CBS News Sunday Morning" is broadcast on CBS Sundays beginning at 9:00 a.m. ET. "Sunday Morning" also streams on the CBS News app beginning at 11:00 a.m. ET. (Download it here.)

Hosted by Jane Pauley



COVER STORY: Seeking relief from chronic pain

About one in four American adults lives with chronic pain, defined as pain lasting more than three months. Most are still suffering for a year or longer. CBS News chief medical correspondent Dr. Jon LaPook examines some of the current treatments aimed at alleviating chronic pain, from medications and surgery, to nerve stimulation, biofeedback and self-hypnosis.

U.S.: The SS United States and her final destination

She was the fastest ocean liner in history, widely known as America's flagship, and in her nearly two decades in service, the elegant SS United States carried four presidents, countless celebrities, and tens of thousands of happy voyagers. But the jet age took her out of service, and she eventually wound up docked at a Philadelphia berth for close to 30 years. Now, the SS United States is scheduled to sink off the coast of Florida, to become the world's largest artificial reef. Correspondent Lee Cowan looks back on the history and future of a maritime legend.

FROM THE ARCHIVES: The SS United States (Video)
