World.title: Carlota de Limón: The Mexican cocktail that transported me to my mother’s kitchen
World.content:
“You have to try one of these; it’s like a refreshing key lime pie,” a hotel guest at the bar said. I walked over to the friendly group, all with the same drink in hand. The cocktail in front of them resembled a blended piña colada that was pale yellow and frothy on top, garnished with a thin lime wedge on the rim.

My friend and I were staying at the Dreams Estrella del Mar in Mazatlán, Sinaloa, for a few days to check out the hotel and all its amenities. After the nightly show, we stopped by the bar for a drink and tasted what would ultimately be the most memorable part of the trip.

The cocktail was tangy from the lemon, sweet from the sugar, and instantly took me to something very familiar. The creamy texture and the balance of tart and sweet also felt familiar, as if I had tasted this combination many times before.

Then it hit me: It was a dessert my mom used to make growing up, and one I’ve always requested when I’m home. It was a favorite of mine that she called “lemon dessert,” which I know now as a Carlota de Limón.

Back in my mother’s kitchen

Carlota de Limón is a Mexican icebox cake made with lemon juice, Galletas María (sweet, thin vanilla cookies), and a creamy mixture of evaporated and condensed milk. Layered and chilled until set, it has the perfect balance between sweet and tangy.

It was one of my favorite desserts growing up. I remember eating it by the spoonful, freshly made and the day after, as well as the feeling of disappointment when it was gone. It wasn’t reserved for special occasions, and my mom made it regularly whether we were having dessert at home or sharing a meal with guests. It was a dish that was made on a whim, ingredients almost always on hand, and one that didn’t last long.

In other words, it was always a hit.

My mother’s kitchen was where our family came together and where some of our deepest conversations happened. While water boiled for pasta or soup simmered in spices, we would all gather around the island, almost like magnets pulling us closer, filling the space with conversation, laughter and connectedness. That feeling is still there today when I visit my parents, especially around the holidays or special occasions.

An unexpected connection

At the hotel, I pulled up a bar stool and watched the bartender make another drink. Curious about its inspiration, I struck up a conversation with him. He was 23 and working his first hotel bartending job, where he had been experimenting with flavors and creating cocktails, something he found to be a fun, creative outlet.

When I described the dessert the cocktail reminded me of, he recognized the Carlota de Limón, a favorite of his, too. He had been experimenting with ingredients to create the drink, combining Licor 43, the vanilla and spice notes echoing the María cookies, and the fresh lemon juice, sugar and heavy cream to match the creamy layer. He would then shake it vigorously with ice until the mixture turned frothy and cold, adding a simple lime wedge as the finishing touch.

What began as an experiment in flavors had unexpectedly recreated something familiar to me. The bartender didn’t know my personal backstory of the dessert, but his experimentation with a new cocktail and my memories of my mother’s kitchen had led us to the same place.

Why flavors stay with us

Research from the National Library of Medicine has a name for the way a familiar smell or taste can bring back a personal memory: the Proust effect, named after the French writer Marcel Proust. The theory is that taste and smell can trigger autobiographical memories, leading to powerful emotions. Research on the brain’s olfactory pathways also shows direct connections between smell processing and the regions involved in emotion and memory, which makes sense given my strong and positive response to the citrus cocktail.

To me, Carlota de Limón was more than just a dessert; it was something my mother made regularly, in a kitchen where conversations and laughter occurred. The flavor was familiar, but so was everything I associated with it.

When I returned home, I found myself thinking less about the resort’s beautiful pools, manicured grounds or nightly shows, and more about that cocktail. A drink I’d encountered on vacation that had brought back a dessert so familiar that I hadn’t thought much about what it meant to me until that moment.

On the drive home from the airport, my husband asked how the trip went. My answer was simple: “Do we have any lemons? I have a drink in mind.”

Sandra Lee is a contributor to Mexico News Daily.

World.title: My family always travels during Día de Muertos. Here’s what we’ve enjoyed most
World.content:
There are certain magical aspects of living in Mexico that simply cannot be replicated elsewhere — its foods, traditions and seasons. And because of Mexico’s vast geography and cultural topography, many of those elements can be heightened by being in the right place at the right time.

In that regard, nothing compares to Día de Muertos: A time of year in which colors are blooming, communities are celebrating and honoring loved ones, and regional gastronomy, customs and superstitions are on display for everyone to be collectively immersed in.

Beyond the obvious, increasing importance of the Mesoamerican holiday in Mexico for so many native families and local households, Día de Muertos means something especially personal for me and my family since it marks our anniversary of having moved to Mexico from California. The holiday always reminds me of arriving in Mexico after having gained dual citizenship and being received by festive parades, open-armed friends and relatives, and getting a dose of Mexico’s fullest, most complex flavors that have come to define what we most enjoy about living on this side of the border.

Building our own annual tradition

My wife’s and my own appreciation for Día de Muertos extends further back, years before we had fully relocated to Mexico. In 2019, we visited my mom, who is Mexican-born and was living on my abuelo’s ranch in Oaxaca at the time. We spent a month traveling the state of Oaxaca with her. The highlight? A full week of Día de Muertos in Oaxaca City.

I’ll never forget when we arrived, hopped off the bus, dropped our things off and went into the loud, colorful streets as Oaxaqueños had already kicked off their days-long celebration in the middle of the afternoon. A man wearing a Spider-Man mask saw us standing among the crowd, and as we soon found out would be a common occurrence and part of the local hospitality, he offered to pour out a shot of mezcal from the bottle in his hand.

As an outsider, there is no warmer welcome on the planet than someone picking you out of the masses on the street and pouring you mezcal. It’s a spirit and energy that would come to embody every Día de Muertos holiday we’ve experienced — the sense of connection and togetherness.

Since then, we’ve turned it into our own tradition to celebrate the holiday in different parts of Mexico as often as we can.

The regional nuances of Día de Muertos

My wife recently shared a visual map with me that outlines the different kinds of pan de muerto that are prepared throughout Mexico, based on each state’s history and gastronomic influences. Her point, besides nudging me to pick up another round of pan de muerto for our house, was that Mexico offers more to try than we know, especially whenever Día de Muertos rolls around.

It’s true. Everywhere we’ve been during this season has always presented a new way through which to experience and understand the multidimensionality of how the holiday is celebrated and revered.

Nearby, in the town of Naolinco, Veracruz, and its surrounding mountain communities, the festival is largely centered on the cempasúchil. This year, the community of San Pablo Coapan welcomed thousands of visitors for its fifth annual Festival del Cempasúchil, in which the local cempasúchil farms open to the public with a festival-like array of activities, food and Instagrammable photo ops.

The flower fields are decorated with playful calaveras that are decorated in Veracruzano style, ranging from a 25-foot-tall Jarocho skeleton to a human-sized fútbolero in the afterlife wearing a Tiburones Rojos soccer uniform from the 1990s (a team that no longer exists but certainly evokes memories for anyone who recalls the historic Veracruz team and grew up watching Liga MX).

In the pueblo of Naolinco proper, just a few miles up the mountain, Día de Muertos is celebrated with “La Cantada” (or a townwide serenade), where locals go around singing from the cemeteries to the streets throughout the night.

Major cities and regional rituals

Of course, there are the more globally popular and large-scale interpretations of Día de Muertos that can be seen in Oaxaca or Mexico City. In both cases, the holiday draws countless international and domestic visitors who join in on the fun and traditions as local families honor their deceased relatives with a mix of humility and bombast.

In both Oaxaca and Mexico City, expect massive gatherings of happy-go-lucky tourists and locals, as you’ll have to shuffle your way around the crowds and generally pay higher prices. The celebrations are bigger, louder and, to a degree, more capably geared toward tourism than other locales. I’d say for starters, both Oaxaca’s capital and Mexico City are a comfortable entry point into Mexico’s sprawling multiverse of Día de Muertos, as they provide broadly appealing and easy-to-navigate celebrations, both of which my family has enjoyed and experienced ourselves multiple times.

Of course, we still have a bunch of places to visit on our wishlist that I’ve been told about by my Mexican family members and other travelers. In the Huasteca jungles, “Xantolo” brings the holiday to life with “La Viejada,” a regional masked dance in which townspeople dress up as elders (similar to Veracruz’s “El Viejo del Año Nuevo” custom at the end of every year) to remember their relatives.

1 of 17

Indigenous customs from Huasteca to Campeche

In parts of Michoacán, there is a lake procession where the Purépecha fishermen use torches to light their path across the water and celebrate with all-night vigils.

Choo Ba’ak, a bone-washing ritual that happens every year in the Campeche pueblo of Pomuch, is part of Hanal Pixán (the Maya Day of the Dead) and offers an idiosyncratic version of the holiday unlike the contemporary mainstream version that is usually portrayed.

National Geographic described the ceremony as such: “…families wash the tombs and clean the bones of their deceased. After the cleaning they keep the ossuaries, or the box where the bones are deposited, open so the skulls and bones receive sun and air, as dictated by tradition. Relatives also arrange, paint and adorn the ossuaries and cover them with an embroidered white tablecloth bearing the name of the deceased.”

In Huaquechula, Puebla, unique altars — three to four stories tall, resembling a pyramid — are on display inside homes, with each layer of the altar representing a different aspect of life and death (the earth, the heavens and a celestial summit). The elaborate designs are typically defined by white cloth and marigolds.

As a taxi driver in Oaxaca once told me, you’d need more than a few lifetimes to truly experience all that Mexico has to offer regionally for Día de Muertos.

Our highlights from this year in the mountains of Puebla

The Pueblo Mágico of Cuetzalan del Progreso is tucked away in the northernmost edge of the state of Puebla, high up in the Sierra Norte mountains.

Unlike the majority of Puebla, which is commonly known for its arid plateaus and Talavera pottery in its state capital and surrounding areas, northern Puebla offers a microclimate and culture of its own that more closely resembles the humid, tropical and high-altitude Indigenous communities of Papantla in northern Veracruz, which is located just a few miles away on the other side of the mountain.

It’s not what one might think of when thinking of Puebla. And yet, it’s where regional customs for Día de Muertos are flourishing. We drove roughly four hours north of Xalapa (or about five hours northeast from Mexico City) to experience it for ourselves this year.

We weren’t disappointed, to say the least.

The town’s architecture alone is worth the winding mountain curves that one must navigate to reach the small, ages-old village that is — because of its elevated location in the mountains — famously drenched in drizzly mist and rainfall. The narrow alleys and steep, cobblestone paths (which all lead to the gorgeous Parroquia de San Francisco de Asís and its Totonac voladores, who perform their flying ritual on a sky-high wooden pole at the center of the plaza) resemble a miniature version of Guanajuato’s capital city, without the overcrowded tourism and with a hyper-local texture.

Flying globos de Cantoya into the night

I was told by a couple of young locals that families don’t commonly celebrate Día de Muertos by visiting the graveyards overnight (which is the tradition elsewhere). Instead, they light “globos de Cantoya” (miniature hot-air balloons made from paper and other materials) and send them off into the night.

From groups of high schoolers to older professionals who’ve mastered the craft, the town gathers on Día de Muertos weekend, as everyone takes turns setting up and sending off hundreds of their custom, artisanal balloons. The balloons — and their makers — vary in style, decoration and success (often, the small balloons will self-combust in flames and come burning back to earth, which can sometimes cause fires in the area). But generally, it’s a safe and spectacular tradition to witness in person.

The tradition, as it was explained to me in the pueblo, is meant to represent a path back to the heavens for the souls who are visiting their altars to enjoy the ofrendas laid out. Each globe, as it ascends brightly and colorfully into the night sky, is meant to guide family members back to the spiritual realm.

In recent years, Cuetzalan has turned the tradition into a legitimate state-funded festival, known locally as “El Vuelo del Quetzal” (The Flight of the Quetzal), and officially as Festival Internacional de Globos Artísticos de Papel. Surprisingly, the festival is only in its second year of formal operation, which helps it retain a charmingly niche, DIY feeling.

Local flavors and looking ahead

During the day, it is all preceded by local dances, voladores, Catrina costume contests and the general ambiance of a Pueblo Mágico worth its salt: excellent food, tianguis and a dense number of historic stairways and nooks to explore.

Among the standouts in town, you cannot skip TAOL, which is led by Chef Adriana Márquez and offers elevated, accessible takes on local dishes, including tlayoyos, chilpozontle, itacate, pipián, coffee and more. It’s the kind of chic eatery that would draw lines out the door in Mexico City, but since it’s hidden behind an unassuming stone exterior in Cuetzalan, it is able to offer ample space and friendly prices for what I would consider among the best cuisine I’ve tasted this year.

Paired with Día de Muertos activities and the hordes of costumed kids making their rounds on Halloween night to ask for their calaverita at local shops, which my son participated in, a few nights in Cuetzalan is a slept-on destination for late October and early November.

Though we elected to stay home last year to dedicate our time and resources to building and decorating an altar inside our home — with the help of my mom, who supplied many photos of our relatives — we’ve enjoyed going on the road to see how others embrace the spirit of the tradition.

I’m already thinking about where we might end up next year and what it will impart.

World.title: Why Tuesday’s US midterm results are a historic opportunity for Mexico-US relations: A perspective from our CEO
World.content:
Most of us intently watched Tuesday night’s midterm election results in the United States, regardless of political affiliation. As the MND team is committed to remaining apolitical, I will not weigh in on my personal thoughts on the results. I will, however, comment on what they mean for Mexico and for Mexico-U.S. relations.

It’s important to understand that the hardline approach of the Trump administration over the past two years against both Mexican immigrants and Mexico effectively silenced leaders on both sides of the border. Mexico was constantly on the defensive against the U.S. on tariffs, cartels, deportations, the rights of Mexican citizens abroad and many other topics. Mexican Americans, regardless of status, watched with anxiety as their communities came under threat from aggressive ICE raids. For many people and for Mexico in general, it was a time to keep your head down and stay quiet. The focus became on surviving the storm rather than thriving, leading or growing.

But the midterm election results have dramatically changed that dynamic.

First of all, I am happy for Mexican Americans. They will hopefully no longer have to fear the heavy-handed tactics often deployed by members of ICE. I recently wrote about the death of the 18th Mexican-American in ICE custody here: Yet another Mexican national dies in the custody of ICE: A perspective from our CEO.

People living in the United States — either legally or illegally — shouldn’t have to fear for their lives at the hands of the government. The data shows that the raids have often gone far beyond focusing on criminals, as the administration suggested it would do. Too many good people have been demonized by ICE as the agency has become increasingly extremist.

I am also happy for Mexico. The country has been the brunt of countless threats by the Trump administration on everything from tariffs to immigration to drug policy and cartels — despite historic cooperation from the Sheinbaum administration on many of these issues. Businesses on both sides of the border have had to deal with near-constant tariff threats, which oftentimes defy standard logic and strategic rationale for the North American region. Both Trump and members of his administration have repeatedly claimed that Mexico is run by the cartels, that President Sheinbaum is “afraid of the cartels,” and threatened to take unilateral action in the country. Hopefully, the unprecedented cooperation will continue and the unhelpful threats will diminish.

I am happy for the states of California and Texas, which both elected Mexican American governors. These two states — the largest and most economically prosperous in the United States — now account for more than half of the people of Mexican origin in the United States. Mexican Americans represent 40% of the total population in those states, which, if they were stand-alone counties, would be the fifth- and eighth-largest in the world in terms of GDP. Children of Mexican immigrants to the U.S. now lead both states. The newly elected lieutenant governor of Nevada is also of Mexican heritage.

Mexican Americans stood up, voted, and were heard — loudly and clearly. Their collective action presents a tremendous opportunity for Mexico. Let me give two examples:

1. I recently wrote about the huge, untapped opportunity that the Mexican diaspora in the U.S. represents for Mexico. The engagement of Indian American businesspeople with India stands in stark contrast to the lack of engagement of many Mexican American businesspeople with Mexico. Post-election, the timing is perfect for this to change. The opportunity for Mexican American businesses to further connect with Mexico to find talent, suppliers or customers is massive and could unleash economic growth in both countries.

2. It’s time for Mexico and the U.S. to think BIG on binational projects and initiatives. If not at the national level, most certainly at the state level. Some great examples already exist or are in process. In California, think of the Tijuana airport, which actually straddles the border into California. The airport has experienced phenomenal growth and is a perfect example of how the two countries can work strategically to develop closer ties. In Texas, think of the newly-opened second railway between Laredo and Nuevo Laredo or the proposed expansion of the World Trade Bridge from eight to 18 lanes. Think of the soon-to-be-opened Pharr project adding a four-lane bridge in Reynosa, or the Colombia-Solidarity highway projects to better connect Nuevo León and Laredo. Or even consider the Green Corridors planned project for an autonomous system to transport cargo from Monterrey to Laredo.

It’s a historic time for real leadership — strategic, long-term, big thinking that can foster engagement and economic prosperity between the two countries. Far too much time has been lost dividing, threatening and silencing bilateral collaboration and cooperation. The current circumstances offer an opportunity to take the relationship to a whole new level. Leaders on both sides of the border, stand up! The time is now.

Travis Bembenek is the CEO of Mexico News Daily and has been living, working or playing in Mexico for nearly 30 years.

World.title: Mexico City’s Quintonil named best restaurant in Latin America
World.content:
Quintonil, a contemporary Mexican restaurant in Mexico City, was recognized as the best restaurant in Latin America and the fourth best globally in the 2026 edition of The World’s 50 Best Restaurants, presented Wednesday at the Municipal Theatre of Lima, Perú.

Led by married couple Chef Jorge Vallejo and restaurateur Alejandra Flores, Quintonil was the only Mexican representative among the top 50 in the ranking.

View this post on Instagram A post shared by The 50 Best Restaurants (@theworlds50best)

“With a reputation for weaving fresh, local ingredients and traditional Mexican flavours and techniques into modern preparations, [Quintonil] has cemented its place as a Mexico City classic,” 50 Best said.

Asador Etxebarri, a Basque restaurant in Atxondo, Spain, was ranked best in the world.

Despite securing a place in the top five, Quintonil dropped one spot in the rankings, falling from third to fourth place this year.

Founded in 2012 by Vallejo and Flores, Quintonil has built its concept around Mexican fresh local produce and a contemporary interpretation of traditional flavors and techniques. Many of its ingredients are sourced from an urban garden just 30 meters away from the restaurant.

Located in the high-end neighborhood of Polanco, the restaurant is named after an edible wild plant belonging to the amaranth family, widely used in traditional Mexican cuisine and featured in some of the dishes and drinks served there.

The power duo brings complementary expertise to Quintonil: While Vallejo leads the kitchen, Flores oversees the service experience in the dining room.

“Quintonil is the setting for chef Jorge Vallejo’s boundary-pushing Mexican cuisine and his wife Alejandra Flores’ exceptional hospitality,” 50 Best said.

50 Best highlighted dishes including roasted duck with coconut manchamanteles mole (a fruit and chile sauce) and a beetroot reduction, wild mushroom chileatole soup with cacahuazintle (a traditional corn variety) and beans, and ice cream made with honey from stingless melipona bees, served with papaya and lavender marmalade.

The tasting menu costs around 4,900 pesos (US $233) featuring four pairing options that include wines from around the world, Mexican wines, a selection of terroir-driven wines and rare finds, and a non-alcoholic option.

It also features a cocktail menu incorporating Mexican ingredients.

The recognition from 50 Best adds to Quintonil’s list of accolades, which includes two Michelin stars, a distinction it shares with only one other restaurant in Mexico: Pujol, also located in Mexico City.

With reports from El País

World.title: São Paulo Ex-Council Head Indicted by Police
World.content:
Brazil: Crime and Politics

Key Facts Who. Milton Leite, ex-president of São Paulo’s city council, and at least 12 others are indicted by the state’s investigative police.

What. Police indicted 13 people in most reports for joining a criminal organisation, in a probe of gang infiltration of São Paulo buses.

Next. A court has not ruled on the arrest request; state prosecutors are expected to review it in the coming week.

As of. 8 November 2026, 00:00 GMT.

A former leader of São Paulo’s city council faces an arrest request over a gang case. Police allege Milton Leite was responsible for running bus companies held by the PCC, a large Brazilian criminal gang based in São Paulo.

What We Know

Police in São Paulo, Brazil’s largest city, have indicted a former city council president in a gang case. The city’s bus network is a core part of daily life for its residents, and the PCC is a large Brazilian criminal gang.

São Paulo state’s Civil Police, the force that investigates crimes, has concluded its inquiry called Operation Vectura Corrupta. The findings, reported on 7 November 2026, cover how the PCC, short for Primeiro Comando da Capital, is alleged to have infiltrated public-transport companies in São Paulo state.

Police indicted Milton Leite and 12 other people, 13 in total in most reports, for taking part in a criminal organisation. An indictment is a police finding, not a conviction, and everyone named is presumed innocent.

Police also asked a court to order preventive arrest (prisão preventiva) of all 13. That means detention before trial with no end date, and the court has not yet ruled on the request.

Leite is a former president of São Paulo’s city council, the Câmara Municipal. He belongs to União Brasil, a Brazilian political party.

According to the police report, Leite was responsible for running bus companies held by the PCC. Police also say he is the real owner of Transwolff, a bus operator, which is an allegation and not a proven fact.

Leite has been in temporary detention (prisão temporária) since Friday 18 September 2026, when he turned himself in. Temporary detention is a limited period of custody that a judge can extend.

On Tuesday 20 October 2026, Leite was moved from the public jail in Mogi das Cruzes, in Greater São Paulo. He went to Provisional Detention Centre 2 in Guarulhos, over suspected privileges during his detention.

The state prosecutors’ office, the Ministério Público (MPSP), is expected to review the arrest request in the coming week. It will also decide whether to file formal charges.

If a court accepts the charges, the 13 become defendants, known in Portuguese as réus, on a criminal-organisation count. Even then, a defendant is not a convicted person.

The Palácio da Justiça, the São Paulo state court building in the city centre. Photo: Simone Cristina de Brito / Wikimedia Commons (CC BY-SA 4.0)

Who Else Is Named

Levi dos Santos Oliveira, a former president of SPTrans, São Paulo’s municipal bus authority, is among the 13 indicted. Danilo Morgado Silva, a member of Brazil’s Liberal Party (PL), is also named.

Silva was a candidate for mayor of Praia Grande, a coastal city in São Paulo state, in an earlier election. Carla de Paula Muller, another of the 13, is the wife of Antônio José Muller Junior.

State prosecutors say Muller Junior is a PCC leader known as “Granada”. The defences of Oliveira, Silva and Muller have denied the accusations.

Other people among the indicted are not named in this article. Leite said on 18 September, when he turned himself in, that he denies any involvement; his defence had not commented on the new indictment.

What Is Not Known

It is not known when the court will decide on the preventive-arrest request. It is also not known whether prosecutors will file charges.

Reports differ on the exact number of people indicted, and it is unclear whether any charges would cover all of them. Those answers depend on the prosecutors’ review and on the court’s own timetable, which has not been announced.

The full police report has not been published. Leite’s own response is also unknown, since his defence had not commented when the news broke.

What It Means for Readers Abroad

An indictment is not a conviction, and all 13 people are presumed innocent. What happens next depends on prosecutors and a court, not on the police.

São Paulo is Brazil’s largest city, and its bus network is a core part of daily life for its residents. A case about who controls bus companies therefore touches a core part of city life.

The PCC is a large Brazilian criminal gang, and this inquiry examines its reach into public-transport firms. Readers should treat the claims as police allegations until a court has tested them.

Our earlier reports describe Leite’s surrender in Mogi das Cruzes on 18 September and an earlier police search in Sorocaba. More coverage is collected on our Brazil page.

The next signals to watch are the court’s answer on the arrest request and the prosecutors’ decision on charges. Neither has a confirmed date.

Frequently Asked Questions

Who is Milton Leite?

Milton Leite is a former president of São Paulo’s city council from the União Brasil party. Police indicted him with 12 others for taking part in a criminal organisation, and he has been in temporary detention since 18 September 2026.

What have police asked the court to do?

Police asked a court to order preventive arrest of all 13 indicted people. Preventive arrest means detention before trial with no end date, and the court has not yet ruled on the request.

Is Milton Leite guilty?

No court has found him guilty. An indictment is a police finding, not a conviction, and everyone named is presumed innocent. Police allege he was responsible for running bus companies held by the PCC.

What happens next?

State prosecutors are expected to review the arrest request in the coming week and decide whether to file formal charges. If a court accepts the charges, the 13 become defendants on a criminal-organisation count.

Sources: São Paulo Civil Police inquiry report on Operation Vectura Corrupta; São Paulo state prosecutors (MPSP) statements as cited in the report.

World.title: Small South African Party Doubles Its Vote
World.content:
File photo. The round Ponte City tower above central Johannesburg, seen from the Carlton Centre, May 2010. Photo: Jorge Láscar, CC BY 2.0, Wikimedia Commons.

SOUTH AFRICA · LOCAL ELECTIONS

A small South African party has more than doubled its national vote in the 4 November 2026 local elections, and that may make it the kingmaker in the country’s biggest cities. ActionSA, founded in 2020 and led by former Johannesburg mayor Herman Mashaba, won 5.68% of the national vote, up from 2.33% in 2021.

For US readers, the result matters because Johannesburg, Tshwane (the capital region around Pretoria) and Ekurhuleni, South Africa’s main industrial and business belt, have no party with a majority yet. The Democratic Alliance (DA), the second-largest party nationally and the leader of the vote in these cities, will need partners to govern them.

The cities Ekurhuleni and Tshwane are hung; in Johannesburg the DA leads with about 35% of votes.

What next The Electoral Commission of South Africa (IEC) has not yet declared final results; 99% of wards are counted.

Prediction markets Polymarket, a real-money betting market, gives DA’s Helen Zille 53% to be Johannesburg mayor (7 November, 6:39 p.m. ET).

What the Count Shows

With 99% of wards counted, the IEC, the state body that runs South African elections, put ActionSA on 1,684,273 votes. That is a rise of 3.35 percentage points on its 2021 share, so the party now holds about 2.4 times the share it won last time.

The African National Congress (ANC), the party that has led the country since 1994, stood at 30.81% nationally, and the DA at 24.6%. The Umkhonto weSizwe (MK) Party, founded by former president Jacob Zuma, had 9.71%.

ActionSA’s 275 seats are a small slice of the 8,825 on offer across the country, and the IEC had allocated 95% of all seats at the time of reading. Its weight comes from where the seats sit, because it is competing for the same big-city voters as the DA and the ANC.

A street median in Maboneng, an inner-city district east of central Johannesburg, March 2020. Photo: Gsalamander, CC BY-SA 4.0, Wikimedia Commons.

Why Three Cities Hang on One Party

A metro is a large city council that runs its own budget, water and electricity services. In a hung council no party has more than half the seats, so a mayor can only be elected with a coalition deal.

The IEC marks both Ekurhuleni and Tshwane as hung. In Johannesburg, a 270-seat council where 136 seats make a majority, the DA led with 34.84% of votes and the ANC had 20.26%, with seat counts still being completed.

Herman Mashaba, ActionSA’s leader, resigned as Johannesburg mayor and left the DA in 2019, a year before he founded his own party. Helen Zille, the DA’s candidate for Johannesburg mayor, is now his main rival for the job.

What Prediction Markets Say

Polymarket, which lets users bet real money on outcomes, gave Zille a 53.0% chance of becoming Johannesburg mayor and Mashaba 24.9% on 7 November at 6:39 p.m. ET. About US$148,838 had been traded on that market; prices are bets, not polls.

Why we show this: prediction markets turn real-money bets into a live probability that moves within minutes of the news, which is why investors, campaigns and newsrooms in the United States now follow them closely. We show them next to polls and official results, never instead of them.

What It Means for You

Johannesburg is South Africa’s largest city and its main business centre, so the coalition that runs it shapes budgets, basic services and investor confidence. Travellers and firms with staff there should expect weeks of bargaining before mayors are elected and council meetings begin.

The pattern also cuts both ways: a deal that includes ActionSA could stabilise a council, while a stalemate would leave city hall without a clear majority. For anyone following the national coalition government in Pretoria, local deals are an early test of how far the DA and ANC will cooperate or compete.

What Is Not Known

ActionSA’s final share and seat count in each metro are not yet published, and the IEC had not declared final results at the time of writing. It is also unknown whether the DA will meet ActionSA’s terms, and whether talks over Johannesburg, Tshwane and Ekurhuleni will start before the results are formally declared.

Related reading: how the hung councils are forming, South Africa’s coalition politics explained, the early Johannesburg count and the Ekurhuleni result. More on the South Africa hub.

Frequently Asked Questions

How much did ActionSA win in the 2026 local elections?

The Electoral Commission of South Africa (IEC) had ActionSA on 5.68% of the national vote with 99% of wards counted. That is up from 2.33% in the 2021 local elections.

What is a hung council in South Africa?

A hung council is one where no party holds more than half the seats. Parties must then agree a coalition to elect a mayor and pass a budget.

Are the South African election results final?

No, the IEC had not declared final results at the time of writing. Until it does, the figures can still change.

World.title: Nigeria Oil Firm Denies Gas Pipes Hit Power
World.content:
NIGERIA · ENERGY

On Friday, 6 November 2026, NNPC Limited, Nigeria’s state oil company, said its gas pipelines face no constraints and do not explain why power plants are producing less electricity. The statement, posted on its website on Saturday, 7 November, answers the national grid operator, which had pointed to thin gas supply and low river water.

What NNPC says its gas pipeline network faces no constraints in delivering gas to power stations.

Who NNPC Limited, Nigeria’s state oil company; its pipeline arm is NNPC Gas Infrastructure Company (NGIC).

When Statement signed Friday, 6 November 2026 and posted Saturday, 7 November 2026.

Why it matters NNPC says other factors must be checked before the cause of the decline is clear.

What it means for you Anyone with business or travel plans in Nigeria should expect the cause of the shortfall to stay disputed for now.

Nigeria’s electricity generation has declined, and the oil company that owns the gas pipelines says they are not the cause. It wants gas suppliers, pipeline operators, power generators and the grid operator to review their data together.

NNPC says the pipelines run by NGIC, its gas infrastructure subsidiary, remain available to deliver gas to power stations nationwide without any constraints. NGIC’s operational records, it says, show no transport constraint that explains the current decline in electricity generation.

The statement was signed by Andy Odeh, NNPC’s Chief Corporate Communications Officer, in Abuja, the capital. It follows a statement by the Nigerian Independent System Operator (NISO), the body that runs the national grid, on 5 November.

What NNPC Says

NNPC says gas production, supply contracts and actual deliveries to each plant must be judged separately from whether the pipelines are open. Those factors, it says, decide whether the gas that is supplied can be turned into electricity.

The company says the review should also cover how many generating units are available, when plants are being maintained and how much gas each plant actually takes. It calls for a joint look at the data by gas suppliers, pipeline operators, power generators and NISO.

NNPC says gas production volumes grew by about 10% in 2026 to date, and that gas supply availability is therefore not a challenge. NISO, by NNPC’s account, had cited limited gas availability and reduced water inflows to hydroelectric stations.

In Plain English

NNPC is Nigeria’s state-owned oil and gas company. NGIC is its subsidiary that runs gas pipelines. NISO runs the national power grid. A generating unit is one turbine or engine inside a power station.

What Is Not Known

The statement gives no figures for gas delivered to power plants, for electricity generated or for the size of the shortfall. It does not say how much of the decline comes from gas, from low water at hydroelectric stations or from plant maintenance.

NISO’s 5 November statement is reported here as NNPC describes it. The dispute is about causes, and NNPC’s statement itself includes no plant-by-plant data that would settle it.

What It Means for You

For readers with money, family or travel plans in Nigeria, the point is that responsibility for lower power output is still being argued. NNPC says gas supply, plant readiness, maintenance and gas intake all have to be checked together.

NNPC’s call for a joint data review is the next step to watch. Until that data appears, the cause of the shortfall stays open.

For more on the company, see our reports on NNPC’s September profit, Nigeria’s plan to sell part of the state oil firm and calls to list NNPC on the stock market. More stories are in our Nigeria coverage.

Frequently Asked Questions

Is NNPC to blame for Nigeria’s lower power output?

NNPC says its pipeline network is not the cause and shows no transport constraints, and that gas supply availability is not a challenge. It says gas production, supply contracts, plant availability and maintenance must be checked too.

What is NGIC?

NGIC is NNPC Gas Infrastructure Company Limited, a subsidiary of NNPC. It operates the gas transportation network that carries gas to power stations.

Who is NISO?

NISO is the Nigerian Independent System Operator, which manages Nigeria’s power grid. NNPC says NISO’s 5 November statement cited limited gas availability and reduced water flows to hydroelectric stations.

Sources: NNPC Limited press statement “NNPC Confirms Gas Supply & Network Availability” (nnpcgroup.com, signed 6 November 2026, read 7 November 2026), which also describes the NISO statement of 5 November 2026: https://www.nnpcgroup.com/insights/press-statement-nnpc-confirms-gas-supply-and-network-availability.

World.title: Five Paths for Cuba After the US Midterms
World.content:
CUBA · POLITICS

Key Facts The bet Cuba’s next two months depend on Washington’s sanctions, Havana’s power, and whether any talks open.

What exists Five paths are plausible: tighter sanctions, Chinese pushback, quiet talks, migration stress, or force.

Congress Final control of the new Congress is not confirmed in the official sources we could reach.

Prediction markets Polymarket bets, 7 Nov: US-Cuba meeting by 30 Nov 40.5%; US strike on Cuba by 31 Dec 11.5%.

As of Saturday, 7 November 2026, 23:30 UTC; election tallies not yet certified.

Four days after the US midterm elections, Washington is tightening its pressure on Cuba, and five different futures are open for the island.

Four days after the United States voted on Tuesday, 3 November 2026, Cuba faces a choice between five paths, and the first one is already under way. The US Treasury added new targets to its Cuba sanctions on Thursday, 5 November.

For readers in the United States, this matters for travel rules, money sent home by Cuban families, and companies that sell to the island. The latest US actions point to more sanctions, but the wild cards are Beijing, Havana’s power grid and any quiet channel.

Scenario 1: Sanctions Keep Widening

The lever is Executive Order 14404, a presidential order that lets Washington sanction named sectors of Cuba’s economy, including electronics, manufacturing, marine and technology. On 5 November the Treasury’s Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC), which enforces US sanctions, listed two Cuban nationals, six companies and two ships under it.

The targets include Tecnosime and Petromarca, two Havana-based companies. On 30 September, OFAC also barred indirect financial dealings with entities on the Cuba Restricted List, a US government list of Cuban entities with which Americans face restrictions.

Watch for more additions to that list and for wider use of Title III of the Helms-Burton Act, a 1996 law that lets US nationals sue over seized property. The strongest counter-argument is trade: US goods sold to Cuba reached US$1.1 billion in the first nine months of 2026, so a total squeeze is not what the numbers show.

Our report on US exports to Cuba has the monthly figures.

Scenario 2: China Pushes Back

The 5 November update added Beijing H&C Technologies, a Chinese company, and also tagged CEIEC, a Chinese state trading company, under the Cuba programme. On Friday, 6 November, China’s Foreign Ministry spokesperson Guo Jiakun said Beijing would “take all measures necessary to resolutely protect the legitimate rights and interests of Chinese businesses.”

He called China-Cuba cooperation “completely above-board” and rejected what he called long-arm jurisdiction. He named no specific countermeasures, so the next step is a Chinese reply or a new US listing.

The counter-argument is that Beijing has so far given only words. Our report on China’s warning to the US has the full statement.

Scenario 3: A Quiet Channel Opens

The lever here is a direct meeting between US and Cuban officials, which neither government has announced. Traders on Polymarket, a prediction market, put the chance of a US-Cuba diplomatic meeting by 30 November at 40.5%, and of an economic deal by 31 December at 6.0%.

The meeting market has traded only about US$1,000, so it is thin. The case against talks is plain: Washington is adding sanctions, not relaxing them, and the White House has said nothing about a channel.

Scenario 4: Pressure Pushes More People Out

The lever is life on the island itself, where long power cuts and an economy under sanctions can push people to leave. We found no official migration figure for this month, so this path rests on logic rather than data.

The counter-argument is that departures need boats, visas or money, which many Cubans lack. Watch official migration statistics from US Customs and Border Protection and the Coast Guard.

Scenario 5: Force Enters the Picture

Polymarket puts a US strike on Cuba by 31 December at 11.5% and a full invasion in 2026 at 2.5%. Those are bets, and no US official has announced such a plan.

The counter-argument is that nothing official points that way, and the cost would be high. Our note on a US warship calling at Guantánamo covers the naval side.

What Prediction Markets Say

On Polymarket on Saturday, 7 November: US-Cuba diplomatic meeting by 30 November, 40.5%; a US strike on Cuba by 31 December, 11.5%; economic deal by 31 December, 6.0%. The strike market has traded about US$5.5 million, the meeting market about US$1,000.

Why we show this: prediction markets turn real-money bets into a live probability that moves within minutes of the news, which is why investors, campaigns and newsrooms in the United States now follow them closely. We show them next to polls and official results, never instead of them.

What Is Not Known

We could not confirm final national results at the Clerk of the House or Senate.gov, and states are still counting and certifying their totals. Control of Congress is not settled in the official sources we reached.

That matters because the embargo is written into US statute, so lifting it needs Congress, while the president can change executive orders alone. We have no verified data on how Cuban-American voters in Florida cast their ballots.

What It Means for US Readers

Travellers should know that group people-to-people trips were removed on 30 September, with a grandfather rule for trips already booked. Banks are told to block accounts of Cuban private entrepreneurs unless licensed, so check any remittance route before sending money.

Florida companies that sell food and goods to Cuba should watch the sector listings, because ties to a sanctioned entity can end a deal. The next hard signals are further OFAC updates, a Chinese reply and the certified election results.

Frequently Asked Questions

Did the US midterms change Cuba policy?

Not yet. Executive orders on Cuba can be changed by the president alone, and we could not confirm final control of Congress. Congress would matter most for the embargo laws.

What did the US Treasury do on 5 November?

OFAC added two Cuban nationals, six companies and two ships to its sanctions list under Executive Order 14404. It also updated tags on other listed parties and vessels.

Can Americans still travel to Cuba?

Some travel categories remain, but OFAC removed group people-to-people travel and professional-meeting authorisations on 30 September 2026. A grandfather rule covers groups that had booked earlier. Check OFAC’s Cuba FAQs before booking.

What do prediction markets say about Cuba?

On Polymarket, 40.5% for a US-Cuba meeting by 30 November and 11.5% for a US strike on Cuba by 31 December. These are bets, not polls.

World.title: Colombian Firms Back Brazil Before Lula Win
World.content:
BRAZIL · BUSINESS

Key Facts What happened Colombian groups Ecopetrol and GEB closed major Brazil deals in 2026, all agreed before Lula’s 25 October win.

Where Brazil’s oil fields and power-transmission grid, backed by Colombian state-linked companies.

Who Ecopetrol, Colombia’s state oil group; GEB, a Bogotá energy company; and its sister group ISA, a Colombian grid company that Ecopetrol controls.

Why it matters Ecopetrol trades in New York as EC, so its Brazil exposure reaches US portfolios.

As of Saturday, 7 November 2026, 23:30 UTC; Banco Central do Brasil rate R$5.5013 per US$1 on 6 November.

Colombian companies are deepening their bets on Brazil in oil and power lines, but the biggest deals were signed months before Lula won a fourth term.

The timing matters for the story. Company filings show the main Colombian deals were agreed or completed before the vote, and no filing links them to it.

For US readers, the link is direct. Ecopetrol, Colombia’s state-controlled oil company, trades on the New York Stock Exchange under the ticker EC, so its Brazil exposure reaches American portfolios.

What We Know

Brazil’s Superior Electoral Court, known as the TSE, says Lula received 64,256,232 votes, or 51.79% of valid votes. His rival Flávio Bolsonaro of the Liberal Party received 59,826,041 votes, or 48.21%.

Ecopetrol announced on 17 August 2026 that it had completed the purchase of about 51% of Brava Energia, a Brazilian oil and gas producer. It paid about US$1.2 billion, based on an average rate of R$5.12 per US dollar.

The stake came in two parts. A public tender offer on the B3 stock exchange in São Paulo delivered about 25%, and a share purchase agreement dated 23 April 2026 added about 26%.

Ecopetrol says Brava held proved reserves of about 459 million barrels of oil equivalent at the end of 2025. Ecopetrol also says Brava produced about 78.8 thousand barrels a day in the first half of 2026, and funded the deal through a loan from another Ecopetrol subsidiary.

Grupo Energía Bogotá, known as GEB, completed on 16 July 2026 the purchase of the remaining 49% of four Brazilian power-transmission companies. The seller was Axia Energia, a Brazilian power company, and the deal now gives GEB full ownership of lines that total 1,086 kilometres in six states.

GEB says the four companies earned an EBITDA, a measure of operating profit, of R$212 million (about US$39 million) in 2025. Brazil’s power regulator ANEEL, its competition authority CADE and the development bank BNDES gave their approvals.

On 15 May 2026, GEB and the Canadian pension investor La Caisse agreed to merge their Brazilian grid assets into a 50/50 company called Verene Energia. It would hold 26 transmission concessions, more than 9,000 kilometres of lines and operations in 17 states.

Neither partner has disclosed a price, and La Caisse says financial close is expected by the fourth quarter of 2026. We found no closing notice from either partner, so we treat the deal as agreed and its completion as unconfirmed.

ISA Energia Brasil, the Brazilian arm of Colombian grid company ISA, opened Brazil’s longest underground transmission line in São Paulo in March 2026. According to the company’s statements at the opening, the Riacho Grande project cost R$1.1 billion (about US$200 million) and was delivered ahead of its contract deadline.

Background in Plain Words

Brazil needs new power lines to carry wind and solar output to its cities. Its regulator awards transmission concessions that pay fixed, inflation-linked revenue, which is why foreign utilities like the business.

ISA is part of the Ecopetrol group, which bought the Colombian state’s majority stake in ISA in 2021. Ecopetrol’s own filings describe that purchase, so the oil company now has exposure to both Brazilian oil and Brazilian grids.

All dollar figures here use the Banco Central do Brasil rate for Friday, 6 November 2026, of R$5.5013 per US$1. Ecopetrol’s own figure uses the rate it states.

What Is Not Known

Whether Lula’s win changes any company plan has not been confirmed. We found no filing from Ecopetrol, GEB or ISA that links a new Brazilian investment to the election result.

The final price of the Verene merger is unknown. We did not find a company filing that gives it.

What It Means for US Readers

Investors holding Ecopetrol’s New York shares now own part of a business that earns reais as well as dollars. A weaker Brazilian currency lowers the dollar value of those earnings.

Colombian groups are buying in that market for the long term, and the deals above were struck at earlier prices. More coverage is on our Brazil page.

Frequently Asked Questions

Did Colombian firms invest in Brazil because Lula won?

No filing says so. Ecopetrol completed its Brava purchase on 17 August, and GEB closed its transmission purchase on 16 July, both before the 25 October runoff.

How much did Ecopetrol pay for Brava Energia?

Ecopetrol says it paid about US$1.2 billion for roughly 51% of Brava. It used an average rate of R$5.12 per US dollar.

Is the GEB and La Caisse merger finished?

We could not confirm it. The agreement was signed on 15 May 2026, and La Caisse then expected financial close by the fourth quarter of 2026.

Why should US investors care?

Ecopetrol trades on the New York Stock Exchange as EC. Its earnings now include Brazilian oil production and, through ISA, Brazilian power lines.

All read 7 November 2026.

What We Know

The US Geological Survey, the American government’s earthquake agency, recorded magnitude 4.7 at 17:17:38 UTC. It placed the epicentre at 1.85 degrees south, 81.14 degrees west, about 45 km north-north-west of the coastal town of Salinas.

The agency set no tsunami flag on the event. It lists a depth of 10 km, which it describes as a default value assigned by the operator.

Ecuador’s Geophysical Institute, the national seismology body at the Escuela Politécnica Nacional in Quito, also records earthquakes there. We could not open its bulletin, so its figures are not used here.

We could not open the bulletins of Ecuador’s navy oceanographic institute, INOCAR, which issues the country’s tsunami warnings. We therefore report only what the US survey data shows and what we found: no tsunami alert.

No damage or injuries have been reported so far. We have not seen a report from Ecuador’s risk agency on the shaking.

How Tsunami Alerts Work in Plain English

A tsunami is a series of long ocean waves, usually triggered by a large undersea earthquake that lifts or drops the seabed. Small quakes, like this one, release far too little energy to move that much water.

Ecuador sits on the Pacific “Ring of Fire”, a belt of volcanoes and earthquakes around the ocean, so strong offshore quakes are watched closely. INOCAR issues tsunami bulletins when a wave is possible.

Our earlier report on a Panama earthquake and tsunami alert shows what such an alert looks like when the threat is real. Coastal towns in Ecuador run drills so residents can reach high ground quickly.

What Is Not Known

The depth is only a default value of 10 km assigned by the US survey, so it may be revised. Official figures from Ecuador’s own agencies were not available to us.

We have not seen a damage report from the national risk agency or from coastal towns. Local checks may take time.

What It Means for US Readers

Nothing we found suggests any change for trips to the Galápagos or the mainland coast. Visitors should still know the evacuation routes posted in their hotel or town.

Travellers can follow updates from the Ecuador section of The Rio Times and from INOCAR, the Geophysical Institute and the risk agency. Earthquakes of this size are common worldwide, and one moderate event does not by itself signal a larger one.

Frequently Asked Questions

Was there a tsunami warning in Ecuador?

We found no tsunami alert for Ecuador. The US Geological Survey set no tsunami flag on the event.

How strong was the earthquake?

The US Geological Survey measured magnitude 4.7 at 17:17 UTC on Saturday, 7 November 2026, which is 12:17 in Ecuador.

Is it safe to travel to the Galápagos or the coast?

We found no warning that says otherwise. Check INOCAR and the national risk agency, the SGR, for current notices before you travel.

How do tsunami alerts work in Ecuador?

INOCAR, the navy institute that issues the warnings, publishes bulletins when a tsunami is possible. Coastal residents follow evacuation signs and officials’ instructions.

Sources: US Geological Survey, event us7000twt8 (https://earthquake.usgs.gov/earthquakes/eventpage/us7000twt8, read 7 November 2026); Instituto Oceanográfico y Antártico de la Armada, INOCAR (https://www.inocar.mil.ec); Instituto Geofísico, Escuela Politécnica Nacional (https://www.igepn.edu.ec); Servicio Nacional de Gestión de Riesgos y Emergencias (https://www.gestionderiesgos.gob.ec).

World.title: What to Do in Salvador in November 2026
World.content:
SALVADOR · Culture

Salvador’s November is anchored by Simone, Guilherme Arantes and a Tarsila musical at Teatro Castro Alves. Here is what is confirmed from 8 November, with prices in US$.

Colonial rooftops in Salvador’s historic centre, the old district known as Pelourinho. File photo.

SALVADOR — This is the November culture guide for expats, digital nomads and long-stay visitors in Salvador, the capital of Bahia state on Brazil’s north-east coast. It covers things to do in Salvador in November 2026 with dates, venues and prices converted to US$.

Most of the month’s headline dates sit at Teatro Castro Alves (TCA), the state-run theatre complex in the Campo Grande district. Its main hall is currently in what the theatre calls an “Operação Teste” phase, a test period in the reopening after the renovation works known as Novo TCA.

We list only events we could confirm on an organiser, venue or ticket page. Several listings that appeared earlier in the month either took place before 8 November or could not be confirmed, so they are not here.

Rio Times membership Read everything we publish for US$1 in the first month. Then US$8.99 a month. Cancel anytime. Start for US$1

Prices are in reais (R$) and converted at about R$5.50 per US$1 (the RT rate of 7 November 2026 was 5.4959), so treat the dollar figures as rounded guides.

8 to 14 November: Luiz Caldas and Simone

Sunday 8 November, 20:00 Luiz Caldas Acústico Teatro Castro Alves, Sala Principal, Campo Grande · R$90 to R$200 (about US$16 to US$36) · Sympla, a Brazilian online ticket platform, and the TCA box office Caldas, the guitarist often credited with launching Bahia’s axé music, plays a stripped-back acoustic set that revisits his career. The 17:00 session sold out earlier, so the 20:00 show is an extra date, and the show is rated for ages 12 and over.

Saturday 14 November, 20:00 Simone: Que Mulher É Essa? Teatro Castro Alves, Sala Principal · Rows B to P: R$340 full price (about US$62), R$170 half price (about US$31) · Sympla and TCA box office Simone, one of Brazil’s best-known popular singers, brings the tour marking her 50 years of career. Seats in rows B to P cost R$340 full price (about US$62) and R$170 half price (about US$31). We could not confirm prices for the other rows.

Half-price tickets require proof of eligibility under Brazilian federal, state and municipal law, such as student or senior status. Foreign visitors should check the theatre’s rules before counting on the discount.

15 to 22 November: Holidays and Bahia Folk Ballet

Sunday 15 November is the Proclamation of the Republic holiday, and Friday 20 November is Black Consciousness Day, a national holiday in Brazil. Banks, public offices and many shops close on both dates, though restaurants and cultural venues often stay open.

Saturday 21 and Sunday 22 November O Balé Que Você Não Vê Teatro Castro Alves, Sala Principal · Prices not confirmed · Sympla and TCA box office The Balé Folclórico da Bahia, a Salvador dance company known for Afro-Brazilian folklore, returns to the TCA with this show on the weekend of 21 and 22 November. We could not confirm session times or prices, so check the theatre’s page before you go.

26 to 29 November: Tarsila and a Song Festival

Thursday 26 to Sunday 29 November Tarsila, a Brasileira Teatro Castro Alves, Sala Principal · Price not published in sources we checked · Sympla and TCA box office This musical tells the story of Tarsila do Amaral, the painter often seen as the face of Brazilian modernism. Sessions run at 20:00 on Thursday 26 and Friday 27 November, at 15:00 and 20:00 on Saturday 28 November, and at 18:00 on Sunday 29 November.

Friday 27 November, 19:00 Guilherme Arantes: 50 Anos-Luz Concha Acústica, the theatre’s open-air amphitheatre · R$80 to R$180 (about US$15 to US$33) · TCA box office and Sympla Arantes is a veteran Brazilian singer-songwriter, and this is his 50-years tour. The first ticket batch was R$160 full price (about US$29) and R$80 half price (about US$15), while the second batch is R$180 (about US$33) and R$90 (about US$16).

Sunday 29 November, 18:30 24th Festival de Música Educadora FM Concha Acústica, Teatro Castro Alves · R$25 to R$50 (about US$5 to US$9) · TCA box office and Sympla The festival is a songwriting competition run by the Bahia state broadcaster’s Educadora FM radio station, with a prize pool of R$530,000 (about US$96,000). Tickets cost R$50 full price (about US$9), R$25 half price (about US$5) and R$30 for the social ticket (about US$5.50).

Planning Your Salvador November

The Concha Acústica is an open-air amphitheatre with free seating, so arrive early for a good spot. Access is only through the lower entrance on Ladeira da Fonte, gates open two hours before the show, and bottles, helmets, umbrellas and swimwear are not allowed.

Salvador is tropical and warm in November, so pack light clothes and something for an occasional shower. Taxis and ride-hailing apps are the simplest way home after evening events in Campo Grande or the historic Pelourinho district.

Ticket sales run through Sympla and the TCA box offices at the Campo Grande entrance and the lower entrance of the Concha Acústica. The theatre warns that it takes no responsibility for tickets bought from resellers.

What It Means for You

For a reader in the United States, the practical lesson is cost and timing. A seat for Simone in rows B to P is about US$62, and holidays on 15 and 20 November can make a long weekend trip easy to plan.

Check each organiser page close to the date, because Brazilian venues often release extra sessions, as Luiz Caldas did, or change batches and prices. Note too that several events here run in Portuguese or rely on local references, so the music and dance shows suit visitors with little language comfort best.

We could not confirm prices for Tarsila, a Brasileira or O Balé Que Você Não Vê. For more of Brazil, see our guides for Rio, São Paulo and Recife.

Frequently Asked Questions

What are the biggest events in Salvador in November 2026?

Simone on 14 November, Guilherme Arantes on 27 November and the musical Tarsila, a Brasileira from 26 to 29 November are the main dates.

Which public holidays fall in Salvador after 8 November 2026?

Proclamation of the Republic falls on Sunday 15 November and Black Consciousness Day on Friday 20 November. Both are national holidays in Brazil.

How do I buy tickets for events in Salvador?

Most events in this guide are sold through Sympla and, for Teatro Castro Alves shows, at the theatre’s box offices. Check the event page for current batches and prices.

How much is a ticket for Simone at Teatro Castro Alves?

Seats in rows B to P cost R$340 full price (about US$62) and R$170 half price (about US$31). Half price needs proof of eligibility, and we could not confirm other rows.

What is the Concha Acústica?

It is an open-air amphitheatre run by Teatro Castro Alves in Salvador. Entry is through the lower entrance on Ladeira da Fonte, and gates open two hours before shows.

GABORONE · Culture

Gaborone’s November runs from a free photography show to a black-tie charity dinner on 28 November. This guide covers what is left of the month, day by day, with prices in pula and US dollars.
