World.title: Kazakhstan’s Cities Are Growing. Are Their Economies Keeping Pace?
World.content:
ASTANA — Kazakhstan’s accelerating urbanization is concentrating population growth in its largest cities, while smaller urban centers struggle to retain residents and attract investment. Experts say the challenge is to ensure that expanding cities create productive jobs and accessible public services rather than simply accommodate more people.

“Urbanization is taking place in every country, but in Kazakhstan it is happening at an accelerated pace. Astana and Almaty remain the main centers of attraction, as our experts have noted. (…) But urbanization is inevitable, and we must prepare for it,” said Zhuldyzai Iskakova, chairperson of the Kazakhstan Institute of Public Development (KIPD).

Iskakova spoke at a Nov. 6 meeting of the SARAP expert club, organized by KIPD, which brought together lawmakers, economists and urban planning specialists to examine urban growth following President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev’s State of the Nation Address and plans for nationwide infrastructure development.

Population growth and the economic divide

The growing concentration of Kazakhstan’s population in its largest cities is reflected in figures presented by Nurbolat Kurmetuly, director of the Center for Regional Studies and Quality of Life at the Economic Research Institute.

According to his findings, the combined population of Astana, Almaty and Shymkent increased by 721,800 between 2021 and 2025, including a positive net internal migration balance of 417,800 people. Astana alone recorded a positive net interregional migration balance of 87,500 in 2025, compared with a negative balance of 2,500 in 2015.

Shynar Tuleshova, head of the Demographic Research Department at the Center for Analysis and Forecasting of Demographic Processes under Kazakhstan’s Agency for Strategic Planning and Reforms, noted that migration to Astana currently exceeds that to Almaty, with approximately 100,000 newcomers registering in the capital annually.

“However, when we talk about migration, a person does not necessarily register as a city resident immediately after moving. Some register five or even 10 years later, while others continue living without registration. We can only see registered residents in official statistics, not those who remain unregistered,” she said.

Tuleshova added that migration to the Almaty Region has increased over the past two years, reflecting the metropolitan area’s expansion into surrounding settlements.

Population growth is also transforming surrounding settlements. In the Astana metropolitan area, the rural population of the suburban zone increased from 121,900 to 181,500 over five years, while employment remained concentrated in the capital. Kurmetuly noted a similar pattern around Shymkent, where employment increased primarily in the city itself and declined in some neighboring territories.

“In other words, cities are expanding outward rather than developing in depth. Population and housing are growing, but jobs, transport and social infrastructure are not keeping pace,” said Kurmetuly.

The geographical concentration of investment presents another challenge. According to Kurmetuly, more than 55% of Kazakhstan’s fixed assets are concentrated in the Atyrau Region, Astana and Almaty, while the southern macroregion, home to more than 30% of the country’s labor resources, accounts for less than 9%.

In 2025, approximately 1.29 trillion tenge (US$2.87 billion) was directed toward real estate activities in cities of regional significance, compared with 1.10 trillion tenge (US$2.4 billion) in manufacturing.

“Housing construction is necessary, but it produces a quick, one-time effect. Sustainable income for cities comes from industries and services that sell their products beyond the local market, including manufacturing, engineering, logistics, IT and technical services. These are the sectors that create quality jobs,” said Kurmetuly.

“Astana, Almaty and Shymkent are our national engines. There is no need to restrain their growth. But a country the size of Kazakhstan cannot depend on just three cities. We need a network of strong regional centers,” he said.

Can smaller cities become centers of growth?

Kurultai deputy Yulia Kuchinskaya, a member of the Committee on International Affairs, Defense and Security, also emphasized the need to strengthen alternatives to Kazakhstan’s largest cities.

Kuchinskaya noted that the country’s 90 cities should be assessed according to their ability to create employment, attract residents and provide conditions for long-term economic development.

“Large-scale construction is a very good project, and a very important one. It can give an impetus to economic development, but we must all understand that construction will eventually end. What happens after construction? Where will people work, what will they do, and what will happen to the economy?” she said.

She also noted that infrastructure improvements do not necessarily prevent rural depopulation, and residents who want to relocate may face financial barriers, including difficulty selling their homes.

“There are many villages in Kazakhstan, at least in the northern regions, where all the infrastructure is in place. There are roads, water and lighting, but there are no people. New residents are not moving there,” she said.

This challenge also showed up in Kurmetuly’s findings. He noted that several regional capitals continue to lose residents despite their administrative status, with Semei’s population declining by 7.2% over five years.

To retain residents, he emphasized the need for economic specialization, permanent employment and stronger links with surrounding rural communities, including agricultural processing and logistics.

Human capital and regional competitiveness

According to Kurmetuly, Kazakhstan has approximately 670,000 students, more than half of whom study away from their home cities or regions. Three-quarters of doctoral students are concentrated in Almaty and Astana.

The distribution of educational opportunities also influences migration, as students who move to larger cities often remain after graduation to pursue careers and establish families.

“Moving away to study often becomes a permanent move. A person earns a degree, finds a job, starts a family and does not return. That is why human capital is not simply a social characteristic of a city,” said Kurmetuly.

“What matters is not how much money was invested, but how many permanent jobs were created with wages above the regional average. (…) Link education to the local economy. And track a simple indicator: how many graduates are working in their home region three years later,” he said.

Rethinking urban planning and mobility

Experts also examined how existing cities can manage growth through changes in urban planning.

Nurkozha Yersaiyn, senior urbanist at the Astana Urbanism Center, presented polycentric development as a way to reduce congestion and improve access to essential services.

“Polycentrism means that a city does not have a single center. It is a multicentered city, where all districts develop at the same pace. To put it more simply, everyone should have a recreational space within walking distance of their home,” he said.

Yersaiyn noted that placing commercial facilities and employment opportunities closer to residential neighborhoods could reduce the need for residents to travel across cities for everyday activities.

“Widening roads or increasing parking spaces will never solve traffic congestion. We can see this in the southern states of the United States. Building major highways will never solve congestion; on the contrary, they make cities less comfortable for people,” said Yersaiyn.

According to the principles used by the Astana Urbanism Center, every public space should offer at least seven reasons for people to visit, accommodating different groups and activities. Even a small park should serve older residents, children, couples and other visitors rather than a single recreational purpose.

“We want to live in a comfortable city. The needs of people with limited mobility are particularly important. This includes mothers with strollers and people with mobility impairments. If these groups are comfortable, the city becomes comfortable for everyone,” he added.

Public expectations also extend to existing infrastructure. According to KIPD’s third-quarter 2026 survey, satisfaction with road quality increased from 40% in 2022 to 57.8% in 2026. However, the institute’s 2024 research found that 46.2% of respondents identified environmental concerns as a priority, while 36.3% viewed dense urban development negatively.

According to Iskakova, such findings could help authorities prioritize infrastructure projects based on residents’ needs, particularly as the country prepares for further construction. The broader question is how to ensure that infrastructure investment generates lasting economic opportunities across the country.

World.title: ‘We didn’t even get chance to ask’ – Georgia’s new gambling law takes Patriarchate by surprise
World.content:
The head of the Georgian Patriarchate’s public relations service, Archpriest Andria Jagmaidze, says the Patriarchate was caught by surprise when parliament fast-tracked amendments to the law on gambling. According to him, the process moved so quickly that Patriarchate representatives had no opportunity to examine the draft law in detail or ask questions.

“Events moved so quickly that we didn’t even get a chance to ask anything,” Jagmaidze said.

He said the Patriarchate plans to look into the matter more closely and discuss it with the authorities. The archpriest explained that the Patriarch was in western Georgia while parliament considered the bill, which meant the Patriarchate could not properly engage in the process.

Jagmaidze expressed particular concern about the state of gambling in the country. He believes the authorities and the Patriarchate should discuss ways to reduce the harm caused by the industry.

“The current situation with gambling is already alarming. It would be good to discuss with the authorities how to reduce the harm gambling causes to the population. We need to talk about setting up and funding rehabilitation centres. Gambling addiction is a condition that requires psychological support,” he said.

In the archpriest’s view, the authorities should also discuss the minimum age for players and how they enforce existing regulations. He added that previous efforts to introduce regulations aimed at reducing harm had taken around four years and involved a working group from the Patriarchate.

“It took us around four years to introduce regulations aimed at reducing harm. A working group from the Patriarchate took part in the process. But parliament passed this new law in just two days last week. So there are a great many questions,” Jagmaidze stressed.

What the amendments involve

Georgia’s parliament approved a package of amendments to the law on gambling on 28 October 2026. The changes allow international casinos to organise international gambling tournaments.

Under the draft law, an international gambling tournament is a competition in which at least 80% of participants hold foreign citizenship.

The amendments exempt casinos from paying gambling business tax on a club table if they use it exclusively for an international gambling tournament with a prize pool exceeding 3 million lari (around $1 million). Organisers can still earn revenue from hosting the tournament. They can hold these competitions either inside casino premises or elsewhere.

Georgia’s Prime Minister Irakli Kobakhidze responded to questions from Patriarchate representatives about the bill. He said the amendment was not significant and did not warrant a broad public debate.

According to Kobakhidze, the changes concern a specific type of international tournament, including poker competitions broadcast on international sports channels. He explained that the amendment simply introduces a specific tax framework for such tournaments and does not fundamentally change the existing rules.

“There was no need for a broad discussion on this issue at all. For example, I myself knew nothing about it. That shows how insignificant the amendment is in substance,” Kobakhidze said.

He claimed he only learned about the bill after parliament had already introduced it.

World.title: Russia signals new opportunities for closer ties with Georgia
World.content:
Russian Foreign Ministry spokeswoman Maria Zakharova said Moscow was ready to support initiatives aimed at deepening cooperation between Russia and Georgia.

She also briefly expressed her wish to see a fully fledged Russian embassy in Tbilisi. At present, because the two countries have no diplomatic relations, the Russian Interests Section at the Swiss Embassy performs this role.

At a press conference, journalists asked Zakharova about the activities and initiatives of the Foundation for Russian-Georgian Unity, established by businessman Mamuka Pipia. She replied that she viewed positively all initiatives aimed at developing bilateral cooperation in education, culture and humanitarian affairs, involving representatives of civil society, academic and cultural circles.

Maria Zakharova

“We believe that the new foundation’s activities will make a significant contribution to further strengthening ties between the peoples of the Russian Federation and Georgia. We are ready to examine the specific projects the foundation plans to undertake and consider providing any necessary assistance.

“We are open to this. You can contact us or our… We would, of course, like to say embassies, but unfortunately we have to say interests sections,” Zakharova said.

Who is Mamuka Pipia?

Mamuka Pipia is a businessman with dual Georgian and Russian citizenship and one of the leaders of Solidarity for Peace, a pro-Russian, Putinist political party. He is publicly known for supporting Kremlin policies and justifying Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine.

Pipia’s name also came up in the case involving Otar Partskhaladze, Georgia’s former prosecutor general, who faces US sanctions. Pipia appeared as a defence witness in the case and publicly confirmed his links to Partskhaladze.

Pipia recently posted a video on social media showing him training on a Russian tank while wearing a Russian military uniform. In a statement accompanying the video, he said he stood ready to take part in Russia’s war if necessary.

Maria Zakharova and Georgia

Maria Zakharova is the official spokesperson for Russia’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs. She regularly sets out Moscow’s foreign policy positions, including on relations with Georgia.

Her statements on Georgia mainly focus on the need to normalise relations, expand economic and humanitarian ties, and justify Russia’s position on the 2008 war.

Georgia severed diplomatic relations with Russia on 2 September 2008, following the August war. The decision came after Russia recognised the independence of Abkhazia and the Tskhinvali region (South Ossetia) and occupied Georgian territories. Since the break in diplomatic relations, Russia and Georgia have each maintained an interests section at the Swiss embassy in the other country.

Zakharova has repeatedly called for the restoration of diplomatic relations with Georgia. In June 2024, she said Moscow supported efforts to normalise Russian-Georgian relations and stood ready to respond to initiatives from Tbilisi in that direction. Around the same time, she welcomed a call by Georgia’s pro-Russian Solidarity for Peace party to restore diplomatic relations.

In October 2024, Zakharova described statements by Georgian officials about the possibility of apologising to the people of South Ossetia for the 2008 war as an encouraging signal for Moscow. However, she also demanded concrete steps from Georgia, including the signing of a legally binding agreement on the non-use of force.

In April 2025, Zakharova reiterated that Russia stood ready to restore relations with Georgia and faced ‘no restrictions’ in this process. At the same time, she linked closer ties to a change in Georgia’s approach to Abkhazia and the Tskhinvali region.

In June 2026, Zakharova said Russia stood ready to expand relations with Georgia, but stressed that the process required steps from both sides. She also welcomed the ‘pragmatic policy’ pursued by the Georgian authorities and highlighted trade, transport, tourism and humanitarian ties.

However, Moscow’s position on Georgia’s territorial integrity remains unchanged in Zakharova’s statements. Russia recognises Abkhazia and the Tskhinvali region as independent states, while Tbilisi regards this as Russia’s occupation of Georgian territory.

On Russia’s rapprochement with Georgia

World.title: Armenia takes a step closer to EU with launch of biometric passport system
World.content:
Introduction of biometric passports in Armenia

Armenia launched a new system for issuing biometric passports on 1 November. The system fully complies with international standards. The Armenian authorities say its introduction marks the most significant reform under the country’s visa liberalisation process with the European Union.

Marta Kos, the European Commissioner for Enlargement, wrote on Facebook that the new passports would make border crossings easier for travellers. She also stressed that Armenian citizens had moved one step closer to visa-free travel to EU countries.

“Armenia is choosing closer ties with Europe, and we are working to make this choice benefit its citizens,” Kos said.

The private company HayPass will provide the new services. The relevant government agencies assure citizens that this partnership will deliver high-quality services and secure, reliable documents.

The new system has moved the entire document application process from paper to digital format. Applicants can submit their applications and complete preliminary registration online. They then receive a QR code by email and must visit a service centre at their appointed time to verify their documents and personal details.

At the centre, staff take photographs and fingerprints and record signature samples. Applicants can collect their biometric passports from the same centre 14 days later.

The biometric passport will remain valid for 10 years and cost 28,650 drams ($80). The government plans to introduce discounts for certain social groups, although it has yet to specify how much of the cost it will cover.

The authorities do not require citizens to replace their existing passports with biometric ones. People can continue using their current passports until they expire.

Which other documents will become biometric?

The Interior Ministry has announced that several other types of documents will also become biometric, in addition to passports:

Identity cards (IDs);

Diplomatic passports;

Residence permits;

Identity cards and passports for stateless persons;

Identity cards and travel documents issued to refugees under international conventions.

The risk of document forgery will be minimal

The Interior Ministry says the introduction of the biometric passport system will help address several issues at once. These include:

Ensuring reliable identity verification;

Reducing the risk of document forgery or the use of another person’s personal data.

Nelly Davtyan, head of the Migration and Citizenship Service, says the new system will minimise the risk of forgery at every stage, from data processing at service centres to the production of the actual document:

“The previous system depended entirely on human factors. As a result, during the preparatory stage, we identified numerous inaccuracies in the State Population Register.”

Davtyan believes a biometric passport is more than just an identity document. It also provides an important safeguard for a person’s legal rights:

“The particular value of the new system lies in the fact that international standards guarantee the establishment, identification and mutual recognition of a person’s legal status worldwide. This is not simply our assessment. We built the entire system in strict compliance with these standards.”

Gold-number passports to go on sale at auction

Armenia also plans to introduce a scheme offering “special” passport numbers, known as “gold numbers”. Some of these will go on sale at auction.

“We will launch the programme next year using two approaches. Passports with repeating digits will cost more, while numbers with ‘special’ combinations will go on sale at auction,” Nelly Davtyan said.

Faster service at HayPass offices: 3–5 minutes instead of 25

HayPass received 7,700 applications within just a few days. Some 2,700 people have already visited the company’s offices and completed the first stage of the process by submitting their biometric data.

According to Nelly Davtyan, head of the Migration and Citizenship Service, the previous document application process took 25 minutes. The new system allows applicants to complete registration in just 3–5 minutes:

“For all 2,700 citizens who have already used the service, data processing took no more than five minutes.”

Staff from the Migration and Citizenship Service have also visited regional branches. They say these offices are operating normally and have no queues either.

“This does not mean that we are providing fewer services. It means that we can now handle a much higher volume of applications,” Davtyan stressed.

Company has already invested €20 million

Interior Minister Arpine Sargsyan said the private partner, HayPass, had already invested €20 million in the project and continued to invest in it. She also stressed that citizens pay the private company 28,650 drams for a biometric passport and 5,950 drams for the accompanying identity card. These payments cover the company’s services. The state, she said, makes no profit from them.

The minister also rejected claims that the company receives payments for its services from both the state budget and citizens.

“We do not pay HayPass any money. Nothing has been paid from the state budget,” she assured.

HayPass operates 14 offices across the country

On 1 November, the first day of biometric data collection, HayPass opened service centres in two Yerevan shopping malls: Yerevan Mall and Mega Mall. Twelve regional branches began operating the following day.

Interior Minister Arpine Sargsyan said the government plans to increase the number of service centres to 23 by March 2027.

“Overall, we will have two branches in each region,” the minister said.

Introduction of biometric passports in Armenia

World.title: Divorce rates are rising in Armenia: divorced women and experts explain why
World.content:
Divorce in Armenia: women share their stories

For some, divorce means a painful separation; for others, it is a happy “liberation” from each other. Either way, former spouses remain part of each other’s lives, albeit in a different capacity.

For some, divorce marks the beginning of a new life. For others, it leads to a prolonged struggle, with endless disputes over issues such as property division and access to their children. Mutual accusations often accompany the process.

In Armenia, divorce can also spark heated public debate. This can be a real ordeal, particularly for women.

Women who have divorced told JAMnews why they decided to end their relationships. Experts offered their explanations for the rise in divorce rates in recent years.

“When you realise nothing can be saved”

Juliette Babayan is 38. She separated from her husband after 15 years together and has been raising their two sons on her own for the past two years. She says divorce had always seemed like a last resort:

“When I got married, I could never have imagined that one day I would have to make such a decision. But when a relationship reaches a dead end, there is no other way out. My children were no longer very young at the time. When we divorced, one was 12 and the other 14. They had seen our arguments and the tension between us. Then one day I realised it was better for them to see us apart, living separately but happy, rather than together and miserable.”

She felt that people around her did not understand how difficult it was to decide to divorce:

“But that is not how it works. You do not decide to separate in a minute. You think about it for a long time and give each other another chance. But when you realise there is no other way out and nothing left to save, you eventually reach that decision. Everything good has a beginning and an end. Once you come to terms with that, separation becomes easier to bear.”

She explains that women face both practical and psychological challenges after divorce. She notes that many women in Armenia face hostility from their former husbands and their families, who accuse them of “breaking up the family”.

She is happy with her relationship with her ex-husband. He provides financial support, pays child maintenance and often spends time with their children.

“I believe both parents have equal rights, both during a relationship and after it ends. I respect my children’s father and stay in touch with him. It is very important to me that the children feel both parents are present in their lives and take part in them. I want to make sure they never feel they have no mother or no father, even if we no longer live together,” Juliette says.

“I got married for life”

Araksi Poghosyan is 40. She married at 23 and separated from her husband after 11 years of marriage. She says it is impossible to explain in a few words why they divorced. But after thinking for a moment, she adds: “We no longer loved each other.”

She insists that they tried to save their marriage and decided to divorce only when they realised there was no other way:

“People talk about divorce more than ever now, especially on social media. Many think it is easy to make such a decision. But it isn’t. I belong to a generation that married believing it was ‘for life, until death do us part’. It was very difficult for me to accept that reality had turned out differently and that I needed to get divorced. It took me around three years to reach that decision. I worked with a psychologist and tried to get back on my feet financially because I was leaving with my son, who was seven at the time. I had no idea what would happen next or how I would manage.”

She explains that women face both practical and psychological challenges after divorce. She notes that many women in Armenia face hostility from their former husbands and their families, who accuse them of “breaking up the family”.

It is very important to me that the children feel both parents are present in their lives and take part in them. I want to make sure they never feel they have no mother or no father, even if we no longer live together,” Juliette says.

I belong to a generation that married believing it was ‘for life, until death do us part’. It was very difficult for me to accept that reality had turned out differently and that I needed to get divorced. It took me around three years to reach that decision. I worked with a psychologist and tried to get back on my feet financially because I was leaving with my son, who was seven at the time. I had no idea what would happen next or how I would manage.”

Statistics and reasons

According to official statistics, the number of marriages in Armenia has fallen in recent years, while the number of divorces has risen:

2022 – 16,795 marriages and 4,525 divorces (26.9%)

2023 – 16,330 marriages and 4,525 divorces (27.5%)

2024 – 15,324 marriages and 4,689 divorces (30.5%)

2025 – 13,821 marriages and 4,881 divorces (35.3%)

Domestic violence, infidelity, financial difficulties and everyday problems are commonly cited as reasons for divorce.

“In the past, couples who had been married for many years tended to divorce. Now, even those who have been married for just three or four years are splitting up. The main reasons for divorce are arguments, accounting for 50%; incompatibility, 14%; and going abroad for work, 8%,” says Tsovinar Harutyunyan, a development and demography expert who has held senior positions at the United Nations Population Fund (UNFPA).

However, some psychologists say these factors have taken a back seat in recent years.

Family psychologist Naira Kharatyan says most of her female clients cite their husbands’ indifference as the reason for seeking a divorce. She believes women marry for love, but men become less attentive as the years go by:

“Women mostly say they feel neglected and that their partners have become indifferent towards them. Marriage is not just about everyday life and money; it is also about emotions and psychological connection. Women want to feel heard and understood.

“The second reason I would highlight is unmet expectations. Women have certain expectations of marriage, and when these are not fulfilled, they become disappointed. Another factor is unspoken competition within the couple. When a woman earns more or holds a higher position, a man may feel jealous. As a result, they stop acting as a couple and become unspoken rivals, each waiting to see who will win.”

Arus, 37 (not her real name, at her request), says that nowadays women “do not marry for money”.

In her words, “women marry for love and divorce because it is no longer there”. This is what happened to her. Arus left her husband after 13 years of marriage, taking their two children with her.

“My husband subjected me to psychological abuse. He put pressure on me and humiliated me. In the last few years, he did not earn any money. I was the only one working. But he told me I was worthless and that nobody wanted me. He told the children I was a bad mother. He said I could not even cook a decent meal. He did not feel like a proper man and wanted to crush me and humiliate me too. When I stood up to him, he threatened to beat me and take the children away,” she says.

While preparing this article, we spoke to many women who had experienced physical and psychological abuse. But all of them, like Arus, refused to speak on camera. They explained that they feared their former husbands might start harassing them.

“It took everything I had to get away from my husband. I am finally living in peace. Now, if he sees me on screen talking about him, he will turn up again and demand answers,” Arus says.

She adds that her former husband provides no support. She does not need financial help from him and wants no further contact with him.

“On my way home from work, I would pick up the children from nursery and school, get home and make dinner. He would come home in the evening, throw his lunch in the bin or spit into it. He would say it was inedible and that I had never learned how to run a household,” Arus says through tears.

The mother-in-law factor

Psychologist Naira Kharatyan argues that mothers can also contribute to the breakdown of their sons’ marriages:

“When sons remain overly attached to their mothers from childhood, they struggle to build strong families of their own. They have wives, but they listen to their mothers and follow their advice. Mothers encourage this dynamic without realising that they are creating a problem. As a result, the woman and the man never truly become a couple. A mother should tell her son: you are married now, and you must make decisions together with your wife. But in many cases, we see men whose wives were chosen for them, whose marriages their families arranged, and whose mothers then interfered in raising their children. The man never grew up.”

She says the “mother-son-daughter-in-law triangle can lead to tragic consequences”. Even when young couples do not live with their parents, the bond can remain so strong that the man still struggles to establish an independent family life.

Psychologist Mariam Manukyan also believes that marriage is more than a union between two people. She notes that the institution of marriage has acquired new dimensions and meanings over the centuries:

“It is a relationship in which two different people’s habits and ideas about life come together. When people enter a relationship, they begin to go through different stages. At the first stage, for example, a couple learns to share everyday responsibilities. At the second stage, after the birth of a child, they become parents and learn how to raise a child. This can also trigger a crisis and become a challenge for young couples. Relationships go through many such stages and crises. When couples fail to resolve them and the problems deepen, they separate because divorce becomes the only possible solution.”

At the same time, divorce brings new problems for many people. Couples struggle to agree on the terms of separation, while disputes arise over child custody, maintenance payments and the division of property.

“I divorced four years ago, and in all that time I have probably spent just four hours having proper conversations with my children. After the divorce, their father decided that they should stay with him. He wanted to punish me, and he succeeded. The court awarded him custody. We spent four years fighting in court. Eventually, the guardianship authority, which decides which parent the children should live with, concluded that staying with their father was in their best interests.

“My former husband’s close relatives work on that council, and its head is one of his friends. They knew what kind of mother I was and how attentive I had always been to my children, but… For four years, I collected documents to prove that I was a good mother so that my children could live with me. But no one cared about the children’s interests. They cared about my former husband’s interests,” says Susanna (not her real name, at her request).

All the women we interviewed on this subject agree on one thing: divorce does not always end on the day two people decide to stop living together. They also say that society often judges divorced women without considering what led them to make that decision.

“It is easier to talk about the importance of keeping a family together than to consider what it takes to achieve that. A family is not simply people living under one roof. It is also an environment where a child learns what love means, how people treat each other, what women and men deserve, and whether it is possible to live without fear,” one divorced woman says.

Divorce in Armenia: women share their stories

World.title: ‘The purge has only just begun’? South Ossetia’s new authorities arrest ‘chief baker’
World.content:
The authorities in South Ossetia have placed Vadim Tskhovrebov, the long-serving director of the local bread factory, under house arrest for two months, from 31 October to 29 December. They have opened a criminal case against him on charges of abuse of office.

This is no routine arrest. It forms part of a sweeping purge, one of the key campaign promises made by the new president, Marat Kambolov.

A hotel at the bread factory

According to investigators, Tskhovrebov appropriated a plot of land on the bread factory’s premises, leased it to his wife at a below-market rate and built a hotel, a billiards room and commercial premises there.

Some Telegram channels have also alleged that Tskhovrebov installed cryptocurrency mining equipment on the factory grounds, while the state budget covered the huge electricity bills.

In addition, unofficial reports suggest that the company owes millions in unpaid taxes, which may simply have been written off.

Alina Chochieva, deputy prosecutor of Tskhinval, explained that the General Prosecutor’s Office had requested Tskhovrebov’s house arrest. His defence team tried to persuade the court to impose a travel ban instead, citing a positive reference from his workplace and numerous awards recognising his contribution to the development of South Ossetia.

Tskhovrebov himself fully accepts both the charges against him and the restrictive measure.

“I admit my guilt and am ready to compensate the damage in full as soon as the investigation determines the final amount,” South Ossetia’s “chief baker” said.

An enterprising bun

For many years, Vadim Tskhovrebov, whom Tskhinval residents affectionately nicknamed “Bun”, was actively involved in politics and even served as a member of parliament. But he took the greatest pride in keeping production running during the August 2008 war. The factory never stopped operating, not even for a day, and continued supplying bread to residents of the South Ossetian capital.

Vadim Tskhovrebov

“Bun” took over as head of the bread factory around 20 years ago.

Over the years, he survived two assassination attempts and efforts to seize his business. He secured state funding and expanded production, while gradually raising the price of his products.

During Tskhovrebov’s time in his “bread kingdom”, South Ossetia went through five presidential administrations. “Bun” managed to get along with every one of them.

Many people now believe that previous presidents may have turned a blind eye to abuses of office in exchange for certain financial arrangements.

It seems, however, that he failed to strike a deal with Marat Kambolov.

Gaps in the logic

However, some JAMnews sources in Tskhinval question the logic behind the new authorities’ actions.

“How does this make sense? The director of the bread factory has been arrested, while his former boss, Atsamaz Kabisov, has actually been promoted to deputy prime minister in the new government, despite long-standing suspicions that he too abused his office,” one of our sources said.

Atsamaz Kabisov previously headed the Committee for Industry, Transport and Energy, which oversees the bread factory.

Local bloggers report that South Ossetia’s debt to Russia for gas and electricity had already exceeded 1 billion roubles [around $12 million] in 2024 and has not fallen since. One of the main reasons is losses in the power grid, which Russian specialists estimate at 40–50%. Unofficial sources link these losses to illegal cryptocurrency mining operations. Kabisov, who oversees electricity consumption records, may have provided protection for these mining farms.

Has the purge only just begun?

Nevertheless, Tskhovrebov’s arrest fits the purge of corrupt officials and those accused of misappropriating public funds that Marat Kambolov announced. “Bun” is not the first person to face scrutiny. Criminal cases have already been opened against several businessmen from the inner circle of former president Alan Gagloev and former prime minister Konstantin Dzhussoev.

One of them is Oleg Bosikov, a close relative of Dzhussoev and CEO of the construction company Megapolis-T. Investigators allege that the company served as a money-laundering operation through which hundreds of millions of roubles from Russia were siphoned off. The money came under an investment programme for South Ossetia’s socio-economic development.

The General Prosecutor’s Office has also turned its attention to former Interior Minister Erislav Mamiev and his first deputy, Atsamaz Sagkaev. Investigators say Sagkaev illegally registered two service firearms in his superior Mamiev’s name.

World.title: Erdogan to visit Baku after hijab dispute: what concessions has Ankara made, and what does Baku want?
World.content:
Turkey–Azerbaijan relations

Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan told journalists on 5 November that he planned to visit Azerbaijan on 8 November, Victory Day, provided no extraordinary circumstances arose. He also said he had spoken by phone with President Ilham Aliyev and sent Turkey’s intelligence chief and foreign minister to Baku.

“The unbreakable ties between our countries rest on a shared history, culture and destiny – and, God willing, a shared future.”

However, Erdoğan’s planned visit comes amid a two-month cooling of relations between the two countries. On 30 October, President Aliyev skipped the summit of the Organisation of Turkic States in Ankara, even though the meeting marked the transfer of the organisation’s chairmanship from Azerbaijan to Turkey.

We reported in October on Turkish Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan’s visit to Baku.

What steps has Ankara taken to resolve the disagreements, what does Baku want, and what does the current situation reveal about relations between the two countries?

How did the dispute erupt?

In September, new school uniform requirements came into force in Azerbaijan. Although the rules do not explicitly mention the hijab, schools began turning away pupils who wore one. Speaking at the UN General Assembly, Erdoğan criticised bans on wearing the hijab in schools without naming any specific countries. In Baku, his remarks were seen as an indirect criticism of Azerbaijan.

The subsequent events unfolded as follows:

2 October. At a congress of the New Azerbaijan Party (YAP), Aliyev declared: “We do not need anyone’s help or anyone’s patronage.” He also stressed that Azerbaijan’s foreign policy should be shaped in such a way that “no one interferes in our affairs”.

At a congress of the New Azerbaijan Party (YAP), Aliyev declared: “We do not need anyone’s help or anyone’s patronage.” He also stressed that Azerbaijan’s foreign policy should be shaped in such a way that “no one interferes in our affairs”. 12 October. The Interior Ministry reported that police had detained 37 people during protests against the new school uniform requirements. On the same day, Erdoğan’s chief adviser Oktay Saral wrote on X: “It is unacceptable to deny girls who wear the hijab the right to education in Azerbaijan! The hijab is not an obstacle, but a requirement of faith!”

The Interior Ministry reported that police had detained 37 people during protests against the new school uniform requirements. On the same day, Erdoğan’s chief adviser Oktay Saral wrote on X: “It is unacceptable to deny girls who wear the hijab the right to education in Azerbaijan! The hijab is not an obstacle, but a requirement of faith!” 13 October. The New Azerbaijan Party described Saral’s remarks as “populist and irresponsible” and called on Turkey’s ruling Justice and Development Party (AKP) to “abandon this harmful policy”.

The New Azerbaijan Party described Saral’s remarks as “populist and irresponsible” and called on Turkey’s ruling Justice and Development Party (AKP) to “abandon this harmful policy”. 19 October. The Azerbaijan Press Council reported what it called a “biased campaign” in the Turkish media. In the council’s view, reports had taken the school uniform decision out of context and portrayed it as a “ban on wearing the hijab”.

The Azerbaijan Press Council reported what it called a “biased campaign” in the Turkish media. In the council’s view, reports had taken the school uniform decision out of context and portrayed it as a “ban on wearing the hijab”. 21 October. Azerbaijan banned 31 Turkish citizens from entering the country. The list included New Welfare Party leader Fatih Erbakan, MP Ömer Faruk Gergerlioğlu and several journalists. The authorities cited their social media statements against Azerbaijan’s constitutional order and leadership as the reason for the ban. Turkish media reported that Erdoğan called Aliyev the same day and invited him to the Ankara summit.

Azerbaijan banned 31 Turkish citizens from entering the country. The list included New Welfare Party leader Fatih Erbakan, MP Ömer Faruk Gergerlioğlu and several journalists. The authorities cited their social media statements against Azerbaijan’s constitutional order and leadership as the reason for the ban. Turkish media reported that Erdoğan called Aliyev the same day and invited him to the Ankara summit. 25 October. Erdoğan dismissed Oktay Saral from his post as chief adviser.

Erdoğan dismissed Oktay Saral from his post as chief adviser. 30 October. Aliyev did not attend the Ankara summit. Azerbaijan’s Foreign Minister Jeyhun Bayramov represented the country at the meeting.

What concessions has Ankara made?

The most significant step was Erdoğan’s dismissal of Oktay Saral as his chief adviser. According to Middle East Eye, which cites its own sources, Baku made three demands of Ankara:

Dismiss Erdoğan’s adviser, prosecute commentators who insulted Aliyev, and block the social media accounts named on a list. The publication reports that Ankara has already blocked some of those accounts.

Saral himself, however, has not retracted his remarks. He said he left his post at the president’s request but stressed that he had said nothing that warranted an apology: “Azerbaijan is my homeland too.”

According to Middle East Eye, Turkish officials have described the disagreements as a “misunderstanding”. Speaking at the summit, Erdoğan made no direct reference to Azerbaijan but said:

“There is no room for division, hostility or discord in the family photograph of the Turkic world.”

On 3 November, while travelling to South Korea, Erdoğan also sent Aliyev Victory Day greetings as his plane passed through Azerbaijani airspace. He delivered the message over the radio through the aircraft’s pilot.

What does Baku want?

Baku has not officially explained why Aliyev skipped the summit. According to APA, the president was due to attend the closing ceremony of the FIFA U-15 World Cup in Baku that day.

Baku has also taken issue with other statements from Ankara. Middle East Eye reports that, at an event organised by a foundation in October, Erdoğan said Turkish children no longer had to go abroad to study because of restrictions linked to their clothing or political views. Azerbaijan also interpreted these remarks as another rebuke.

An Azerbaijani source cited by Middle East Eye summed up Baku’s position as follows: Turkey must recognise the principle of “one nation, two states”. In other words, Baku does not want Ankara to interfere in Azerbaijan’s domestic affairs.

Elman Fattah, head of the Khazar Centre for Research and Analysis, shares a similar view. In an interview with Radio Free Europe/Radio Liberty, he said: “This means rejecting Turkey’s right to veto.” Fattah believes Aliyev is “deliberately shifting the hidden tensions between the two countries into the religious sphere”.

Political analyst Asif Narimanli, meanwhile, argues that

“The tensions between Baku and Ankara have deeper roots.”

Speaking to TodayPress, he noted that Aliyev’s absence…на саммите дает основания для такого вывода.

What lies behind the disagreements?

One of the deeper sources of tension concerns Israel. In Turkey, Azerbaijan’s close ties with Israel have caused considerable discontent, particularly since the start of the war in the Gaza Strip. Middle East Eye reports that Erdoğan declined to attend the October summit of the Conference on Interaction and Confidence Building Measures in Asia (CICA) to avoid meeting Israeli President Isaac Herzog. Turkish Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan also boycotted Herzog’s address. Baku saw this as an unfriendly gesture towards Aliyev.

Another source of disagreement concerns Armenia. According to an analysis by OC Media, Ankara wants to normalise relations with Yerevan, while Baku insists that this process must remain linked to a peace settlement between Azerbaijan and Armenia.

At the same time, the two countries share significant interests. According to OC Media, on 30 September they signed defence contracts worth around $500 million in total. In early 2026, they also reached a 15-year agreement on gas supplies from the Absheron field to Turkey. Azerbaijan accounted for around 22% of all the gas Turkey imported in 2024. According to figures from Turkey’s Ministry of Trade, bilateral trade reached $4.3 billion in 2025.

What could the visit change?

Political analyst Elkhan Shahinoglu described Erdoğan’s decision to visit Baku as “the right one”. He said:

“If tensions arise between two allies for any reason, they should not delay resolving them.”

Shahinoglu recalled that Erdoğan also visited Baku and addressed the Milli Majlis in 2009, when Turkey was moving closer to Armenia. Relations between the two countries returned to normal afterwards.

There is another sign that tensions may be easing. According to the newspaper Karar, when Turkey considered nominating former Foreign Minister Feridun Sinirlioğlu for the post of UN secretary-general, Azerbaijan backed a candidate from the United Arab Emirates instead. However, in late October, Azerbaijani Foreign Ministry spokesman Aykhan Hajizada welcomed Turkey’s nomination of Sinirlioğlu.

The next test for relations will be the UN climate conference COP31, which will take place in Antalya this month. Middle East Eye reports that Ankara hopes Aliyev will attend the conference. Baku has yet to confirm his visit.

World.title: Abkhazia to raise electricity tariffs for businesses by 40% to pay for Russian power imports
World.content:
Electricity tariffs for commercial customers in Abkhazia will rise by 40%. However, the increase will apply only during the autumn-winter period, when the region imports electricity to cover its energy shortfall.

The Inguri hydroelectric power plant is Abkhazia’s only source of electricity. However, its output falls from around November until March or April as water levels in the Inguri River drop. Electricity consumption in the region, meanwhile, rises.

In 2025, a shortfall of 500 million kWh was covered by electricity imports from Russia. Russia provided some of this electricity to Abkhazia free of charge as humanitarian aid, but the authorities had to buy the rest at market prices.

This comes at a high cost for Abkhazia: Russian electricity is significantly more expensive than the domestic tariffs charged to consumers. The current rate is 2 roubles [$0.02] per kWh for households and 3 roubles [$0.03] for legal entities. Under the agreement with Russia, however, Abkhazia will have to pay 5.5 roubles [$0.06] per kWh for imported electricity.

This is why the authorities decided to raise tariffs for businesses.

“When we pay 5.5 roubles per kWh for imported electricity but sell it to households for 2 roubles, this is also an example of the state’s social responsibility towards its citizens.

“But for commercial enterprises and institutions – where businesses make money – the tariff should match the purchase price during periods when we import electricity,” Abkhaz President Badra Gunba said. He instructed the government to approve this as the republic’s new tariff policy.

World.title: The evacuation from Oleshky: How Russia turned a humanitarian mission into a propaganda story
World.content:
The evacuation from Oleshky

The evacuation from Oleshky (Oleshky, formerly known as Oleshky/Aloshky) in Ukraine’s Kherson region, during which around 800 civilians were evacuated and aid was delivered to those who remained, was a rare example of Ukraine and Russia working together under international mediation. For Russian state media and Z-bloggers, it also became an opportunity to launch a new information campaign.

The Ukrainian side stressed the need to save lives and continue humanitarian missions. Russian media, meanwhile, portrayed the evacuation as an act of concern by Moscow for the residents of occupied territories, sought to discredit Ukraine and tried to intimidate those considering returning to territory under Kyiv’s control.

Four narratives stood out in the media coverage: Russia cast as a humanitarian intermediary; residents’ alleged unwillingness to return to Ukraine; attempts to frighten men with the prospect of forced mobilisation; and efforts to shift responsibility for threats to civilians onto Ukraine.

Some of these claims contradicted both the circumstances of the operation and statements by official representatives of the parties involved.

A report by Novosti Donbassa By Yulia Tararui.

A catastrophe whose causes the propaganda ignores

Oleshky has been under Russian occupation since February 2022. After Ukrainian forces liberated the right-bank part of the Kherson region in the autumn of that year, the city found itself on the front line.

The situation deteriorated dramatically in June 2023, when the Kakhovka Hydroelectric Power Plant was destroyed. Flooding, damaged infrastructure, disruptions to electricity and water supplies, and restrictions on movement made life extremely difficult for residents.

By 2026, the situation had become critical. Fighting, landmines and drone attacks had left the city in urgent need of food, medicine and other essentials, while opportunities to leave safely were almost nonexistent.

Russian publications described the hardships faced by residents in detail, but avoided the central fact: Oleshky had been under the control of Russian occupation authorities throughout this period.

Russian media circulated the account of a local woman who tried to leave in an ambulance but could not get even as far as the outskirts of the city because the road was mined.

Other reports described elderly residents cycling to Radensk during a ceasefire to buy food and medicine – a journey of around 20 kilometres each way.

These stories conveyed the scale of the catastrophe. But they also helped construct a narrative convenient for Moscow: the suffering was blamed on the proximity of the fighting, while the occupation administration’s responsibility for meeting residents’ basic needs was left out of the picture.

A joint operation turned into a story of Moscow’s concern

Agreements on a temporary ceasefire and the evacuation were reached with international mediation, including the active involvement of US First Lady Melania Trump.

According to figures she cited, around 750 people left the city. Reports mentioned 25 buses.

Residents were free to choose their destination: territory under Ukrainian control or Russia.

Those who chose Ukraine were evacuated via Belarus. The Russian side arranged an airlift from Anapa to Gomel using military transport aircraft.

Evacuees who chose Russia were taken to a temporary accommodation centre in Simferopol.

Food, water, medicine, fuel for generators and hospital equipment were brought into the city. A total of 105 pets were evacuated from Oleshky.

According to Ukraine’s human rights ombudsman, Dmytro Lubinets, the ceasefire lasted five days, 19 hours and 59 minutes. The operation also made it possible to arrange the repatriation of the bodies of fallen soldiers and civilians from morgues in Oleshky and other settlements.

The Ukrainian and Russian human rights commissioners said that both sides had fulfilled their obligations and thanked each other.

Russian media coverage, however, focused on Moscow’s role: the military aircraft, the transfer of evacuees to Simferopol, medical assistance and the work of Russian officials. In this way, the joint operation helped promote the image of a state that not only controls occupied territory but also looks after its residents.

The fact that an international operation was needed to evacuate people from a city that had been under Russian control for more than four years was barely examined in these reports.

The story of evacuees being mobilised: What a Z-Blogger claimed

One revealing episode involved Russian Z-blogger Sergei Kolyasnikov, better known as Zergulio. He circulated a claim that men who chose to travel to Ukraine were detained by staff from territorial recruitment and social support centres (TCCs and SPs, Ukraine’s equivalent of military enlistment offices) immediately after the evacuation and sent to the front.

The story drew on a familiar image of Ukraine, where men of conscription age are supposedly bound to become victims of forced mobilisation. But it had a problem with the timeline.

When the claim began circulating, evacuees heading towards Ukraine had, according to published reports, been flown to Gomel, the regional capital of Belarus. The allegation that they were detained by TCC staff after arriving in Ukraine did not match the known evacuation route.

The reports provided no publicly available evidence of mass detentions of evacuated men.

Lubinets stressed separately that no screening had taken place during the evacuation, including for people with problems concerning their documents. He said: “There was no screening whatsoever. Moreover, we had people who said they had problems with their documents – for example, they had lost them. There were no problems.”

He added: “There was not only no screening, there were no checks of phones or documents either.”

These remarks concerned the evacuation procedure and did not describe all subsequent actions by state authorities after people returned to Ukraine. But they offered no support for the blogger’s claim.

▇ Disinformation exploits people’s genuine fears of war and mobilisation, attaching them to a specific event.

Such a message could also have been aimed at residents of occupied territories, particularly men of conscription age and their relatives.

For people who have lived in information isolation for years, a story about evacuees being sent to the front could become a reason not to leave, even in the absence of evidence.

Why people chose to leave: An attempt to undermine their decisions

The Russian military blog Kotsnews claims that most men of conscription age refused to travel towards Ukraine. According to the blog, those who left were mainly elderly people, women and children, and they did so for personal reasons rather than out of political conviction.

The author of the post writes: “Not out of any great love for ‘independent Ukraine’, but to sort out their personal affairs. People in Oleshky have long felt no gratitude towards Ukraine.”

This explanation serves several purposes at once. It diminishes the significance of people’s decisions by portraying them as pragmatic choices – for example, a chance to reunite with relatives or move to Europe.

It creates the impression that residents of the occupied city no longer see their future as being tied to Ukraine. It also reinforces the narrative of inevitable mobilisation.

The result is a self-reinforcing argument: men do not want to go to Ukraine because they fear the TCCs, while those who do make the journey are supposedly immediately confronted with mobilisation. Russian commentators provide no reliable statistics on the evacuees’ reasons for leaving.

Lubinets said the parties had agreed not to disclose how many people chose Ukraine and how many chose Russia. According to him, honouring that agreement was necessary to ensure that humanitarian operations could continue.

Meanwhile, various figures circulated in the Russian information space. Russian Z-war correspondent Romanov initially reported that 17 buses had travelled to Ukraine and four to Russia, but later deleted the figures from his post.

Newsmax journalist Alex Salvi reported 11 buses heading to Ukraine and four to Russia.

Without official figures, these reports do not make it possible to establish how the evacuees were divided between the two destinations. But the very attempt to interpret their choices as an indication of political allegiance became part of the information war surrounding the operation.

Accusations of violating the ceasefire

At the same time, Russian officials accused Ukrainian forces of breaching the agreement. Rodion Miroshnik, the Russian Foreign Ministry’s ambassador-at-large, claimed that a Ukrainian drone had attacked a civilian vehicle leaving Oleshky.

According to Miroshnik, the vehicle was carrying civilians travelling to Radensk to buy food. Two people were injured. He alleged that attacks on civilians had resumed before the agreed ceasefire had expired.

These accusations contradicted statements that the terms of the agreement had been observed. After the operation, Lubinets said that both sides had fulfilled their commitments.

Russia’s human rights commissioner, Yana Lantratova, gave a similar assessment. International media also reported that there had been no confirmed violations of the local ceasefire.

Miroshnik’s statement therefore remains an accusation made by the Russian side, not an established fact.

Such reports serve an obvious purpose. They portray Moscow as willing to take part in humanitarian initiatives while reinforcing the image of Ukraine as the side posing a threat to civilians.

Even during an operation that officials from both countries described in positive terms, the Russian information space continued to recycle familiar accusations.

The ceasefire ended, but the problem remains

Russia refused to extend the ceasefire. According to AFP, Ukraine’s Foreign Ministry had proposed prolonging the agreement, but the Russian side rejected the offer.

The ceasefire ended on 1 November. The ombudsmen said they were considering organising further humanitarian missions.

The need for evacuation has not gone away. Ksenia Arkhipova, a volunteer who has been helping residents of Oleshky since 2022, told the Agency that not everyone who wanted to leave had been evacuated.

According to her, some residents of the city’s suburbs were turned back at checkpoints, while no transport arrived for some people with limited mobility. The most vulnerable are elderly people, people with disabilities and those unable to reach an evacuation point on their own.

Lubinets said 22 ambulances had to be deployed. Some people were too unwell to withstand the planned journey.

In one case, medical staff initially approved a person for transport but, after examining them on site, decided they would not survive the journey. An alternative arrangement had to be made. Several families are now continuing their journey to Ukraine by road.

The ombudsman also said that the Ukrainian side had managed to deliver medical equipment and medicines to the hospital in Oleshky. But he acknowledged that it was still impossible to assess the quality of medical care there.

Russian reports focused on the number of vehicles involved, the aid delivered by Russia and the organisation of transport. The fate of those left behind amid the crisis received far less attention.

Why this poses a threat to future evacuations

Disinformation can put people’s safety at risk. If a resident of an occupied city believes that returning to Ukraine will mean being detained and sent to the front, they may refuse to evacuate even when a safe route is available.

Claims that large numbers of people are unwilling to return can make those who remain feel that choosing Ukraine is dangerous, unpopular or pointless. The reality is more complicated.

People choose where to go based on their health, whether they have relatives there, their documents, housing and access to assistance.

For an elderly person, for example, reuniting with children or grandchildren may be the priority. A person with a disability may need medical care. For a family with children, safety and the ability to continue their education may matter most.

None of these decisions, in itself, reveals a person’s political beliefs. Turning evacuation figures into a vote for either Ukraine or Russia is therefore a form of manipulation.

▇ Choosing an evacuation destination is not the same as voting for Ukraine or Russia.

The information war could also complicate future humanitarian missions, the need for which both sides acknowledge.

World.title: U.S. military disables merchant vessel in Gulf of Oman
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, November 8. The U.S. military has disabled a merchant vessel in the Gulf of Oman.

According to U.S. Central Command (CENTCOM), the incident occurred on November 7.

The command said the vessel’s civilian crew repeatedly ignored warnings and made several attempts to breach the Iranian naval blockade.

" The vessel's civilian crew ignored repeated warnings and made several attempts to break through the Iranian naval blockade," the statement said.

According to CENTCOM, the strike was carried out using precision-guided munitions targeting the vessel’s aft section.

World.title: Nine killed in road accident in southeastern Türkiye
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, November 8. At least nine people have been killed and five others injured in a road accident in Türkiye’s southeastern Van province.

According to the local administration, Van Governor Ozan Balci announced the casualties.

The accident occurred on Saturday, shortly after rainfall, on the Van–Ozalp highway, where a minibus collided with a truck.

"According to preliminary information, nine of our citizens lost their lives in the accident, five of them women. Another five people were injured and hospitalized," the governor said.

The circumstances and causes of the accident are under investigation.

World.title: Azerbaijan’s Victory Day commemorated in Mexico (PHOTO/VIDEO)
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, November 8. A commemorative event marking Azerbaijan’s Victory Day was held in Mexico on November 7, 2026.

The day symbolizes the end of nearly 30 years of occupation of Azerbaijani territories as a result of the 44-day Patriotic War, led by Supreme Commander-in-Chief, President Ilham Aliyev.

According to the Embassy of Azerbaijan in Mexico, the official ceremony took place at the Mexico-Azerbaijan Friendship Park, located on the historic Paseo de la Reforma, one of Mexico City’s most prominent avenues. The park features a monument depicting a map of Azerbaijan.

The event served as a symbol of the strength of the Azerbaijani people and national pride.

During the ceremony, the Symphony Orchestra of the Mexican Navy performed the national anthems of Azerbaijan and Mexico. A wreath was also laid at the monument depicting the map of Azerbaijan.

The event was attended by representatives of the Embassy of Azerbaijan in Mexico, members of the Azerbaijani diaspora, and representatives of the Mexican public.

World.title: President Ilham Aliyev: The leader who achieved what no one else could
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, November 8. Azerbaijan is celebrating Victory Day. Six years ago, on November 8, 2020, Supreme Commander-in-Chief and President of Azerbaijan Ilham Aliyev announced the liberation of Shusha.

Today, it is clear that Azerbaijan did not simply win a war. It brought to an end a conflict that had been considered insoluble for 30 years. As recently as 2019, Karabakh was cited as an example of a problem with no solution in sight – and seemingly no prospect of one in the future. President Ilham Aliyev, however, had a different view.

To understand the scale of this achievement, one need only look around the world. Cyprus has remained divided since 1974. The Annan Plan, on which the international community spent years of work, was rejected in a 2004 referendum, and the island has remained divided by a demarcation line ever since. Transnistria has been frozen in conflict since 1992, while Abkhazia and the Tskhinvali region have remained unresolved since the early 1990s. The Minsk agreements on Donbas were intended to provide a diplomatic solution but proved to be little more than a pause before a major war. Serbia and Kosovo signed agreements in Brussels and Washington but have yet to establish normal relations. India and Pakistan have spent decades fighting over Kashmir, periodically exchanging strikes, with neither side able to secure victory or reach an agreement. Ethiopia and Eritrea signed a peace deal in 2018, for which Ethiopia's prime minister received the Nobel Peace Prize, yet the region was plunged into war again just two years later.

In all these cases, influential politicians, major powers, and respected mediators were involved. Some relied on negotiations, only to see them turn into an endless process without results. Others relied on force, which brought temporary gains that could not be consolidated. Almost no one managed to see the process through to the end.

The Karabakh conflict required solving three distinct challenges, each of which would, on its own, be considered a major achievement in a political career.

The first was military. It was not enough simply to win the war; it had to be won before the international community could intervene and prevent the achievement of its objectives. The 44 days of fighting in 2020 were the culmination of 17 years of preparation – in the military, economic and diplomatic spheres, as well as in relations with Türkiye, Russia, the West, and neighboring countries. The war began when Azerbaijan was ready for it and ended when its main objectives had been achieved. Knowing when to stop is a skill no less rare than knowing how to win.

The second challenge was bringing the conflict to a definitive end. After 2020, armed formations and a Russian peacekeeping contingent remained in Karabakh. Many believed at the time that this status quo would persist for years. The anti-terrorist measures in September 2023 lasted less than a day, and by spring 2024, the peacekeepers had left Azerbaijani territory. The country's sovereignty was fully restored, with no gray areas or "special arrangements" remaining.

The third challenge was diplomatic – and perhaps the most difficult. Military victory almost always creates the conditions for another conflict: the defeated side harbors resentment, seeks revenge, and waits for circumstances to change. This was the case with Germany after World War I and with dozens of other local conflicts that followed. Ilham Aliyev did what victorious leaders rarely do: he turned victory into a negotiating position, and that negotiating position into peace. On August 8, 2025, the leaders of Azerbaijan and Armenia signed a Joint Declaration at the White House in the presence of the US President, while the two countries' foreign ministers initialed a peace agreement. A year after the Washington meeting, there is no gunfire along the border, and discussions between Baku and Yerevan are focused on transport, trade, and reopening communications.

The main lesson of Karabakh is not that force solves everything. If that were true, many powerful countries would have resolved all their outstanding conflicts long ago. The lesson is that force works only when backed by a clear political objective and an understanding of what comes next.

From the outset, Ilham Aliyev said that Azerbaijan wanted neither someone else's land nor endless hostility. It wanted its own territory and peace on its own terms – in accordance with international law and the principle of territorial integrity. This position did not change during years of fruitless negotiations, throughout the war, or in its aftermath. That is precisely why victory did not turn into endless confrontation, and why peace does not look like a temporary ceasefire.

Speaking at the World Forum on Intercultural Dialogue in Baku in October, the President recalled that the Karabakh negotiation format had initially been structured not to resolve the conflict but to freeze it, and that major powers appeared to have accepted this approach. They made one mistake: they failed to take into account what the Azerbaijani people wanted and what the Azerbaijani state was determined to achieve.

Today, the world is going through perhaps its most difficult period since the Cold War. Conflicts that were considered manageable for decades are once again turning into open hostilities. Leaders are searching for formulas that would allow them to end wars without creating new ones. In almost every case, those formulas are proving elusive.

Against this backdrop, Azerbaijan's path stands out as an exception. In six years, the country has moved from war to the full restoration of its sovereignty, and from there to peace recognized in Washington, Brussels, Moscow, and Beijing. Many leaders have faced and continue to face similar challenges: occupied territories, fruitless negotiations, and indifference from international institutions. Many have tried to resolve them through force, while others have relied on diplomacy. Ilham Aliyev has proved to be one of the very few leaders capable of combining the two and seeing the process through to the end.

That is why November 8 is more than a day of remembrance and pride. It is a day to recall that no conflict is frozen forever. What is often lacking is the political will to unfreeze it and the wisdom to build peace afterward. President Ilham Aliyev has shown that both can come together in one leader.

Happy Victory Day!

World.title: Chronicles of Victory: November 8, 2020
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, November 8. The Azerbaijani Army launched a counter-offensive operation, later called the "Iron Fist", on September 27, 2020, in response to the large-scale provocation of the Armenian armed forces along the frontline.

The 44-day second Karabakh war ended with the liberation of Azerbaijan’s territories from nearly 30-year Armenian occupation and the restoration of territorial integrity.

Chronicle of the 43rd day of the Second Karabakh War:

- President of the Republic of Azerbaijan, victorious Supreme Commander-in-Chief Ilham Aliyev addressed to the nation from the Alley of Martyrs on November 8 announcing that the city of Shusha was liberated from occupation.

- Supreme Commander-in-Chief Ilham Aliyev congratulated General Hikmat Mirzayev on victory.

- President of Azerbaijan Ilham Aliyev and First Lady Mehriban Aliyeva visited the Alley of Honors and the Alley of Martyrs.

- President Ilham Aliyev received Turkish Foreign and National Defense Ministers.

- First Vice President Mehriban Aliyeva congratulated the people of Azerbaijan on the occasion of the liberation of Shusha on her official Instagram page.

- Armenian troops were forced to retreat, suffering losses.

- The list of Armenia's military equipment destroyed in one day has been announced.

- Armenia violates ceasefire on state border.

- Armenian troops fired on Tartar, Aghdam and Aghjabadi.

- A video of the liberated Balasoltanli village of Gubadli has been released.

- The Azerbaijani Army is increasing the advantage of the front in the direction of Khojavand.

- High-ranking Armenian officials were destroyed in the direction of Khojavand.

- A video of the liberated Tsakuri village of Khojavand has been released.

- Heavy blows were inflicted on the Armenian troops as a result of the operation carried out by the Azerbaijan Army in the Khojavand direction of the front.

- The Azerbaijani Army has full control over the city of Shusha.

- Video footage of the liberated Vejnali village of Zangilan region was released.

- A video has been spread of Armenian troops fleeing from the Khojavand direction of the front.
