World.title: Arise, Sir Kev: The league legend who lost his best mate to MND and then set out to eradicate it
World.content:
Kevin Sinfield being made a Knight Bachelor by The Prince of Wales at Windsor Castle last month.

Former Great Britain captain Kevin Sinfield has raised $26 million dollars for MND research and support in the last seven years, and he’s headed to Australia next year for his next charity run.

Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

It says a lot about Kevin Sinfield that soon after Prince William knighted him, the future king wondered why it had taken so long. “Frankly, he should have been Sir Kevin years ago,” Prince William told the BBC, adding that awarding the knighthood to Sinfield at Windsor Castle last month was “probably the easiest decision anyone has ever had to make”. The honour – and the genuine admiration of the Prince of Wales – was earned by Sinfield thanks to his extensive work raising funds and awareness for Motor Neurone Disease over the past seven years. Kevin Sinfield waving to the crowd before the Super League grand final in Warrington, having just completed a charity ultra-marathon. Getty Images The former Great Britain rugby league captain has so far raised a remarkable $26 million through his tireless efforts – and that’s a very literal description. Sinfield, who is an assistant coach of the England rugby side who will meet Australia on Monday, has done the bulk of his fundraising by pounding the pavement in seven exhausting running challenges, including multiple completions of seven marathons in seven days. This year, Sinfield finished his seventh challenge by knocking off an ultra-marathon (50 kilometres) every day, for seven days.



“I am worried about his knees,” Prince William told the BBC. Sinfield laughs when you follow up. Seriously, how are the knees? “No, they’re good,” he told this masthead in London this week. “Honestly, the knees are still fine.” The “seven” theme of Sinfield’s challenges is no coincidence. The number is at the heart of why the 46-year-old from Oldham began running. Kevin Sinfield speaks with Rob Burrow after completing his Extra Mile Challenge at Headingley Stadium in 2021. Getty Images Sinfield’s best mate was his long-time Leeds and Great Britain league teammate Rob Burrow. The former halfback was diagnosed with MND in 2019 and died in 2024. “I played alongside Rob for 15 years, so we sat next to each other in the dressing room. As you probably know, in sport, dressing rooms accelerate friendships. So that 15 years, it’s probably 60 or 70 years in real life,” Sinfield explains.



After Burrow’s diagnosis in December 2019, Sinfield promised his mate that by the following Christmas he’d raise a certain sum of money. But COVID lockdowns shut down the world and, with it, chances to hold big fundraising events. Kevin Sinfield running in one of many marathons. CameraSport via Getty Images “We got to September of 2020 and I’d made a promise, but we were going to fall short of that promise,” he said. “So I was like, I’ve got to try and do something.” Sinfield was then director of rugby at the Leeds Rhinos and he submitted a proposal to authorities to do a charity running challenge around Oldham and Leeds in November, using all the professional sports COVID protocols. “Remarkably, we got it signed off. And then we got a TV station: the biggest news breakfast show in the UK decided to follow us because there was nothing else going on at the time,” Sinfield said. “And it just went crazy. So that was the start.” Sinfield ran seven marathons in seven days, aiming to raise £77,777 (about $150,000). The public forked out more than £2 million. The next year he ran 101 kilometres in under 24 hours, and in following years upped the stakes to repeatedly run seven ultra-marathons in seven days. At each run, Sinfield also does a mile (1.6 kilometres) with MND families, meeting people and providing his support.



In 2023, he pushed Burrow in a chair in the Leeds marathon, before carrying his mate across the line in highly emotional scenes. “I had no idea I’d end up where we’ve ended up,” Sinfield said. “It was never planned. Like I said, the first one was very fortunate in terms of timing because we create a lot of momentum. And on the back of that, it’s enabled us to carry that on. We’ve been able to raise awareness and funds but also change the way people understand MND across the UK and Ireland. “So, yeah, it’s been great to continue with Rob’s name. Sadly we lost him just over two years ago. But we continue fighting for his legacy. And now for so many other families as well, who’ve become friends because you meet people along the way. You’re drawn to these families because of how tough they are, how inspirational they are, and I’ve got so many friends in the MND community now. Kevin Sinfield when he played for Great Britain. Fairfax Photography “That’s been probably the biggest part of this. It’s been less about the running in the last couple of years, and more about spending time with families and connecting and pulling them all together, so that we try and crack this as one big unit.” Sinfield believes a cure for MND can be found, and money will hasten its discovery. But he is also motivated to provide better support facilities and systems for MND sufferers and their families.



“I made a commitment [to Burrow] that I would support this community for the rest of my life. Now, that may look differently to what has been done the last seven years. Whilst I can still run, I’ll continue to try and run. But there are other ways of fundraising and raising awareness and pulling people together. “The families need to be looked after better than what we currently do. So it’s two-pronged, really: the care side, and trying to find a cure and give our researchers and medical professionals some more money to go after a cure. Retired South Sydney player Jai Arrow and former Wallaby Nathan Charles take part in a lap of honour before the NRL grand final. Getty Images “I’m very hopeful. There’s some very smart people working on MND research … and the better we are at collaborating and sharing means we’ll do it quicker. I just think MND has been underfunded for too long. With the right amount of funds we’ll find a cure.” Sinfield noted with sadness the recent MND diagnoses of NRL star Jai Arrow and former Wallaby Nathan Charles. He says he was also inspired by the fundraising work of the late AFL great Neale Daniher. It’s why Sinfield has decided to lace up again next year and do a charity challenge in Australia and New Zealand. The final plan is yet to be set in stone, but it is likely to be in May, with Sinfield running seven marathons in seven days in different cities, finishing at various sporting events.

World.title: Macklemore says major US arenas refused to book ‘Free Palestine’ tour
World.content:
CultureMusicIsraeli-Palestinian conflict Macklemore says major US arenas refused to book ‘Free Palestine’ tour Ben Sisario November 8, 2026 — 11:24am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Macklemore, the indie rapper who was kicked off Ed Sheeran’s stadium tour in September over his public support of Palestinians, said on Saturday (AEDT) that nine arenas in the United States refused to book him for a “Free Palestine” benefit tour he had planned. In a social media post, Macklemore wrote that in mid-September, after being removed from Sheeran’s tour, his team contacted arenas in the United States and “received available dates at these arenas through the end of the year.” “But once they found out these were my benefit shows for Palestine,” his statement continued, “those dates were suddenly off the table.” In a social media post, rapper Macklemore said a number of arenas in the US have refused to book his tour. Getty Images Macklemore named nine venues: Madison Square Garden, Barclays Center and UBS Arena in New York; Prudential Centre in Newark, New Jersey; Intuit Dome, Kia Forum and Crypto.com Arena in and around Los Angeles; Chase Centre Arena in San Francisco; and Climate Pledge Arena in Seattle, Macklemore’s hometown.



In a statement, a spokesperson for Madison Square Garden said: “We have some of the busiest venues in the world with extremely limited availability and he’s not an arena-level act.” Related Article Israeli-Palestinian conflict Macklemore dumped from Ed Sheeran’s tour over pro-Palestine comments A spokesperson for Kia Forum said the venue had no comment. None of the other venues responded to requests for comment. Macklemore, who had breakout success in the early 2010s with songs like Thrift Shop and Can’t Hold Us, was removed from Sheeran’s tour after he appeared at two shows at MetLife Stadium in East Rutherford, New Jersey, in early September.



There, he proclaimed “Free Palestine” and performed Hind’s Hall, his protest song against Israel’s conduct of the war in the Gaza Strip, which came in response to the Hamas-led attack on Israel on October 7, 2023. In that song, Macklemore accuses Israel of genocide. Macklemore said that owners of the venues where the Sheeran tour had been scheduled demanded he be removed. Robert Kraft, whose company owns the New England Patriots and Gillette Stadium outside Boston, said that his venues do not allow “hate speech,” and that Macklemore’s statements at MetLife had crossed that line. Macklemore was removed from Ed Sheeran’s tour in September over his Free Palestine comments. Getty Macklemore’s removal renewed debate about the power of billionaires to control free speech, and the power of artists to resist it. After Sheeran said he had played no part in the decision, every other musician associated with his tour, including opening acts and his backing band, dropped out in solidarity with Macklemore. Sheeran continued the tour, at first alone and then picking up other musicians.



Editor's pick Israeli-Palestinian conflict Country artist breaks Gillette Stadium attendance record while wearing ‘Free Palestine’ shirt In his statement on Friday, Macklemore added: “We live in a country that prides itself on freedom of speech. Yet we’ve reached a point where a handful of billionaires can decide which causes are acceptable, which voices are welcome and which human lives are worth defending.” In late October, Macklemore played arena shows in London, Paris and Dublin as part of a benefit tour. When that tour was announced, representatives of Macklemore said they expected additional dates to be booked in the US, but none were. Though Macklemore has never been a stadium-level touring attraction, he has maintained a steady fan base for years. In October, he played a solo concert at Red Rocks Amphitheatre, near Morrison, Colorado. In 2023, he went on a tour of arenas and theatres, including Climate Pledge Arena.

World.title: Socceroos name under-strength squad for Jordan friendly amid player safety fears
World.content:
Updated SportSoccerAustralian soccer Socceroos name under-strength squad for Jordan friendly amid player safety fears Anna Harrington and and Vince Rugari Updated November 8, 2026 — 12:35pm ,first published November 6, 2026 — 11:22am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Football Australia will continue to assess security ahead of the Socceroos’ planned friendly against Jordan after an under-strength squad was named amid player concerns over safety. Tony Popovic’s squad was released at 10:30pm on Saturday night for upcoming friendlies against Qatar in Doha on November 13 (November 14, AEDT) and Jordan in Amman three days later. Loading The friendlies were initially meant to serve as preparation for the Asian Cup, which has since been pushed back from January to December 2027 due to security concerns in host country Saudi Arabia. Professional Footballers Australia on Friday said players had “overwhelmingly expressed their view that the Jordan match should be rescheduled or relocated”.



Captain Maty Ryan and fellow veterans Jackson Irvine and Milos Degenek, plus midfielder Aiden O’Neill, are the most prominent omissions from coach Tony Popovic’s squad, which includes seven uncapped players. It is unclear whether those players made themselves unavailable for safety reasons. As yet, there has been no movement on the Amman fixture, despite Indonesia recently cancelling their own planned friendly in Jordan. Diesel Herrington, the younger brother of Socceroo Lucas Herrington, is in line to make his Australian debut. Getty Images “For the match against Jordan, we will continue to assess the security environment and provide players and staff with timely, comprehensive updates, including relevant safety advice and risk assessments,” FA chief executive Martin Kugeler said in a statement. “The safety and wellbeing of our players and staff remains our highest priority.” There are eight changes to the squad from September’s friendlies against Brazil in Australia.



New call-ups are Central Coast defender Diesel Herrington, older brother of Hull City ace Lucas Herrington, Portsmouth striker Thomas Waddingham and FC St. Pauli midfielder Sam Klein. Attacker Daniel Arzani returns after finding form at Ferencvaros, along with defender Gianni Stensness (Viking FK), who scored against Bayern Munich in the Champions League. View post on X Striker Kusini Yengi joins brother Tete, while goalkeepers Joe Gauci (Lincoln City) and Tom Glover (RB Omiya Ardija) have been recalled. “While the Asian Cup has been rescheduled, that does not take away from the importance of this window,” Popovic said in a statement. “We have limited opportunities to be together as a group, so every camp and every game is important.



“We will have an eye on continuing to evolve the squad for the future, with our World Cup 2030 qualifying campaign and the Asian Cup both now in the second half of 2027. This camp gives us another chance to work with new players and see how they fit into what we are building.” Qatar and Jordan were finalists from the last Asian Cup, and were viewed as ideal opponents for the Socceroos in their preparation for the next edition of the tournament. Socceroos squad For friendlies against Qatar and Jordan * denotes uncapped player Goalkeepers: Patrick Beach, Joe Gauci, Tom Glover* Defenders: Kealey Adamson*, Aziz Behich, Kasey Bos*, Alessandro Circati, Jason Geria, Diesel Herrington*, Lucas Herrington, Jacob Italiano, Harry Souttar Midfielders: Sam Klein*, Riley McGree, Connor Metcalfe, Paul Okon-Engstler, Gianni Stensness, Patrick Yazbek Forwards: Eli Adams*, Daniel Arzani, Nestory Irankunda, Thomas Waddingham*, Kusini Yengi, Tete Yengi, Marcus Younis The postponement has not only thrown those plans into disarray, but raised questions over the future of Popovic, who signed a short-term contract extension earlier this year which officially ends in March. To remain in the job for the 2027 Asian Cup’s new dates – which take place over the Christmas and New Year’s period to avoid Ramadan, which begins on January 28, 2028 – Popovic and Football Australia will need to agree terms on a new contract, whether it be another 12-month term or encompassing the full World Cup cycle through to 2030.



Related Article Asian Cup Socceroos set Christmas deadline for Popovic decision as rival coaches circle Garriock has set a Christmas deadline to sort out Popovic’s future, warning that other coaches were “knocking on the door” – including, sources say, Kevin Muscat, who shapes as their primary target if Popovic decides to step away from the Socceroos. Muscat’s contract with Chinese Super League club Shanghai Port expires at the end of the year, and the former Melbourne Victory and Yokohama F. Marinos title-winning coach has long held ambitions of steering the national team. with AAP

World.title: It only takes three songs before every seat in the Palais is hastily abandoned
World.content:
CultureLive reviewsMelbourne live reviews It only takes three songs before every seat in the Palais is hastily abandoned Michael Dwyer and Bridget Davies November 8, 2026 — 12:28pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Key points MUSIC: Courtney Barnett returns to the Palais for the first time since 2017

OPERA: This new production of La Bohème is a shiny successor to what came before

MUSIC

Courtney Barnett ★★★★

The Palais, November 7 It takes three songs for Courtney Barnett’s Melbourne return to feel like 2017. The comical near-death experience of Avant Gardener was already an Aussie suburban classic when she played this esteemed venue nine years ago and again, every seat becomes a hastily abandoned inconvenience. Courtney Barnett performs at the Palais on November 7, 2026. Martin Philbey What’s changed? A slow churn of albums mapping the agonies of indecision, procrastination and rumination has culminated in the aptly titled Creature of Habit. “Feels like I’m going backwards, each day I preach my practice,” she rants in the opening blast of Stay In Your Lane. The backwards bit is an illusion. There’s more grey hair out here now and more confidence on stage. But Barnett’s three-piece grunge attack does feel as casually comfortable as her white jeans and T-shirt. It’s as if the stasis anxiety in her songs is exorcised in the act of simply doing what she does.



The bashful grin no longer tries to contain itself as she strolls to the lip of the stage to strangle those raggedly torn chords from her guitar. Our silence is “intimidating”; she squirms after the relative gentility of Mantis. But there’s very little of it as she interleaves ancient favourites with all 10 tracks from the new LP. Early EP tracks History Eraser and Canned Tomatoes (Whole) must feel like another lifetime to the singer, but from here, the consistency of her craft is striking. The same thread of restless, poetic self-examination is carried by a familiar racket conjured by unfussy bassist Bones Sloane and drummer Stella Mozgawa. It only takes three songs before everyone is on their feet. Martin Philbey Barnett gives herself and her overdriven guitar room to breathe in the slowed coda of City Looks Pretty and other improvised breakdowns, and the noise default is leavened by the likes of singalong favourite Depreston. The solo spell of Mostly Patient stills the beer-hoisting crowd like magic. The fact that any of the new songs might have fit neatly enough on her first album puts a lid on the evening’s surprises. But Barnett’s musical vocabulary is a reflection of an inner monologue that strives to accept what won’t change. “Reborn every morning, still somehow getting older,” she sings in a song called Another Beautiful Day. To her fans, the gift is in feeling the same. They’re still the kid in Elevator Operator and they know Nobody Really Cares If You Don’t Go To The Party like a thing only your best friend would tell you. Growing older hasn’t made any of us less ourselves. Some habits are just keepers.

Reviewed by Michael Dwyer



OPERA

La Bohème ★★★★

Opera Australia, The Regent Theatre, until November 18 Bohème is back, baby. And not the Gale Edwards production that returned in almost every Opera Australia season in the past 15 years, but a new, shiny successor. This new production of La Bohème is a shiny successor to what came before. Peter Foster Beloved by novices and veterans alike, Puccini’s La Bohème sits at the centre of basically every opera company worldwide. With Edwards’ loyal moneymaker put out to pasture, OA entrusted young Australian director Constantine Costi to make its golden goose anew. They could not have made a finer choice. Costi has assembled a brilliant creative team in fellow thirty-somethings, Dann Barber (sets) and Sabina Myers (costumes). There are many jaw-droppingly stunning moments: from Rodolfo and Mimi singing literally suspended in mid-air to the sheer scale of Café Momus. Visually, it’s everything you ever wanted in an opera.



The sound, regrettably, was less convincing. At no fault of young British conductor Finnegan Downie Dear, who led with passionate precision, nor Orchestra Victoria, who dutifully acquiesced whenever Downie Dear gestured for them to effectively turn it down. It’s the unforgiving acoustics of the Regent, where the orchestra is in front of the stage, rather than in the pit. But such is Bohème’s aforementioned perennial appeal, a revival – in another theatre – is not far away. Galina Cheplakova as Mimi and Kang Wang as Rodolfo. Peter Foster As bohemians Marcello, Colline and Schaunard, OA stalwarts Luke Gabbedy, David Parkin and Shane Lowrencev really do feel like old friends; their chemistry unforced. Making her hometown OA debut, Alexandra Flood (Musetta) is now, deservedly, on a Siobhan Stagg-esque trajectory, beloved at home and overseas. Flood has dynamo stage presence and shimmering vocals with perfect pianissimo high notes.



Tenor Kang Wang has long been an excellent Rodolfo, and Russian Galina Cheplakova’s heartbreaking Mimi was flawless, with the most beautiful array of vocal colours. This is what a national arts company should be doing, allowing inspired young Australian creatives to breathe new life into the classics. The art evolves and so too does our relationship with the piece. Costi’s Bohème will ensure that this tryst will endure.

Reviewed by Bridget Davies The Booklist is a weekly newsletter for book lovers from Jason Steger. Get it delivered every Friday.

World.title: ‘On to the next chapter’: UFC boss Dana White says he’ll meet with Trump over press secretary job
World.content:
Updated WorldNorth AmericaTrump's White House ‘On to the next chapter’: UFC boss Dana White says he’ll meet with Trump over press secretary job Michael Koziol Updated November 8, 2026 — 12:19pm ,first published November 8, 2026 — 5:56am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Washington: Ultimate Fighting Championship boss Dana White said he was flying to Washington, DC to meet with Donald Trump after the US president publicly offered him the role of White House press secretary. Trump said White was “a violent fighter and warrior”, and that he should bring mixed martial arts fighters from around the world – including Russians Islam Makhacev and Khabib Nurmagomedov – as “assistants” for the press secretary job. Loading “We need these people to defend us against the Lunatic Left,” Trump wrote on Truth Social. “Dana will be a press secretary like none other. Dana, please take the job!” The president’s offer might have been tongue-in-cheek, given the UFC president’s business commitments. His post included a mock-up of White in a suit behind a podium, and pictures of various MMA fighters.



The Washington Post has reported that a White House official, who spoke on the condition of anonymity because they weren’t authorised to speak about the matter publicly, said the offer was made as a joke. Donald Trump posted a collage of images alongside the Truth Social post calling on Dana White to take up the job. Truth Social However, at a press conference in London on Saturday (Sunday AEDT), White said that he was “flying to Washington DC right now”, and acknowledged that he had “a lot of jobs already”. “I’m going to meet with him, we have a meeting on Monday so I’m sure I’ll have more to talk about after that,” White said. White earlier posted an Instagram story resharing Trump’s post, adding the caption “on to the next chapter”.



The two men are friends, and Trump hosted a UFC fight at the White House in June as part of official celebrations for America’s 250th anniversary. US President Donald Trump and UFC president and CEO Dana White arrive for the UFC Freedom 250 event at the White House in June. AP The White House press office already has a former UFC spokesperson in White House Director of Communications Steven Cheung, who worked for White’s organisation from 2013 to 2016. Trump has a long history of using social media to troll Democrats, progressives and political enemies. Even so, the post suggests the White House is leaning into the perception that it is in “fight” mode after Democrats won control of the House of Representatives and the Senate at last week’s midterm elections. It comes a day after Trump replaced White House chief of staff Susie Wiles with hardline lieutenant Stephen Miller, widely seen as the start of an aggressive staff restructure as Democrats prepare to investigate the administration in Congress.



Miller was homeland security adviser and the deputy chief of staff for policy at the White House. AP Also on Saturday (US time), the president said he was ordering the Department of Justice to investigate what he termed “Weaponisation and Lawfare” by Democrats who were threatening to impeach or investigate senior administration officials. Trump claimed Democrats were threatening Republican donors with imprisonment – potentially a reference to Democrats’ intention to probe corporate donations to the president’s new White House ballroom. “This is extortion at the highest level, and they should be held accountable for this,” Trump claimed, without evidence, on social media. “These SLEAZEBAGS should go to jail for what they are doing.” Typically, the Department of Justice operates at arm’s length from the president, but Trump has involved himself directly in the department’s operations, including publicly pressuring his former attorney-general Pam Bondi to hasten investigations into his political enemies.





With Caitlin Fitzsimmons, Reuters Get a note directly from our foreign correspondents on what’s making headlines around the world.

World.title: Superlative: This Fiddler on the Roof rises to and exceeds expectation
World.content:
Key points MUSICALS: Fiddler on the Roof arrives at Her Majesty’s Theatre

MUSIC: The Brahms Festival by Melbourne Symphony Orchestra has begun

MUSIC: 5 Seconds of Summer perform at Rod Laver Arena

THEATRE: Before I Forget by Kamarra Bell-Wykes is centred on early-onset dementia

DANCE: Orbit at Dancehouse kicks off with Agitato and Charcoal

MUSICAL THEATRE

Fiddler on the Roof ★★★★★

Her Majesty’s Theatre, until December 27 Fiddler on the Roof has strummed through thousands of performances since its first run in 1964 on Broadway and its Australian premiere three years later. This latest version comes from director Jordan Fein’s 2024 London season. Troy Sussman as Tevye in Fiddler on the Roof. Daniel Boud Its decades-long popularity is a testament to the musical’s enduring themes of generational conflict and the inevitability of change. There are, of course, also the rousing songs, joyful choreography, and characters who are idiosyncratic enough to appear as individuals rather than simply emblems of stasis or progress. Set in 1905 in a small village in Russia, it follows the hardscrabble life of a Jewish milkman, Tevye (Troy Sussman) and his wife, Golde (Alexis Fishman) as they uphold rigorous traditions handed down about marriage, gender roles and social interactions.



Unfortunately, three of their five daughters are determined to thwart the matchmaker’s choices. As a parent, Tevye knows that if they choose their spouses unwisely, their fates are as precarious as the titular fiddler trying to ply his craft on a roof. The heart of the production rests upon whether Tevye bends to their autonomous desires or remains patriarchally inflexible. Sussman plays his role with humour, warmth, and commanding gravitas. Fishman’s bossy, sharp-tongued Golde is a perfect foil. You know she’s the one wielding the real power in their relationship. Sigrid Thornton and Alexis Fishman as Yente and Golde. Daniel Boud Tzeitel (Freya Boltman), Hodel (Ellen Ebbs), Chava (Caity Plummer) are the daughters whose love and respect for their father mean their rebellion is necessarily tempered by the push and pull of filial duty and antagonism. All three acquit their roles with the earnestness and passion of young women desperate for independence. As the gossipy matchmaker Yente, Sigrid Thornton’s performance is on point; so too is John Waters as the querulous Lazar Wolf— a wealthy, aged suitor who is rejected by Tzeitel. She’s already pledged her love to her childhood friend, Motel (Felix Star). Hodel, too, is soon smitten with Perchik (Maxwell Simon) the progressive thinker, while Chava becomes enamoured with bookish Fyedka (Jacob Steen) – who, even more daringly, is not Jewish.



Tevye’s beloved traditions – the most important one being that papa knows best – are no longer being upheld by his strong-minded daughters. Tom Scutt’s set is simple: a hay roof is hung over the stage, which rises and descends as the narrative unfolds. Other than that, the space is sparse, with wheat fields on either side. There’s no need for elaborate high-tech wizardry. The rituals of community are beautifully portrayed, from candle-lit chiaroscuro tableaux that look like Caravaggio portraits to set pieces of raucous merriment. As the Fiddler, Ben Adler’s virtuoso playing is interwoven into the narrative, lending a whimsical charm to the weighty matters at stake. John Waters (centre) as Lazar Wolf. Daniel Boud Outside of familial life, the threat of pogroms is imminent. The villagers are forced to leave abruptly and without ceremony. Given the continued climate of religious discrimination and antisemitism, Fiddler on the Roof’s continued relevance remains assured. (The oppression of women is also, and forever, a pertinent topic.) This musical demands a whole palette of emotions, and this triple-threat ensemble rises to and exceeds expectations; it’s a superlative production that focuses on a man bedevilled by changes on the domestic front and beyond, and wondering how, “Sunrise, Sunset” he and his scattering family can best navigate an uncertain future.

Reviewed by Thuy On



MUSIC

Brahms Festival: First Symphony & Piano Concerto ★★★★

Melbourne Symphony Orchestra, Hamer Hall, November 7 Composer Johannes Brahms It is tempting to typecast Brahms as the stern, grand old man of romanticism, putting him on a dusty plinth with his precursors, Bach and Beethoven. Hopefully, the Melbourne Symphony Orchestra’s survey of his symphonies, piano concertos, A German Requiem and a little of his chamber music will provide a more rounded image of this pivotal but all-too-human personality of 19th-century music. Taking a roughly chronological approach, the five-concert festival opened with the first piano concerto and first symphony. Although premiered 17 years apart, both are highly dramatic works. Russian pianist Denis Kozhukhin capitalised on the concerto’s titanic drama but was also highly alert to its many emotional contrasts. This paid handsome dividends in the central adagio, where he wrung enormous pathos from the solo part, surrounded by a halo of beautifully hushed string tone.



By contrast, the orchestra seemed reluctant at first to unleash the fiery passion demanded of the opening, developing greater confidence only later. In the sprightly concluding Rondo, chief conductor Jaime Martín ensured that the many rhythmic and contrapuntal challenges were neatly navigated, aided by Kozhukhin’s constant alertness to his orchestral interactions. Related Article Arts Melbourne Symphony Orchestra chief speaks for first time since court win After ample displays of bravura technique, Scriabin’s solo Etude, Op. 2, No. 1 offered a further demonstration of Kozhukhin’s subtle, lyric poetry. Many of the orchestra’s strengths were on show in Symphony No. 1 in C minor, Op. 68. Concertmaster Natalie Chee’s poignant solo in the second movement, mellifluous winds in the flowing third movement and the stirring horns that ushered in the finale all bolstered a strong sense of occasion. Even if the upper strings did not project sufficient heft and bite into the hall for the symphony’s searing opening, the orchestra did gather considerable momentum, not least in its fevered rush to an exultant finish, where any Brahmsian gloom was definitively banished.

Reviewed by Tony Way



MUSIC

5 Seconds of Summer | Everyone’s a Star! World Tour ★★★★

Rod Laver Arena, November 2 There has always been something a bit cringe about boy bands – the Britney mics, the gelled hair, the synchronised dancing. Few are more aware of this than 5 Seconds of Summer. They just so happen to be a boy band themselves. One thing that will never change about 5SOS, though, is their refusal to take themselves seriously. Richard Clifford The Sydney quartet’s world tour is coated in this irony, positioning them as the “biggest, best boy band in the world”. “There’s us, The Beatles and Jesus,” guitarist Michael Clifford says early on, totally deadpan.



Through a pre-filmed 60 Minutes-style mockumentary, we see 5SOS conquer the world, fall to pieces and then reunite, behaving as if their fame were the elixir of life. It’s both an ode to their rapid journey to fame and a biting takedown of it. Michael Clifford of 5SOS performs at Rod Laver Arena. Richard Clifford The true irony here, however, is that for those in the crowd – including myself – 5SOS actually is the world’s best boy band. I’ve followed them since their side-bangs and floppy beanie days, jamming out to Heartbreak Girl and Unpredictable. I pushed through hordes of feral fans to get my hands on 5SOS tees before sobbing through their 2015 Rock Out With Your Socks Out Tour. I plastered their posters on my bedroom wall. Eleven years have since passed, but that teen girl is still somewhere inside me, swooning over Calum Hood, naively thinking I may actually have a shot with him given we’re both Australasian. Tonight, that girl re-emerged – and she was in raptures. Older tracks like Voodoo Doll and She Looks So Perfect have everyone in a collective delirium, screaming along to lyrics we’ve sung a million times. Amnesia, meanwhile, has a teary woman beside me admit the song “makes her cry every time”. As my inner teen resurfaces, so does every other woman’s in the arena. It’s intoxicating.



Any band that has performed together for 15 years will inevitably evolve. 5SOS’ biggest change arguably comes with their latest album, Everyone’s a Star!, a grittier alt-rock record that wades through their complicated feelings about fame. Editor's pick Literature Kisses, chaos and Dustin Hoffman’s memoir: The 15 must-reads of this month Though different and slightly slower to heat up, Not Ok and Telephone Busy eventually send us into exaltation, tapping into the teen angst we’ve long buried. Blistering guitar solos from Clifford and lead vocalist Luke Hemmings send shockwaves through the arena, reminding us boy bands can be punk rock, too. One thing that will never change about 5SOS, though, is their refusal to take themselves seriously. Late in the show, they welcome The Wiggles for an Everyone’s a Star! dance party, encouraging the Tree of Wisdom to do the worm on stage. These guys may be the “biggest boy band in the world”, but they’ll never be too cool for The Wiggles, and neither will we. So yes, boy bands may be slightly cringe, and 5SOS may be painfully aware of this. But if loving 5SOS is wrong, I don’t ever want to be right.

Reviewed by Nell Geraets



THEATRE

Before I Forget ★★★★

Melbourne Theatre Company, Fairfax Studio - Arts Centre Melbourne, until November 28 The debilitating creep of early-onset dementia is the focus of this new play, developed through MTC’s Next Stage writers’ program, a commissioning and residency initiative that seeks to foster emerging theatre-makers. Loosely based on lived experiences, Before I Forget is the work of Kamarra Bell-Wykes, whose capacity here is as both the playwright and the director. Melodie Reynolds-Diarra, Roxanne McDonald and Tyallah Bullock in Before I Forget. Pia Johnson It paints a portrait of a woman, once vital and vibrant, who’s losing the contours of her days. Faith Wells (Roxanne McDonald), a renowned First Nations academic and linguist, once had a wicked tongue and a fierce intellect, but her language – and, indeed, her life skills – are now mired in forgetfulness and confusion. While Faith is in the middle of giving a lecture, she becomes disoriented and hears voices. The play begins with her losing her keys and handbag, and as the disease takes a firmer grip, she fails to recognise her grandchild, Hope (Tyallah Bullock), and mistakes her son, Jet (Nathan Wright), for her own father.



But when plans are discussed to relocate her into an aged care home, Faith rages and refuses to go gently into that institution, much to the chagrin of her daughter, Karma (Melodie Reynolds-Diarra). McDonald is brilliantly convincing as the erstwhile leader, activist and trailblazer who now needs round-the-clock care for basic daily tasks. There is a mischievousness and playfulness to her even as she battles both memory fog and her daughter’s and granddaughter’s ministrations, and it’s this humour that leavens the otherwise serious intent of the play. Before I Forget explores loss of all kinds. Pia Johnson Also funny in a feckless way is Wright, who makes a brief appearance as Jet, who loves but leaves, and is unable to do any actual caring for his mother. We’re reminded of how much caregiving is relegated to the domain of women. To afford the fees for residential care, Faith’s home has been sold – its new owners are days away from moving in. The set features two beds on either side of a couch, with an ominous “For Sale” sign in the far corner. There are documents and folders in disarray on the floor as Karma and Hope try to pack away Faith’s research papers.



What’s particularly egregious is that for a linguist whose job and passion was to reclaim and restore Indigenous languages, Faith’s memory loss means aspects of her own life have disappeared, her cultural legacy compromised. Editor's pick Visual art Whistleblowers, children and stateless men: The artist telling stories one image at a time Before I Forget explores three generations of women grappling with change and transition. As the dutiful daughter trying to manage the household, Reynolds-Diarra is a tightly coiled ball of anger and frustration, while Bullock is sweetly earnest as she teases and plays with her grandmother, hoping for connection. Sometimes she’s rewarded by moments of lucidity. Tonally, the play’s emotional arc moves back and forth from fear, hurt, outrage, and tenderness. The play is all about loss – not just of identity, but of a home, independence, and dignity. But Bell-Wykes has a broader reach in her remit than just the interpersonal interactions of one family – one that reaches back into the annals. The living wake, a eulogy that the three women conduct to acknowledge each other’s strengths and to celebrate each other, is a balm to counter the fact that, as Faith points out, there were no burials for ancestors massacred by colonialists. Before I Forget is as much a story about remembrance and honouring the Indigenous matrilineal line as it is about ageing, illness and death. The set opens up to reveal the luminous skyline and a scattering of stars, offering us a greater sense of spirituality and transcendence that goes beyond earthly mortality.

Reviewed by Thuy On



MUSIC

Night Music ★★★★

Melbourne Symphony Orchestra, Melbourne Recital Centre, October 31 Coincidentally presented on Halloween, this program, beginning with allusions to night but ending in a blaze of glory, delivered a few neat tricks as well as several treats. Flute virtuoso Eliza Shephard Cameron Jamieson Centred around the Melbourne premiere of The Vicious Circle, a flute concerto written for virtuoso Eliza Shephard by Joe Chindamo, the concert began with his Fantasie auf Nachtmusik (tipping its hat to Mozart’s Eine kleine Nachtmusik) and was counterbalanced by Mozart’s Symphony No. 36 “Linz”. While Chindamo’s “poly-stylistic” reimagining of Mozart makes good use of elements from baroque and minimalist style, mid-20th century modernist influences seem predominant, whether in the opening Britten-esque gestures or later nods to the neoclassicism of Stravinsky. Even so, this amalgam remains uniquely Chindamo’s and was conceived and delivered with wit and a lightness of touch.



Taking musical influences from the other side of the Atlantic, the concerto was inspired by writer Dorothy Parker, member of the 1920s Algonquin Round Table (known as “the vicious circle”). Traces of Gershwin and Copland pervade its deftly orchestrated three movements. City of Myths evokes New York with a slow blues feel, worthy of film noir. Tender is the Night projects interior melancholy through a slow waltz before a short preamble (Vertigo) leads into the fevered finale, The Brightest Hour, with its echoes of Hollywood. Editor's pick Art From a refugee camp to global acclaim: Atong Atem finds her place Shephard is a dynamo of a performer, brimming over with irrepressible enthusiasm and astonishing technique, present not only in the concerto but two literally breathtaking encores. Precociously written in under a week, the “Linz” symphony reflects the grand court for which it was written. From the imposing opening to the exultant finale, the Melbourne Symphony Orchestra, amiably and expertly directed by concertmaster Natalie Chee, brought effervescence and elegance to this finely crafted masterpiece. Revelling in their task, the players did indeed provide listeners with a final treat.

Reviewed by Tony Way



DANCE

Orbit Week 1: Charcoal and Agitato ★★★★

Dancehouse, Carlton, until October 31 It’s a familiar lament: contemporary dance rarely travels in Australia. We almost never get the chance to see the work of independent dance artists based in other cities. For that reason, a new national touring initiative called Orbit should be welcomed. Charcoal by Keia McGrady Gregory Lorenzutti The program comprises two double bills, which tour through five venues across Victoria, South Australia and NSW. The first program opens with Charcoal by emerging choreographer Keia McGrady, from south-east Queensland. This delicate, sensitively shaped duet responds to the regenerative power of cultural burning: the First Nations practice of using low fires to manage Country.



Crouched on a large sheet, the dancers crush sticks of charcoal and scrawl loose forms, suggesting a landscape viewed from above. As if rising from the ashes, they gradually stretch and unfold, then quicken, with fleeting animal imagery emerging as the work reaches its climax. McGrady and Amelia Jean O’Leary give earnest, attentive performances, sustaining the duet’s gentle, nurturing atmosphere as its movement slowly gathers intensity. Agitato by Jo Lloyd. Gregory Lorenzutti The progression from quiet beginnings to fuller activity is straightforward but handled with assurance. McGrady focuses on developing her theme, allowing the simple image of regeneration to progress with clarity. The second piece, Jo Lloyd’s Agitato, a standout work from last year, responds to a short, rackety piano piece by Fanny Mendelssohn, as remixed by Duane Morrison, with whirling, spasming figures.



Yet, it also opens chasms within the music. The four dancers seem to enter these fissures, discovering strange little scenes and fleeting, almost painterly arrangements amid the tumult. Related Article Melbourne live reviews Betrayal and good-intentions gone wrong: Eliza tells the story of the world’s first chatbot With two new dancers in the quartet, Agitato seems an even greater achievement on second viewing: an epic of churning anxieties. This is the sort of gripping theatre that I think vindicates Orbit’s ambitions. It’s fascinating to think what audiences elsewhere make of it.

Reviewed by Andrew Fuhrmann The Booklist is a weekly newsletter for book lovers from Jason Steger. Get it delivered every Friday.

World.title: Khawaja’s explosive confession puts Australian bowlers in the firing line
World.content:
Breaking SportCricketAustralian cricket Khawaja’s explosive confession puts Australian bowlers in the firing line Tom Decent November 8, 2026 — 11:38am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Usman Khawaja has revealed he feared he might never be able to return to the Australian dressing room after the sandpaper scandal of 2018, admitting he was unwilling to “go to war” with his Australian teammates over their refusal to accept collective responsibility for the ball-tampering saga. In a series of extraordinary videos posted on social media on Sunday morning ahead of his book launch on Tuesday, the retired Australian batsman also claimed former captain Steve Smith talked him out of publicly revealing what he knew eight years ago, with the skipper determined to shoulder the blame and serve his one-year suspension. Loading Khawaja has doubled down on his explosive claim that every player in the team – including the bowlers, despite their repeated denials – knew sandpaper was being used on the ball not only during the infamous Cape Town Test in 2018, but also in the preceding match in Gqeberha, then known as Port Elizabeth. Khawaja was speaking on Sunday after a series of inflammatory extracts from his autobiography reignited the scandal and raised questions about why he waited eight years to speak publicly about the events that led to Smith, David Warner and Cameron Bancroft being banned.



Khawaja also claimed Bancroft had used sandpaper on the ball during the second Test, revealed he had confronted teammate Nathan Lyon over dropping the ball on South African batsman AB de Villiers following a runout, and suggested he was overlooked for the interim captaincy at the end of the series because “Australia wasn’t ready for a brown captain”. Khawaja has put renewed pressure on Australia’s bowlers to come clean, arguing the three players who were sanctioned have unfairly carried the burden of the scandal for eight years. Former Test batsman Usman Khawaja says the entire team knew of the ball tampering during the Newlands Test against South Africa in 2018. Dan Peled In his book, Khawaja writes that he was “really pissed off” that two unnamed teammates were unwilling to accept collective responsibility for what happened in South Africa. “Time to clear up some facts,” Khawaja said on social media. “When I mentioned it was all of us, that’s implying that whether we like it or not, we’re all responsible for what happened together as a team. We need to take that collectively.



“Now that everyone’s talking, am I going to deny that everyone knew? Nah, I won’t deny that either. I never speak on behalf of anyone else in my book. “Why now? I’ve been trying to take this as a team right from the start. I wrote everything that happened down a few days later after Cape Town. When the other guys got their penalties, I told Smudge [Smith] that I was going to come clean to the media. I couldn’t believe the penalties he got. Cameron Bancroft and Steve Smith talk with the umpires during the Cape Town Test in 2018. Getty Images “Smudge being the man and leader he was talked me out of it. He wanted to take the blame. I argued with him, but he was having none of it. That’s the first time I tried to come out.” Khawaja said the issue “reared its ugly head again” in 2021, when he contacted then Australian coach Justin Langer and pleaded with him to convince other members of the team to speak publicly together.



He said he also raised the matter with then Australian Cricketers’ Association boss Todd Greenberg. Instead, the four frontline bowlers from the Cape Town Test – Pat Cummins, Josh Hazlewood, Mitchell Starc and Nathan Lyon – issued a strongly worded statement denying any knowledge of a plan to tamper with the ball. “Then that statement came out from the guys. What could I do then? I wasn’t going to go to war with those guys back then. I wasn’t comfortable. That’s the truth,” Khawaja said. “Why didn’t I say anything in those four years while I was still playing? You know what? I never wanted to be the first guy to chat about this. Call me a chicken or whatever you want. I didn’t know how to do it because I was still in the team. How was I ever supposed to bring this up when I knew some of my teammates didn’t want to talk about it? I knew everything I did or said always influenced and affected the team.



“I was always conscious of putting my team first, but I’m not in that team more. What I say now isn’t a reflection of them any more. Now my words don’t influence the team at all. I speak for myself.” Khawaja insisted he had not betrayed his former teammates by speaking out, arguing the real victims were the three players who had been publicly vilified and forced to carry the shame of the scandal. Australia’s Pat Cummins and Usman Khawaja during a net session in 2023. Getty Images “I haven’t thrown anyone under the bus,” Khawaja said. “The guys that are currently in the team right now, and the other people that were there on the South African tour, including me, are not the victims. These three guys took the blame for all of us. They’re the victims. “Yes, it was tough for everyone, including me. I had sleepless nights. I told [wife] Rachel and Justin Langer, ‘I’m not sure if I can go back in the change rooms ever again’. Those three [Smith, Warner and Bancroft] are the ones that had to endure this for the last eight years, quietly. I’m glad everyone else has moved on from this. But I promise you, those guys have not moved on. How can they if the truth has never come out?”



“I made a promise to my childhood friend David Warner that I would tell the truth, so he could tell a story. I’m absolutely 100 per cent unapologetic for that. I stuck up for all cricketers in the past through the ACA, fighting for what I thought was right. This is no different. Related Article Exclusive

Australian cricket ‘It was all of us’: Khawaja blows the whistle on more sandpaper use in South Africa in 2018 “These three guys deserve justice, and I haven’t pointed fingers at anyone. I’m still searching for what I was searching all those years ago. For us, me included, to take the blame together as a team, so we can all move on from this once and for all. You know what? I would do it again in a heartbeat.” Former Australian captain Mark Taylor, who was a CA board member in 2018, said the renewed focus on the events of Cape Town would be “a nightmare” for Cummins this summer. “I’m disappointed because it was eight years ago that this happened,” Taylor said on Nine’s Wide World of Sports on Sunday morning. “You sort of hope it’s going to go away.



“I don’t know if you’re ever going to find out exactly who knew what, where, and when. I’m disappointed that we’re going to keep asking it again and again and again. It’s going to be obviously a nightmare for Pat Cummins and the team leading into the summer of cricket. “Where it goes from here, I don’t know. It’s going to be a great thing for the book sales. I think it’s going to be disappointing for the game of cricket. I’d love to move on, but I don’t think we ever will.” Cummins, Starc, Hazlewood and Lyon have so far declined to comment through their managers. World.title: Arise, Sir Kev: The league legend who lost his best mate to MND and then set out to eradicate it
World.content:
Kevin Sinfield being made a Knight Bachelor by The Prince of Wales at Windsor Castle last month.

Former Great Britain captain Kevin Sinfield has raised $26 million dollars for MND research and support in the last seven years, and he’s headed to Australia next year for his next charity run.

Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

It says a lot about Kevin Sinfield that soon after Prince William knighted him, the future king wondered why it had taken so long. “Frankly, he should have been Sir Kevin years ago,” Prince William told the BBC, adding that awarding the knighthood to Sinfield at Windsor Castle last month was “probably the easiest decision anyone has ever had to make”. The honour – and the genuine admiration of the Prince of Wales – was earned by Sinfield thanks to his extensive work raising funds and awareness for Motor Neurone Disease over the past seven years. Kevin Sinfield waving to the crowd before the Super League grand final in Warrington, having just completed a charity ultra-marathon. Getty Images The former Great Britain rugby league captain has so far raised a remarkable $26 million through his tireless efforts – and that’s a very literal description. Sinfield, who is an assistant coach of the England rugby side who will meet Australia on Monday, has done the bulk of his fundraising by pounding the pavement in seven exhausting running challenges, including multiple completions of seven marathons in seven days. This year, Sinfield finished his seventh challenge by knocking off an ultra-marathon (50 kilometres) every day, for seven days.



“I am worried about his knees,” Prince William told the BBC. Sinfield laughs when you follow up. Seriously, how are the knees? “No, they’re good,” he told this masthead in London this week. “Honestly, the knees are still fine.” The “seven” theme of Sinfield’s challenges is no coincidence. The number is at the heart of why the 46-year-old from Oldham began running. Kevin Sinfield speaks with Rob Burrow after completing his Extra Mile Challenge at Headingley Stadium in 2021. Getty Images Sinfield’s best mate was his long-time Leeds and Great Britain league teammate Rob Burrow. The former halfback was diagnosed with MND in 2019 and died in 2024. “I played alongside Rob for 15 years, so we sat next to each other in the dressing room. As you probably know, in sport, dressing rooms accelerate friendships. So that 15 years, it’s probably 60 or 70 years in real life,” Sinfield explains.



After Burrow’s diagnosis in December 2019, Sinfield promised his mate that by the following Christmas he’d raise a certain sum of money. But COVID lockdowns shut down the world and, with it, chances to hold big fundraising events. Kevin Sinfield running in one of many marathons. CameraSport via Getty Images “We got to September of 2020 and I’d made a promise, but we were going to fall short of that promise,” he said. “So I was like, I’ve got to try and do something.” Sinfield was then director of rugby at the Leeds Rhinos and he submitted a proposal to authorities to do a charity running challenge around Oldham and Leeds in November, using all the professional sports COVID protocols. “Remarkably, we got it signed off. And then we got a TV station: the biggest news breakfast show in the UK decided to follow us because there was nothing else going on at the time,” Sinfield said. “And it just went crazy. So that was the start.” Sinfield ran seven marathons in seven days, aiming to raise £77,777 (about $150,000). The public forked out more than £2 million. The next year he ran 101 kilometres in under 24 hours, and in following years upped the stakes to repeatedly run seven ultra-marathons in seven days. At each run, Sinfield also does a mile (1.6 kilometres) with MND families, meeting people and providing his support.



In 2023, he pushed Burrow in a chair in the Leeds marathon, before carrying his mate across the line in highly emotional scenes. “I had no idea I’d end up where we’ve ended up,” Sinfield said. “It was never planned. Like I said, the first one was very fortunate in terms of timing because we create a lot of momentum. And on the back of that, it’s enabled us to carry that on. We’ve been able to raise awareness and funds but also change the way people understand MND across the UK and Ireland. “So, yeah, it’s been great to continue with Rob’s name. Sadly we lost him just over two years ago. But we continue fighting for his legacy. And now for so many other families as well, who’ve become friends because you meet people along the way. You’re drawn to these families because of how tough they are, how inspirational they are, and I’ve got so many friends in the MND community now. Kevin Sinfield when he played for Great Britain. Fairfax Photography “That’s been probably the biggest part of this. It’s been less about the running in the last couple of years, and more about spending time with families and connecting and pulling them all together, so that we try and crack this as one big unit.” Sinfield believes a cure for MND can be found, and money will hasten its discovery. But he is also motivated to provide better support facilities and systems for MND sufferers and their families.



“I made a commitment [to Burrow] that I would support this community for the rest of my life. Now, that may look differently to what has been done the last seven years. Whilst I can still run, I’ll continue to try and run. But there are other ways of fundraising and raising awareness and pulling people together. “The families need to be looked after better than what we currently do. So it’s two-pronged, really: the care side, and trying to find a cure and give our researchers and medical professionals some more money to go after a cure. Retired South Sydney player Jai Arrow and former Wallaby Nathan Charles take part in a lap of honour before the NRL grand final. Getty Images “I’m very hopeful. There’s some very smart people working on MND research … and the better we are at collaborating and sharing means we’ll do it quicker. I just think MND has been underfunded for too long. With the right amount of funds we’ll find a cure.” Sinfield noted with sadness the recent MND diagnoses of NRL star Jai Arrow and former Wallaby Nathan Charles. He says he was also inspired by the fundraising work of the late AFL great Neale Daniher. It’s why Sinfield has decided to lace up again next year and do a charity challenge in Australia and New Zealand. The final plan is yet to be set in stone, but it is likely to be in May, with Sinfield running seven marathons in seven days in different cities, finishing at various sporting events.

World.title: Macklemore says major US arenas refused to book ‘Free Palestine’ tour
World.content:
CultureMusicIsraeli-Palestinian conflict Macklemore says major US arenas refused to book ‘Free Palestine’ tour Ben Sisario November 8, 2026 — 11:24am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Macklemore, the indie rapper who was kicked off Ed Sheeran’s stadium tour in September over his public support of Palestinians, said on Saturday (AEDT) that nine arenas in the United States refused to book him for a “Free Palestine” benefit tour he had planned. In a social media post, Macklemore wrote that in mid-September, after being removed from Sheeran’s tour, his team contacted arenas in the United States and “received available dates at these arenas through the end of the year.” “But once they found out these were my benefit shows for Palestine,” his statement continued, “those dates were suddenly off the table.” In a social media post, rapper Macklemore said a number of arenas in the US have refused to book his tour. Getty Images Macklemore named nine venues: Madison Square Garden, Barclays Center and UBS Arena in New York; Prudential Centre in Newark, New Jersey; Intuit Dome, Kia Forum and Crypto.com Arena in and around Los Angeles; Chase Centre Arena in San Francisco; and Climate Pledge Arena in Seattle, Macklemore’s hometown.



In a statement, a spokesperson for Madison Square Garden said: “We have some of the busiest venues in the world with extremely limited availability and he’s not an arena-level act.” Related Article Israeli-Palestinian conflict Macklemore dumped from Ed Sheeran’s tour over pro-Palestine comments A spokesperson for Kia Forum said the venue had no comment. None of the other venues responded to requests for comment. Macklemore, who had breakout success in the early 2010s with songs like Thrift Shop and Can’t Hold Us, was removed from Sheeran’s tour after he appeared at two shows at MetLife Stadium in East Rutherford, New Jersey, in early September.



There, he proclaimed “Free Palestine” and performed Hind’s Hall, his protest song against Israel’s conduct of the war in the Gaza Strip, which came in response to the Hamas-led attack on Israel on October 7, 2023. In that song, Macklemore accuses Israel of genocide. Macklemore said that owners of the venues where the Sheeran tour had been scheduled demanded he be removed. Robert Kraft, whose company owns the New England Patriots and Gillette Stadium outside Boston, said that his venues do not allow “hate speech,” and that Macklemore’s statements at MetLife had crossed that line. Macklemore was removed from Ed Sheeran’s tour in September over his Free Palestine comments. Getty Macklemore’s removal renewed debate about the power of billionaires to control free speech, and the power of artists to resist it. After Sheeran said he had played no part in the decision, every other musician associated with his tour, including opening acts and his backing band, dropped out in solidarity with Macklemore. Sheeran continued the tour, at first alone and then picking up other musicians.



Editor's pick Israeli-Palestinian conflict Country artist breaks Gillette Stadium attendance record while wearing ‘Free Palestine’ shirt In his statement on Friday, Macklemore added: “We live in a country that prides itself on freedom of speech. Yet we’ve reached a point where a handful of billionaires can decide which causes are acceptable, which voices are welcome and which human lives are worth defending.” In late October, Macklemore played arena shows in London, Paris and Dublin as part of a benefit tour. When that tour was announced, representatives of Macklemore said they expected additional dates to be booked in the US, but none were. Though Macklemore has never been a stadium-level touring attraction, he has maintained a steady fan base for years. In October, he played a solo concert at Red Rocks Amphitheatre, near Morrison, Colorado. In 2023, he went on a tour of arenas and theatres, including Climate Pledge Arena.



This article originally appeared in The New York Times. Find out the next TV, streaming series and movies to add to your must-sees. Get The Watchlist delivered every Thursday.

World.title: What the world's media made of NZ's election cliffhanger
World.content:
New Zealand's general election has made headlines overseas, with most - though not all - focused on the lack of any clear result.

While the governing coalition of National, NZ First and ACT has a fragile majority in an expanded 131-seat Parliament on the preliminary results, hundreds of thousands of special votes are yet to be counted, which could leave no one with a path to power without the help of newcomer Opportunity.

Here's how the world reacted and reported the outcome.

Australia

New Zealand may not know its government for weeks / New Zealand election remains on a knife edge

In the words of Labour leader Chris Hipkins, "New Zealand has spoken", but exactly what it has said is anything but clear.

Starting with our closest neighbour, Australia's ABC covered the election live before summing it up with Hipkins' election-night comments on the uncertain outcome.

"The two major parties - Labour and National - are in an exceptionally close race, showing that every vote really does count," its Auckland-based team wrote.

ABC also highlighted the role Opportunity might play, and explained to readers how MMP's overhang system works.

NZ PM has a long month ahead with little to crow about

Writing in The Australian, David Cohen noted Luxon would be without many of the big names from his previous Cabinet, and that his party's "campaign lost direction as it moved from law and order to affordability and cultural issues".

He also pointed out both National's governing minor partners, NZ First and ACT, increased their presence in Parliament, and suggested it was over for Hipkins if he didn't become prime minister, since he would have lost two consecutive elections.

United Kingdom

No clear winner after tight New Zealand general election

The BBC focused on the lack of a clear winner too, noting that with 42 seats on the present count, National was far short of governing on its own. The authors wrongly suggested 61 seats would have been enough for a majority, apparently unaware of how New Zealand's MMP system works and what voters delivered on Saturday night.

Cost of living was noted as the campaign's biggest issue, linking the Greens' boost in support to their plan for a publicly owned supermarket chain.

Professor Andrew Geddis from the University of Otago was quoted, calling Opportunity a "wildcard" and noting the results won't be known until at least 27 November.

New Zealand faces weeks of uncertainty with election 'too close to call'

The Guardian too focused on the coalition's narrow lead, and said the "collapse of the two major parties, amid a sluggish economy and stubbornly high inflation, is feeding record support for the smaller parties" and helped Opportunity cross the 5 percent threshold.

It too gave readers a lesson on MMP's quirks, and said the final result would not be known for potentially weeks.

Nicola Willis speaks to the media as she arrives at the National Party’s election night event at Viaduct Event Centre. Fiona Goodall/Getty Images

New Zealand conservatives see path to power after deadlocked election

Conservative UK paper The Telegraph focused on the coalition's chances of remaining in power.

"The National Party looks to have the best chance of forming a government, given its coalition options," it wrote, while also noting its reluctance to work with newcomer Opportunity.

It also pointed out special votes, yet to be counted, tend to favour the left-leaning parties.

United States

New Zealand in political limbo after knife-edge election

Another knife-edge metaphor led CNN's coverage, saying it would take just a "small variance" to change the outcome.

The outlet noted Labour at this stage actually had more party votes, but National - though a "diminished force" - was in a stronger position due to its performance in individual electorates.

"Its struggle to secure an emphatic victory this time signifies the level of public discontent over living costs, stubbornly high unemployment rates and concerns over healthcare."

Conservative bloc takes a slim lead in New Zealand election that's still too close to call

The Associated Press reported the election "produced no definitive victory for the right or the left", but the coalition "hovered on the brink of a wafer-thin majority that could allow it to eke out a precarious return to power".

"Voters instead bolstered power for minor parties on the ideological flanks and propelled to office a centrist political newcomer, Qiulae Wong of the Opportunity party, who has pledged a non-partisan and pragmatic agenda that draws from socially liberal, technocratic and pro-environment ideals."

New Zealand's Election 'Too Close to Call' as Voters Turn to Minor Parties

The New York Times said "minority parties [emerged] as the real winners in a vote dominated by economic sluggishness and political discontent".

"Both [major] parties were polling near historic lows before the vote, signalling a lack of faith in their ability to steer the nation out of its malaise."

Opportunity's rise was covered before any mention of the other minor parties, and the author noted that if the coalition failed to form a government, it would be "the first time in 50 years that a government has lasted just one term".

New Zealand's election results are too close to call

In a short article barely seven paragraphs long, the Washington Post managed to fit in "the battle of the Chrises", Wong's recruitment via  and Luxon's telling-off of a supporter who booed when National's rivals were mentioned.

Opportunity Party leader Qiulae Wong arrives at the Opportunity Party’s election night event. Phil Walter

New Zealand party leader Qiulae Wong's disbelief

News.com.au covered Wong's excitement as she realised Opportunity was going to break the 5 percent threshold, with a focus on her failed effort not to swear.

Middle East and Asia

Two main parties neck and neck after New Zealand vote, near complete count

Al Jazeera, like most other outlets, zeroed in on the lack of any outcome, saying it was "an election dominated by a struggling economy and voter disillusionment with the two biggest contenders".

It quoted former Cabinet minister Peter Dunne, who worked with both National and Labour governments, as saying Labour and National were "carbon copies of the other", leaving "a whole rising generation of voters, who want to see a bit more adventure in politics".

In talking about how long it might be until a result is clear, Al Jazeera noted that New Zealand counts votes "by hand, not by machine".

New Zealand govt holds narrow lead in poll nailbiter
